item.title: Plastic Is Poisoning the Earth—So This Designer Made a Backpacking Kit Without It
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.98
Transcript My name’s Tom Bonamici, I’m an assistant professor of product design at the University of Oregon , and I teach in general product design for undergraduates and also our master’s program in sports product design. So, my research is about lightweight backcountry travel, and I am particularly interested in backpacking, been doing it since I was a kid, and I’m also really interested as an Oregonian in sustainability issues. As we all know, backpacking is just rife with synthetic materials, and they’re really awesome. They’re super lightweight and waterproof and strong and badass, and they’re also made out of petrochemicals, which, you know, on the in end is a problem, on the out end it’s a problem. I was just curious to explore academically what it would mean to use a full backpacking kit without any petrochemicals at all, not to say that everyone should, but just to explore what compromises we’d make if we did that. And going in, I kind of anticipated it was going to be heavier, it was going to not perform as well, it might be weaker, but how cool to make a collection that could actually completely compost. I thought that would just be an interesting experiment and exploration. I think to start with, we can start with the backpack because we’re backpacking, and that’s one of the more more fun things to talk about. Generally throughout this collection, certainly with this backpack, I was using pretty normal ultralight backpacking designs and just adapting materials to be completely petrochemical free. So, this is a really kind of standard issue frameless lightweight backpacking pack. There’s no suspension at all. The sleeping pad forms the back panel and adds some rigidity when it’s all packed together. You know, we’ve got the normal big side pockets, the big back pocket, thick shoulder straps. I keep my pack light enough that I don’t typically use a waist strap, but I could certainly have added one. But the materials are what makes this compostable. So, I used a Ventile material. It’s basically a super strong, densely woven cotton material, and this one especially is ripstop. Same thing for the side pockets, it’s a Ventile, but a much lighter weight version. We’ve got cotton cord forming the drawstring in those side pockets and aluminum toggles with a metal spring, so that’s all plastic free. The back pocket is a stretch 100 percent Merino jersey, and we’ve got some more metal hardware holding that in place, another metal hook for the top closure. And the shoulder straps are lined with that same Merino jersey, Ventile on the outside, cotton webbing, and then I used a thick Merino felt as the padding for that back strap. And it’s a little on the stiff side. The more it gets used, the more it’s going to kind of conform. Felt is really good at that. But the challenge throughout this whole collection, and especially in something like a pack that needs to be really strong, is the thread. So, I used 100 percent cotton thread. This is kind of a super heavy-duty thread that is meant for sewing on buttons, for like a fancy suit coat. I ended up with a lot of formal wear overlaps with the materials I was using here. So, the thread I think is pretty strong, but it’s, you know, I can break it if I really yank on it, this very heavy-duty thread. And that’s not a great sign because with a synthetic, you know, typically backpacking packs are sewn with polyester thread, and I can’t break that, you know, like a Tex 80, Tex 100 thread. So, that’s a pretty heavy gauge. And this stuff I can totally break. So, I did adapt by, you know, sewing several times over some seams. If you sew too many times, you’re just going to over-perforate a fabric, and then it can tear like a check out of a checkbook. But we’ll just see how it goes. As as throughout the whole collection, it’s an experiment. But I’m quite excited about the pack. And again, I wasn’t getting weird with the design of it, just with the materials. For the sleeping bag, I did a sleeping quilt. This is the same quilt design that I’ve done in the past with synthetic materials, which is super light and super comfortable. I use my homemade quilt all the time. It’s the kind of usual idea where you have a somewhat tapered rectangle, and then it forms a footbox, and you can kind of tie up that footbox and cinch it at the bottom, and it works great. Instead of a zipper, although I could use a cotton taped, metal-toothed zipper, I just went ahead and used some little ties because I’ve done quilts with zippers in the footbox and I’ve also done quilts with just snaps across, and they both work just fine. This is for summer backpacking, so I don’t need like full Arctic enclosure. The shell material is a silk-cotton blend. This is meant for the lining material of a formal suit. So, again, one of those like formal wear overlaps with this collection. Cotton tape and cotton cord for the ties and the draw cord, and cotton thread. And then the material on the inside is a wool material. It’s called Lavalan, and it’s this puffy wool batting. Got a scrap here. That’s kind of very, very cleaned from how wool comes off the sheep, and then kind of spun and matted into this lighter weight and fluffy material. It’s really nice, it’s really warm. I used kind of a layer and a half. This is their almost heaviest weight and then I used a little bit more very lightweight quilt batting in there that was Merino quilt batting. This material is nice because it’s a little bit more resilient than some of the synthetic options. It is heavier. This quilt weighs a little under 2 pounds, and my homemade quilt weighs a little over 1 pound. So, it’s definitely heavier, but I think it’s going to be plenty warm. The feeling of that fabric is so nice, and totally compostable as with everything else. So, I’m excited about this one. It’s quite bulky. That’s one of the downsides of using the wool instead of a synthetic and certainly a down. But it actually compresses pretty well once you jam it into the backpack, then it holds its form, and it’s actually kind of nice when you’re backpacking with a frameless pack to let the pack be full because then you don’t have any flopping or shifting. You might wonder why didn’t I use down? Because down is natural. When you make something with down, it needs to use downproof fabric. And typically what that is is a really, really lightweight synthetic material that’s calendared. So, calendering means that you’re taking that material and putting it through these heated rollers, and it’s almost melting it, but it’s just like smushing the the yarns of that woven textile together and closing up all of the gaps in between the warp and the weft fibers, bringing those gaps together. And that means that those little stems on the down puffs can’t work their way through and pop out like they do on your pillows at home. So, there are there are certainly natural materials that could fit the bill. In fact, the Ventile materials that I used are probably dense enough to be downproof or like functionally downproof. And there are some upholstery materials that are all cotton that are meant to be downproof. But they’re super heavy. So, it would end up tripling maybe the weight of the of the quilt and adding to the bulk, too. One of the hardest challenges in this whole collection was doing a sleeping pad . And this is the one, the sleeping pad and the shoes, man, are just, that’s that’s the tough one. So, this, I know this is just kind of a punishing sleeping pad. It’s super narrow. It is full length, and I’m 6’2″, so it’s nice to have, you know, enough length. And it’s so flat. It’s not providing any cushion at all. This is just a thermal break. But I wanted a sleeping pad that could function as a back panel in the backpack, and I needed that thermal break. If you’ve ever had a inflatable pad that deflated during the night, we all know that the ground is just so cold. Imade this with, again, some of that Ventile material, the super lightweight, and then a really thin layer of cork, which is not going to hold up long term, I know it, because it kind of crumbles. And that’s sandwiched in with some Melton wool. And Melton wool is a a very dense, almost felted thick woven wool material. Sometimes it’s made with a Merino, usually it’s more of a strong wool because it’s just felted in so much, you don’t need that softness and kind of luxurious hand of Merino. And then the whole thing is bound with cotton twill tape and, again, cotton thread. And then I sewed across in some channels just to try to hold that cork into place long term. This is something where, as I said, the collection is about exploring compromises, and it’s a big compromise in comfort. I was backpacking last weekend and just loving my big plush, Big Agnes pad, you know, just like sprawled out on that and sleeping like a baby. And this isn’t going to be like that. It’s also heavy. This is just under 2 pounds, which is pretty painful because that’s well over double a Z Lite. So, if I’m going to be less comfortable, I’d rather have a Z Lite. But, you know, that’s just straight petrochemicals, so it didn’t work for this project. So, again, the the collection was about exploring compromises, and I’ve definitely found some compromise area with the sleeping pad. And that’s okay. I did look into whether or not it’d be possible to do inflatable natural pads and also just like thicker, squishier materials, you know, wool felt. I looked into kapok, which is this kind of tree seed pod husk material that was used for insulation and also for life jacket flotation before petrochemicals. It’s not as good as foam for a life jacket, so don’t get any ideas. And all this is possible. Like with natural latex rubber, it would theoretically be possible to make an inflatable pad, but roughly running the numbers, it would be much, much heavier than this, like 5 to 8 pounds for just the pad. They were available, you know, you look in old Abercrombie & Fitch catalogs from the early 1900s, and they had inflatable pads, and they weighed 10 to 15 pounds. So, you know, if you’re horse packing, maybe that’s a good option, but for the purpose of this project, again, I was trying to keep everything as light as possible. For trekking poles, I knew I wanted to use trekking poles, and I need them for my 40-year-old knees, and also to set up the tarp. And I looked into making them out of aluminum because metal was allowed in the confines of this project, but to make them extendable, adjustable, I think it could be done. You know, if I were a really amazing machinist, I’m sure I could make all those parts out of aluminum and have it be fine. I’m not an amazing machinist, and I didn’t want to use those plastic adjusters, which are so great and so good at what they do, but again, for the confines of this project, I wanted to keep it original. So, I ended up using Calcutta bamboo. And this is a species of bamboo that’s insanely strong. It’s still used for ski poles and for fishing gaffs, that’s the like big hook that you use to yank that 200-pound tuna in the boat. It’s way stronger in flexion than aluminum, which is pretty sweet, and not too heavy at all. It has a really thick wall. So, this is a little chunk of it, and it’s got this thicker, denser wall, and it’s just a lot tougher than normal bamboo. And then in Slovenia, of all places, I found a ski pole DIY supply house. With the tariffs, I paid a phenomenal amount of money to get these ferrules, which are meant to be used with bamboo poles. So, these are all aluminum with a carbide tip, just like a normal trekking pole. So, we’ve got a really durable way to hit the ground. I used a suede grip. I made a wrist strap, adjustable with an aluminum buckle, Merino wool lining, Ventile outer shell. And then I even found some I put in a brass threaded insert in the top of the pole and a really nice bolt to hold the whole thing in place. So, it’s super comfortable, it’s super strong, I think stronger than my carbon fiber poles, which I’ve broken, just crossing a river and I don’t think these are going to have that issue at all. And then in order to avoid, you know, I didn’t want this project to look too hippy-dippy or Ren Faire or like, you know, Civil War reenactor or anything, so while the bamboo is beautiful naturally, I just coated the whole thing in some ink, some Sumi calligraphy ink. I had that for woodworking marking, and it applied beautifully. I had to just sand the outside of the bamboo to remove that natural waxy finish, and then the ink went on, and it’s staying on, and it doesn’t rub off or anything. So, these poles I think are going to be maybe the the strongest part of this collection, like physically strongest. I think a lot of the textiles have to be a little bit weaker, mostly because of using a natural thread, but these poles are going to be stronger than the aluminum or carbon fiber equivalents that are at REI. I’d say the only bummer or compromise about these is that they’re not height adjustable. No problem to just make them appropriate for my height for use, but I wouldn’t then be able to adjust it even taller to use with a a tent, for instance. And it’s possible to lash two poles together, but it’s a lot easier with like a Voile strap, or something, you know, synthetic. So, it’s it’s just interesting how the the confines of this project, the rules of the project, just put a lot of constraints on the decision making all throughout. For the tent or shelter, I did a tarp, and I usually sleep under a tarp when I’m backpacking, and they work great. I live in the West, and am blessed to have pretty predictable stretches of good weather and fewer bugs. For the situation we get to backpack in out West, it’s nice to not need to worry about the bugs so much. So, I did this very lightweight tarp design. Again, it’s very similar to tarps that I’ve made in the past. So, it’s basically a 9-foot long tarp, and it’s, you know, catenary-cut curves so that the tension is really even on the seams and on the sides, and tensioning lines, and I use trekking poles to set it up. The difference about this tarp, being petrochemical free, is that it’s made out of oiled silk. And this is a really unusual material nowadays. I found a lot of references to it in literature from over 100 years ago, but almost nothing since then. And that’s probably because synthetics are a lot stronger and a lot more predictably waterproof, and that’s okay. But given the confines of the project, I needed to find something lightweight and waterproof enough. So, this is waterproof enough. I haven’t done a hydrostatic head test on it, but I can fill up a embroidery frame with this material on it with water, and it doesn’t drip through even over 24 hours. And, you know, with a rough garden hose test, it’s managed to just kind of bead that water off really, really nicely. What is oiled silk? It is a silk taffeta, so it’s a really, really lightweight almost a ballgown type material, and then I soak it in a blend of linseed oil and natural turpentine. Turpentine is basically distilled pine tar or pine sap. You distill it like you would distill whiskey and you end up with turpentine. That’s the same stuff that artists use to cut their paints. And I use the turpentine to cut down the linseed oil so that it can flow through the fabric more easily and that I can wring it out more easily. If there’s too much in there, it’ll end up getting really sticky and like, yeah, too too sticky and gross. Ugh. But with with the right blend and the right amount of kind of wringing out and careful drying, I can get it to where it’s this really nice, predictable hand and waterproof enough without being too sticky. You can see that it’s yellowed, and some of my older samples have yellowed a lot more. This is a kind of interesting anecdote because what we read about as oilskins, that’s what fishermen wore, like in Captains Courageous or something, you know, those books from 150 years ago about people fishing in the North Sea, they’re all wearing oilskins. Oilskins are basically a canvas smock soaked in linseed oil. And as it ages and oxidizes, it turns yellow, and that’s why Paddington Bear and, you know, all those traditional raincoats are yellow, because it’s kind of an inheritance from the oilskin. Kind of an interesting detail. When I first made this tarp, it was this like just ivory off-white, and that was 2 months, 3 months ago, and it’s already turned started to turn yellow, and the older it gets, the more yellow it’s going to get. So, I did use some reinforcements at important areas, like the the main seam attachment point of the tarp. I used a kind of a Ventile patch in some areas and just a self-fabric patch in other areas. I used cotton tape to reinforce those attachment points. I did a lot of kind of repetitive straight stitching, but again, not too close together, so it doesn’t get perforated and just rip out. We’ll see how this holds up. This is not nearly as strong as synthetics, but this is one where I’m pleased to say it’s actually lighter weight. I used, due to the width of the fabric, this tarp is even a little bit smaller than the one I usually use, that’s sil- sil-coated polyester. And this is this is 440 grams, so that’s just under a pound. It’s like about, I don’t know, 14 ounces or something, the the weights that we expect out of ultralight shelters.

item.title: Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders Fell 71 Times and Quit Once Before Setting His Latest Appalachian Trail Record
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.64
Dale "Grey Beard" Sanders on his 2026 thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail. (Photo: Courtesy of Dale Sanders) Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders, 91, was about two tenths of a mile from the top of Mount Katahdin when he took a hard fall. Just steps away from becoming the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail in a calendar year, he hit the ground for the 71st time on his 12-month journey. Two days later, he told Backpacker, “I’m a little sore on both legs from that, but it’s simply just small contusions and no bones or anything is broken or damaged.” Out of the 71 falls that Sanders took, the vast majority were “soft falls,” which meant that he quickly got up, brushed himself off and kept walking without pain. But seven of those falls left him in a daze. “I laid down on the ground, and I didn’t care who saw me,” he said. “I was all moaning and groaning for a while.” Sanders says his balance was noticeably worse than in 2017, when he had set a previous Appalachian Trail age record by hiking the trail at 82. “When you get older, it seems that our body starts to deteriorate, and we simply do not physically have the abilities that we had when we were under 40 and below,” Sanders said. “The older you get past say 50 or 60, it starts going down.” In order to claim the age record for a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail, hikers have to tackle the whole 2,200-mile trail within a 12-month period. They must also hike past every white blaze (“in some cases, crawl by,” said Sanders, alluding to his experience on Mount Katahdin). Neither the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) nor Guinness currently differentiate between supported, self-supported, and unsupported age records on the trail. Prior to Sanders’ record, M.J. ‘Nimblewill’ Eberhart last claimed the title at age 83 in 2021, taking the record from Sanders. To Sanders’s knowledge, no other 90-year-old has attempted to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. Compared to his 2017 thru-hike, Sanders had to significantly dial down his mileage. As an 82 year old, he hiked many 20-mile days, but averaged closer to 11 miles per day this year. It was also tough on his mind, which occasionally wavered at the sight of a steep climb. While he trained for six months before setting out on his latest thru-hike, he still underestimated the difficulty of the Appalachian Trail. “I realized quickly that my ceiling of physical ability was much lower than it was at 82 years old,” he said. Most AT thru-hikers blaze through the route, tackling it in four to six months. Sanders nearly took the entire 365 days to complete his trek, hiking for 200 of those days. On one occasion, he even quit the trail. He was in Maine when it happened: A hard fall 142 miles short of the northern terminus landed him in the hospital, where doctors checked for internal bleeding and ran tests to see why he was experiencing numbness in his left arm. One doctor suggested that it was time to hang up his hiking poles to head home and talk to his primary care physician and neurologist. “I didn’t want to go home because it was so close to the end,” he reflected. But after receiving a call about his mother-in-law’s death, his fate was decided: He was going home to Tennessee. After attending the funeral, resting, and scheduling new doctor’s appointments, his neurologist determined that Sanders had experienced bleeding in his brain, but it wasn’t active and it appeared to be old. His numb arm was due to a pinched nerve. Both that doctor and his primary care provider cleared him to hike. Given the short window of time that Sanders had to finish the final stretch of trail, he knew it was unlikely that he’d finish before time ran out. But he decided he wanted to see Katahdin, even if it meant he’d only land the age record for a section hike instead of a thru-hike. With a bit of luck and sheer determination, Sanders ultimately made it to the northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail with 5 days to spare. When asked why he was so determined to get back on trail, Sanders explained that the record felt bigger than he was. “I hold several age records in several different venues, most of them hiking and paddling, and in each and every one of those, it seems that I’ve given people hope. [It’s when] people have hope that they have inspiration,” he said. “Hope is really important.”

item.title: Six US drive-ins where you can stay the night
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.68
Six places in the US where you can sleep at a drive-in From retro 1950s properties to modern glamping sites, these places are reviving one of the US's most enduring pastimes – and offering travellers one last classic summer experience. At the Frontier Drive-Inn, there are no televisions in the guest rooms. Instead, as the property rather cheekily puts it, the biggest TV in southern Colorado is right outside your door. That would be the outdoor screen left over from the Frontier's first life as a drive-in cinema, which opened in 1955 and went dark three decades later. Today, the former cinema anchors a retro-inspired hotel where guests sleep in Quonset-style yurts and vintage trailers, then gather outside for films beneath the famously dark skies of the San Luis Valley. As Labor Day (7 September) approaches, the Frontier and other properties like it are providing a fresh take on one of the US's most enduring warm-weather pastimes – and offering one last classic summer experience before the season winds down. For generations of Americans, drive-ins have been inseparable from summer. The country's first drive-in opened in 1933, but they exploded after WWII, when rising car ownership, suburban expansion and the baby boom helped push their number to nearly 5,000 by the late 1950s, according to April Wright, a drive-in historian and director of Going Attractions: The Definitive Story of the American Drive-In Movie in which she visits roughly 500 open, abandoned or former drive-in sites. "Going to the drive-in was just something you did every summer," Wright said. Though their heyday may have passed, Wright says the appeal of drive-ins isn't purely nostalgic. Plenty of younger visitors are experiencing them for the first time, drawn to the fact that a night at the drive-in is as much about the ritual around the film as the film itself. "What it's always been about, and what it is still about today, is spending time with friends and family, and creating an experience," Wright said. Now, a handful of hotels, motels and campgrounds around the US are turning that experience into an overnight stay. Some have revived long-shuttered drive-ins, while others let guests sleep within sight of giant screens that have been showing films for decades. At these properties, film night doesn't end with the final credits. Frontier Drive-Inn – Center, Colorado Luke Falcone, co-owner of Frontier, said the screen had survived decades of the San Luis Valley's harsh weather and was too important to the site's history to lose. "When doing historic preservation projects, if you come across something that isn't broken, you've hit the jackpot," he said. Despite the name, the Frontier is no longer a traditional drive-in: guests don't pull up in their cars, but settle into lawn chairs or onto blankets to watch fan-favourite films under the stars. "By bringing folks out of their rooms (and cars), we provide an entirely different experience that we can all bond over," Falcone said. The programming leans into nostalgic cult classics, while the accommodation is decidedly modern. Best Western Movie Manor – Monte Vista, Colorado The motel was built beside The Star Drive-In Theatre, which opened in 1955 as drive-ins were booming across the US, and many rooms face one of its two screens through large picture windows, with the film's audio piped inside. Each room is named after a movie star, from Cary Grant to Robert De Niro, and guests can also head outside and watch from their cars. More than 70 years after The Star first lit up, it still shows films seasonally (generally from spring to the end of September). Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday – Sutherlin, Oregon The Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday campground occupies the former Cloverleaf Drive-In, where the original 100ft (30m) screen survived long after the cinema itself closed. When the current owner bought the property in 2006, they chose to keep the screen and eventually added a digital projector and FM transmitter, bringing films back to the site. Today, films are shown most weekends. Some RV sites sit directly in front of the screen (or have private patios angled towards it), allowing guests to watch from their rigs and tune into the film over their radios, much as they would at a traditional drive-in. Tent campers and guests in the rest of the RV sites can bring chairs or blankets to a grassy viewing area just in front of the screen, where the sound plays aloud. Hotel Caravana at Four Brothers Drive-In – Amenia, New York Unlike most of the places on this list, Four Brothers isn't a survivor from the golden age of the silver screen. The Hudson Valley theatre opened in 2013, reviving the format decades after thousands of its predecessors had disappeared. Since then, the family-run property has added mini-golf, fire pits and Hotel Caravana, where guests can sleep in vintage trailers within the drive-in grounds or even pitch their own tent. Ofland Escalante – Escalante, Utah Set along Scenic Byway 12 in southern Utah, Ofland Escalante occupies a former drive-in site within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. Guests spend the day hiking, exploring slot canyons or visiting nearby Bryce Canyon and Capitol Reef national parks, then return in time for the nightly film. "The movie starts just after dusk and it anchors the whole evening," said Noah Ellis, CEO of Ofland Hotels. "It's a key amenity, not an add-on." The old drive-in comes with its own fleet of vintage cars – including a 1957 Chevrolet and Ford Thunderbird – that are parked facing the screen. Guests grab complimentary popcorn and classic sweets from the concession stand, choose a car and settle in beneath the desert sky. "The site was a drive-in long before it was a hotel, so keeping actual cars in the mix mattered to us," Ellis said. "There's something about a row of vintage cars, climbing in with a bag of popcorn, that stays with people." Overnight options range from modernised vintage Airstreams to a variety of cabins. Tiger Drive-In – Tiger, Georgia Tucked into the mountains of north-eastern Georgia, the Tiger Drive-In first opened in 1954, went dark in the 1980s and then sat abandoned for roughly two decades. It returned to life in 2004, and today guests can stay after the movie in one of three vintage 1960s campervans parked on the drive-in grounds (each with a private deck facing the screen), or camp in a tent or RV. --

item.title: Vienna's great surprise: The Globe Museum
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.57
The museum charting how humans understand the world Beautiful, surreal and eerily empty, Vienna's Globe Museum the only public museum on Earth dedicated to globes, and it – quite literally – tells the story of our world. It's a chilly afternoon in Vienna, and the line for the Austrian National Library has already spilled out the door, curling like a ribbon around the grand Josefsplatz square. I'm not in the mood to wait – I've already struck out at several crowded nearby attractions where timed-entry tickets were sold out. Rather than join the queue, I walk down the street and stumble onto a smaller, somewhat hidden site: The Globe Museum. Tucked inside Vienna's 17th-Century Palais Mollard, it's the only public museum on Earth dedicated entirely to globes, and one of Vienna's greatest surprises. Different worlds I soon realise that I've wandered into another world – or more accurately, many of them. Just steps from some of the city's most celebrated, crowded attractions, Vienna's Globe Museum displays more than 220 rare and antique spheres, most created before 1850, ranging from towering Coronelli globes to tiny, foldable pocket orbs. Beautiful and surreal, the museum's extensive collection goes beyond geography to reveal how humanity has mapped and imagined the Earth and heavens above. It's a chronicle of human curiosity, and – quite literally – the story of our world. "Globes show the change in our imagination of our planet," says Nikolaus Schobesberger, the director of museum. "And this is the only place in the world where you can see so many of them at the same time." Visitors start by travelling through the Golden Cabinet, a lavish room with centuries-old frescoes depicting scenes from Greek mythology. It's the backdrop for a stunning array of globe-related instruments, like telluriums, which illustrate the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and armillary spheres, which use a framework of rings to visualise the movements of celestial bodies. As I reach the museum's four main galleries, I realise the whole place is pin-drop quiet. I shuffle slowly from one glass case to another, holding my breath to not disturb the stillness, even though I'm alone with centuries-old objects. I find myself marvelling at two spherical worlds suspended in time. One is terrestrial, with oceans awash in vivid blues and squiggly brown coastlines. The other is celestial, where mythological creatures and constellations spill across a tea stain-coloured backdrop. Barely bigger than beach balls, these two time capsules were made by the same craftsman 10 years apart in the mid-1500s and preserve a world as it was still coming into focus. In one, Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa's coasts are filled with place names, while North America fades into the uncharted Arctic. Asia is distorted, a hypothetical southern continent stands in for Australia and Antarctica and the Pacific is populated by sea monsters instead of islands. In the other, Renaissance astrological observations exist alongside Pegasus taking flight and Perseus brandishing Medusa's severed head. "They're some of the oldest globes we have in our collection," says Schobesberger. Moving from one globe to the next, I notice how these relics extend beyond geography and depict what people once believed. Many fill the space of unexplored oceans with dragons, while some confidently depict my home state of California as an island. Some pieces also preserve colonial-era prejudices with elaborately painted scenes depicting Indigenous people as cannibals. On one, African coastlines are dotted with Spanish and Portuguese flags, showing "ownership". "They're a part of this colonial thinking. And so, they're beautiful art, but you also have to think about the time they were created," Schobesberger says, explaining that every globe is as much a record of what people knew as what they didn't. That's why he believes the museum resonates with all types of people, not just historians or cartography enthusiasts. One of Schobesberger's favourite objects is a lunar globe from 1961. The front portion of the Moon is meticulously mapped. The back, however, is a stark white strip, intentionally left blank because the far side of the Moon had not yet been seen. An updated lunar globe made two years later, also on display, contains the missing portion. I can't help but circle back to a showstopper in the front hall, a replica of the Behaim Globe – completed by Martin Behaim in 1492, the year Christopher Columbus sailed west – which shows a world without the Americas. There's simply an expanse of ocean between Europe and Asia. "A globe is such a great thing because it's a small-scale model of our planet, so you can tell stories about the world on it," he says. "Climate, geology, topography, trade routes, everything." From curios to cultural cornerstones Walking through the museum, visitors can see the globe's own journey unfold. The earliest examples were luxury objects reserved for aristocrats and wealthy merchants. Over time, globes lost their exclusivity, shrunk in size and became more affordable and popular. They entered schools, appeared in living rooms and even became playthings for children. Today, they are so commonplace that my son even won his desktop globe in a classroom raffle. I entered the museum expecting to view globes as historic artefacts, but I'm surprised by how alive they still feel. Even with Google Earth at my fingertips, these tactile objects invite curiosity and imagination in a way that a screen doesn't. "It's not just that the globe is a scientific instrument. It's also an object which lets you dream of foreign countries," says Schobesberger. Globes in pop culture Beginning 24 September 2026, the museum's newest exhibition, Globes in Everyday Life, Art and Culture, will explore how globes evolved from a status symbol to a familiar fixture. It also showcases the globe's enduring place in pop culture, from architecture to art and film, like Charlie Chaplin's famous dance with an inflatable globe in The Great Dictator. "The main idea was to show that globes are almost everywhere as a part of everyday life," Schobesberger says. Schobesberger's own fascination began as a young child, when he became captivated by the ships, sea monsters and mythical creatures that filled the blank spaces of historical maps and globes. He began to draw his own world maps when he was just six years old. "You can think about what's possible on the other side of the world, even when you're sitting here in Europe," he says. "Nothing else can capture the imagination quite like it." More like this: That sentiment resonates with author JF Penn, who stumbled onto the Globe Museum while researching her novel Spear of Destiny, based on a relic housed in Vienna's Imperial Treasury. Like me, she ended up lingering far longer than planned. "I particularly loved the oversized antique globes with the patina of age and use," she says. "I considered how many fingertips have turned them over generations and wondered if they thought of travelling to these far-off places that I do." Even after visitors leave Palais Mollard, the search continues. Across Vienna, some 50 globes are perched on rooftops and facades, hidden in plain sight. The museum even charts them on a virtual map in its new exhibit, encouraging people to look upward as they wander the city. When I finally step back outside, the sky is dark and the streets are even more crowded. Earlier in the day, I had been seeking a quieter corner of Vienna. Instead, I was given a whole new way of seeing the world – a place that's constantly being redrawn and reimagined. --

item.title: The smoky plant goo that Finns can't stop eating
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.52
Pine tar: The surprising, smoky goo that Finns can't stop eating Once used to waterproof boats and treat infections, this smoky plant byproduct is now used to flavour everything from schnapps to bread. But how does it taste? I've been in the sub-Arctic city of Oulu, Finland for only a few hours when I'm caught under a torrent of late summer rain. I take refuge in a cafe and order a coffee and sugar-dusted pannukakku (a thick pancake). The waiter asks me, "What flavour? We have almond, tar, blueberry..." I'm certain I've misunderstood: "Did you say tar?" He nods nonchalantly. Welcome to Oulu, the northern Finnish city where terva (pine tar, usually translated in English simply as "tar") is on the menu. Produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, this thick, dark substance flavours everything from lager to ice cream, lending a distinct, rich smokiness. "It's an intense flavour, so a little goes a long way," says Matti Moller of the Arctic Food Lab, an initiative showcasing northern Finland's culinary culture. "But it's brilliant to experiment with in everything from fish to desserts." To Finns, pine tar's aroma has long been associated with wooden boats, summer cottages and sauna scents. So what's the recent culinary appeal? I've decided to find out. From sealant to meal Yet just two centuries ago, Oulu had a very different reputation. Encircled by dense pine forests and the winding channels of the Oulujoki delta, it was famed as the tar capital of the world. "Oulu has been a major trading hub since the 15th Century thanks to its position on the Oulu River," says local guide Sirpa Törmä. "By the 1860s, it had become the world's largest tar-exporting port." Essential for waterproofing wooden sailing ships, tar was produced by smouldering wood in tar pits across villages along the river, then transported in narrow boats to Oulu's harbour for global export. Thanks to its antibacterial properties, tar had also long been used as a natural wound treatment all over Finland. "As the well-known saying goes: 'If sauna, spirits and tar do not help, the disease is fatal,'" explains Ritva Kylli, a food historian at the University of Oulu. But how did it make its way to the Finnish palate? Tar-as-flavour made its debut on pharmacy shelves. Archives at the National Library of Finland reveal that tar-flavoured medicinal lozenges date back to the early 1900s, and Oulu's local papers advertised tervakaramellit ('tar sweets') as early as 1902. "These were medicinal lozenges sold in apothecary shops for coughs and respiratory diseases," says Kylli. Even if not every Finn enjoys the taste of tar, virtually everyone has tried the iconic black terva pastille. The nation's most famous brand is Terva Leijona (Tar Lion), sold to this day. Launched in 1933, the pastilles were created by Oulu pharmacist YW Jalander after watching locals inhale smoky tar fumes for their health. Facing low profits, he invented a tar essence (tervaessanssi) and infused it into liquorice pastilles, which he sold through his confectionary company, Merijal. Terva Leijona eventually changed hands, but it is still made using his recipe. As popular as they were, tar didn't make the leap from pastille to gourmet treat until the end of the 20th Century, says Kylli, as living standards rose and interest in regional heritage cuisine grew across the country: "[It] seems to be connected to a growing interest in the cultural memory of Oulu's tar economy, a trend spreading beyond northern historical trade routes to all of Finland," she says. "It was reimagined into a distinctive heritage flavour." 'It can be addictive' Matti tells me he buys tar chocolate and syrup a few times a year. "The taste is unique – sweet, smoky, medicinal and completely unmistakable," he says as we walk across the picturesque island of Pikisaari, connected to Oulu's city centre by a short bridge. "Why do we love it? Perhaps we're tasting our roots, the Finnish forest and our heritage." The Oulu region, as the historic heart of the pine tar culture, has also become the symbolic centre of pine tar cuisine, with a high concentration of restaurants, cafes and bakeries that produce terva foods. At Pekka Heikkinen, a family bakery in Kajaani founded in 1913, owner Kaisa Marin bakes traditional bread and pastries. "Tar boats used to sail right past our bakery to Oulu," she explains. "When pine tar food innovations emerged in the '90s, it was natural to start baking tar-flavoured bread." For Marin, the connection is deeply personal: "My grandmother washed my hair with tar shampoo in the sauna, and our cabin's boat was sealed with tar. To me, the scent is cosy, nostalgic and rooted in home. I love it!" She always keeps thinly sliced tar bread in the freezer, ready to fry in butter when guests arrive. Though not for everyone, she warns it can be addictive. "My uncle, a master confectioner, created a rich tar chocolate that we bake every Christmas. We've even made cakes with pine tar and spruce needles." Rina Hirviniemi, owner of the cosy Kahvila Kiikku, also bakes tar bread at least once a week, usually pairing it with gravlax. "In summer, I serve vanilla ice cream with tar syrup, and in winter, we grill with tar outside," she says. "I like keeping tar products on hand, though I don't put them on the menu – I have an eye for people I can recommend it to." So what does it taste like? Convinced, I decide to – literally – bite. According to Marin, ice cream is the best starting point for tar newcomers, so I head to Market Square's ice cream van. Cone in hand, I sit by Toripolliisi, the brawny bronze police statue keeping watch over the square, and take my first hesitant taste. A smoky-sweet aroma rushes from nose to palate – the unexpected whiff of bacon. Yet, it's surprisingly sweet. Intrigued, I can't stop eating. Bite by bite, it completely wins me over. Just as Marin predicted, I find myself becoming addicted. I head next to ChocoSomnia, an Oulu chocolate maker. "We make tar pralines, chocolate bars and tar coffee. We get curious first-timers, but also loyal regulars," says co-owner Mika Lähteenmäki. Sampling a square of dark chocolate infused with pine tar and cranberry, I'm struck by the balance of smoky depth, rich cocoa bitterness and soft berry sweetness; the very taste of a pine forest in midsummer. I can't stop there. My local friend leads me to a supermarket for Terva Leijona pastilles. Like impatient children, we tear open the box and pop the tiny black sweets. Instead of subtle sweetness, an intense, smoky rush clears my airways. My friend introduces me to two of his mates, and I discover that local usage varies widely: some drizzle tar syrup on bacon, others serve tar schnapps before nights out. For others still, tar candies reign supreme. While most Finns buy ready-made tar products, today's skilled chefs craft them from scratch. This is what brought me to Lasaretti, a restaurant tucked into the riverfront oasis of Oulu's Hupisaaret Park. Today, head chef Laurance Robinson is serving smoked whitefish pasta with tar pearls, pickled fennel and red onion. "I can't build a tar pit, so I buy flavouring from Kujala's farm to make my syrup for sweet and savoury dishes," he says. "Balancing its strong, pungent taste took time." Resembling caviar, the tar pearls burst in my mouth against the whitefish, sharp fennel, and sweet archipelago bread. It is pure umami with subtle smokiness. More like this: Originally from the Isle of Man, Robinson cooked across Europe before settling in Finland. "I'll never forget my first taste of tar in 2011 – a sauna soda from my future father-in-law. It tasted like an ashtray at first, but the smokiness mellowed. Later, when I had the freedom to experiment, I said, 'I want to be the tar chef.'" His tar pavlova recently won best dessert at an Oulu culinary contest. "I wonder how far I can push it." Watching passersby drift through the sunny park, I marvel at how tar shifted from a maritime necessity to the flavour of local identity. "You know what," says my friend. "I've had a horrible headache since morning, but after eating this dish, it's completely gone." I can't promise it cures headaches, but in every sense, tar remains a uniquely Finnish ingredient that still works its quiet magic. --

item.title: Why Swedes think standing out is embarrassing
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.29
'You're not to think you're anything special': Why Swedes hate standing out Swedes prize equality, dislike boasting and are famously reluctant to stand out – yet they're also fiercely individualistic and know how to celebrate. The century-old idea of Jantelagen helps explain these contradictions, and offers visitors a fascinating key to decoding Swedish culture. As an utlandssvensk – a Swede who grew up abroad – I've always been fascinated by the unwritten rules that shape Swedish social life. I once got to chatting with a fellow Swede at a party. It was 4 July, and we discussed why our country didn't celebrate its national day as fervently as Americans. No fireworks, no parades – how come? "Well, it would be fairly embarrassing wouldn't it?" she said. "All that self-celebration. It's a bit over-the-top," she added, lowering her voice, as if there was an American hovering inches away from our table. As she explained, setting off fireworks for your nation (and therefore yourself) smacks of back-patting and ostentatiousness – two things that are anathema to much of Scandinavia. When I complimented my companion on how well she'd outlined the issue, she looked askance and waved my praise away like a bad smell. "No, please. That's just my little opinion, of course." A modest code of conduct To understand this aversion to basking in even the smallest of spotlights, many Swedes point to Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante: an unwritten social code embedded across Scandinavia that prizes humility, equality and not placing yourself above others. The term comes from Danish-Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose's satirical 1933 novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional town of Jante. Sandemose used Jante to skewer the conformism of small-town Scandinavian life, laying out 10 "laws" designed to put anyone who considered themselves exceptional firmly back in their place. Rules such as "you're not to think you're anything special" and "you're not to think you're smarter than [anyone else]" leave the reader with a deliberately bruised ego – and that's the point. Nearly a century on, Sandemose's laws remain memorable and highly quotable, helping Jantelagen endure as cultural shorthand. How to connect with Swedes Be proactive: Small talk with strangers isn't the norm, so don't mistake reserve for unfriendliness. "Swedes tend to be very loyal and trustworthy once a friendship is established," says Gossner. "I often advise newcomers to take the initiative. Don't wait for Swedes to come to you, as they appreciate when others make the first move." Suggest fika: The Swedish ritual of cake and coffee offers a low-pressure way to socialise. Meet over coffee and a modest but delicious kanelbulle (cinnamon bun) rather than trying to force conversation in the street. Be punctual: Swedes place a high value on being on time, particularly when you're invited to someone's home. Stefan Dahlberg, a professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, has written a paper on Jantelagen's modern legacy. He sees the rules less as firm laws governing Swedish behaviour. Instead, he explains, "they are better understood as a cultural shorthand for a set of familiar norms […] that you can recognise in everyday Swedish interaction. Status differences tend to be played down, social relations are relatively informal and conspicuous self-promotion can be viewed negatively." Visitors to Sweden will likely see this in action when chatting to locals. Compliment a Swede on their English, for example, and they may quickly play it down – switching to Swedish and muttering, "Äsch, det är ju inte flytande…" (Shucks, it's not like it's fluent…). Sandemose would be proud. The qualities can also be seen in everyday Swedish rituals, from Fredagsmys – unpretentious "cosy Fridays" with friends or family – to Lördagsgodis ("Saturday-candy") that's practiced by parents as the one day that kids can unleash their sweet tooth after a week of modest abstention. That doesn't mean that Jantelagen functions as a literal rulebook – or identically across Scandinavia. Dahlberg's study of Jantelagen in Norway, a geographical and cultural neighbour, found the average respondent tended to disagree with the Jante statements. After all, Dahlberg explains, Sandemose invented the list as a scathing takedown of conformity. "So there are really two things mixed together in the concept: an egalitarian idea that nobody is inherently better than anyone else, and a more negative pressure not to distinguish yourself too much." Jante's mirror image Jantelagen has another, less obvious side. In a culture where seeking the limelight is usually frowned upon, Swedish reserve can disappear at parties when a tradition of snappsvisor (increasingly risqué songs belted out while drinking heroic amounts of aquavit) and performative speeches create safe social spaces to open up. So, while Jantelagen is often used as a reasoning for Swedish reserve and diffidence, it can also reveal the inverse. More like this: As Dahlberg notes, "'Don't think you are better than anyone else' can be read in the opposite direction: don't assume that somebody is better than you simply because they are richer, more successful or have a more prestigious title." With so much bubbling under the surface, Sweden can feel deceptively complex. Luckily, there are classes designed to help mystified foreigners. Yvonne Gossner runs Learn Swedish Culture AB – and business is booming. "I realised there was a big demand for practical insights into Swedish culture, especially for foreigners trying to navigate life here," she says. "Many felt lost or misunderstood in everyday settings, or even when trying to make Swedish friends." Case in point: a South American client once arrived at a Swedish woman's party an hour late, carrying a big dish of food as a surprise. The hostess "was not pleased" as the guests had already eaten, and the immodestly large, late-coming dish was left untouched in a bedroom. Swedes, Gossner says, place a high value on punctuality and politeness; if you're invited to a Swede's house, she suggests sending a post-party message of thanks. "There is even a Swedish joke: 'Don't forget to send a thank-you note for the thank-you note'," she adds. An unasked-for dish can risk looking like a statement that "my food is better than yours", while failing to acknowledge someone's politeness can jar the sense of social balance. Cracking the Swedish ice Lola Akinmade Åkerström, a Nigerian-American author, travel writer and photographer who moved to Sweden more than 15 years ago, was initially "a bit floored by the unspoken ethos" of Jantelagen, as well as the contradictory layers of national character. "Sweden is the most open society, run by the most private people," she says. If you want to deeply discomfit a Swede, she advises, just make eye contact on a quiet train, and hit them with "Hi! How you doing?" Yet they're not being cold, just respectful of the idea that no one should impose themselves on a stranger's space. That preference for understatement extends beyond social interactions. Travel through the countryside and you can see it reflected in the nation's beloved summer houses. "I think Swedes hold the world record in the number of summer houses per capita – around half the population has access to one," says Orvar Löfgren, professor emeritus of ethnology at Lund University. Yet these are rarely flashy second homes; instead, they reflect rustic, rural values, even among wealthy owners. (Don't think your cabin is better than other cabins, Sandemose might say.) While in Sweden, visitors might also notice small Swedish flags on birthday cakes, supermarket products and during student celebrations. "Swedes who love to see themselves as non-nationalistic are actually good at waving the flag," says Löfgren. And despite their quiet reputation, "Swedes are great at celebrating," he adds. Christmas, Easter, Midsummer, birthdays, and student exams are celebrated "with more intensity than in most European countries". You could say these occasions showcase Swedes at their best – not that they'd put it so boastfully, of course. --

item.title: Crispy Potato Kugel
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.07
When many people hear “kugel,” visions of a sweet egg noodle casserole first come to mind, delighting many and confusing others. Savory potato kugel, however, is almost universally pleasing. Landing in between a latke and a Spanish tortilla in flavor and texture, potato kugel is, like all kugels, a baked casserole common in the Ashkenazi Jewish culinary tradition. Filled with grated potato, onion, and egg, it’s a no-brainer side dish for high holidays, like Rosh Hashanah and Passover, or weekly shabbat, but it’s welcome on the table any day alongside meaty mains such as braised brisket or roast chicken. Where latke mixture must be squeezed extremely dry to fry into crisp pancakes, potato kugel’s creamy texture comes from leaving some of that liquid in the mix. Using mayonnaise in the filling—and to grease the pan—instead of traditional schmaltz or olive oil helps ensure the kugel bakes off moist, rich, and crisp—never dry or greasy. Fat wedges of potato kugel are excellent topped with a dollop of sour cream and a sprinkle of chopped chives (but, of course, if you’re keeping kosher and serving meat alongside, you’ll want skip the dairy). Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours - Yield 10–12 servings Ingredients 4 3 1 3¼ 3 3 1 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Brush bottom and sides of a 9"-diameter springform pan, metal cake pan, or cast-iron skillet with 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise. (If using a springform pan, place a baking sheet underneath rack to catch any drips.) Fill a medium bowl with water. Peel 3 lb. russet potatoes (about 4 large) and quarter; place in bowl of water. Quarter 1 medium onion. Using a food processor fitted with a coarse grating disk, grate potatoes and onion. (Alternatively, grate on the large holes of a box grater.) Step 2Transfer potato mixture to a large colander or fine-mesh sieve set over a large bowl. Sprinkle with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to combine. Let sit 5 minutes to allow excess liquid to drain. Step 3Using your hands, press out more liquid from potato mixture (it should not be totally dry). Transfer colander to a plate. Gently pour out liquid from bowl, leaving behind any white starch accumulated at the bottom. Step 4Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture. Step 5Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture.

item.title: Pommes Purée (French Mashed Potatoes)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.67
Pommes purée is France’s answer to mashed potatoes. But instead of simply mashing the spuds, they get passed through a food mill and a tamis (a large fine-mesh drum) to make them as smooth as satin sheets. Think of them as the fancier, more luxe version of the comfort food classic. Here, chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, takes inspiration from chef Joël Robuchon’s famous version, adding a wealth of milk and butter to the potatoes for a truly decadent result. You can serve them as a comforting side next to roast chicken or seared steak, elevating any dinner into a bistro-worthy affair. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 2 1 1 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 lb. 4 oz. large Yukon gold potatoes (5–7) in a large pot and pour in water to cover by about 2". Season generously with kosher salt and bring to a boil. Cook until potatoes are fork-tender, 20–25 minutes. Step 2Meanwhile, heat 1 cup whole milk in a small saucepan over low heat and keep warm. Step 3Drain potatoes. Working quickly so they remain hot, peel potatoes with a paring knife and cut into pieces. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl, then pass through tamis onto a sheet of parchment paper, pressing with a heatproof rubber spatula. Step 4Transfer potato purée to a small pot or large saucepan and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until dried out a little and steaming, about 3 minutes. Gradually pour in warm milk, stirring constantly until smooth and spoonable (you might not need all of the milk). Remove from heat and add 1 cup (2 sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced, a few pieces at a time, whisking after each addition until melted and combined before adding more. Taste pommes purée and season with salt as needed.

item.title: Apple Fritters With Cinnamon Glaze
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.60
Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack. Is it even fall if you haven’t been apple picking? And have you even been apple picking if you didn’t end the day lining up for piping hot cider doughnuts? This recipe is designed to recreate that experience—apple-sweetened dough, a hint of grease, a jolt of sugar and spice—without having to wait for yeast to rise. Ricotta and baking powder deliver tenderness and lift, as with some Central and Eastern European pastry doughs. We then borrowed the best bits from a cake doughnut (crumbly, fluffy insides) and a state-fair fritter (big, juicy chunks of fruit) for a treat that tastes like fried apple pie. Making these chubby little sweets may be even quicker than a drive to the orchard. Cooking the apples in plenty of butter and sugar before adding them to the batter has a twofold effect: The fruit becomes luxuriously tender, and the sugar caramelizes, introducing deep, full-bodied apple-pie-like flavor. Find more great apple recipes here: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Buttery German Apple Cake; and Apple-Walnut Upside-Down Cake. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield 6 servings Ingredients 3 ¼ 4 ½ 2½ 1 2 ½ 1¼ 1 2 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Cook 3 large Honeycrisp or Fuji apples (about 1½ lb.), peeled, cored, cut into ½" pieces, ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. (packed; 75 g) light brown sugar, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, ½ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until apples are softened but still retain their shape and liquid is syrupy, 15–20 minutes. Let cool. Step 2Pour vegetable oil into a medium high-sided skillet fitted with thermometer to come ¾" up sides; heat over medium-high until thermometer registers 325°. Step 3Meanwhile, whisk 2 large eggs and ½ cup plus 2 Tbsp. whole-milk ricotta in a large bowl until smooth. Sift 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour and 1 tsp. baking powder over and, using a rubber spatula, mix until mostly combined (it will look dry and clumpy). Add apple mixture, scraping pan well to get all of the syrup, and fold into batter (it will look broken at first but will come together quickly). Step 4Working in batches of 4 or 5 and using a #16 cookie scoop or ¼-cup measuring cup, drop batter into skillet. Flatten each fritter slightly with scoop and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown, 6–8 minutes. Using a spider or slotted spoon, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet to drain. Step 5Whisk 2 cups (220 g) powdered sugar, a pinch of ground cinnamon, and a pinch of kosher salt in a medium bowl. Add a splash of whole milk; whisk, adding more milk or powdered sugar a little at a time as needed, until a thick but pourable glaze forms. Working one at a time, dip warm fritters in glaze, turning to coat. Transfer back to rack; let sit until glaze is set, about 15 minutes. Do Ahead: Apples can be cooked 1 day ahead. Let cool; transfer to an airtight container and chill. Reheat slightly before folding into batter.

item.title: Pommes Anna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.60
Pommes Anna is a French potato cake made of thinly sliced potatoes cooked in nothing more than butter. While humble in its ingredients, the cake is as dramatic as can be. Baked in a skillet, it gets turned out to reveal a graphic spiral of spuds on top. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, keeps things classic in her recipe, layering paper-thin slices of potatoes with plenty of butter to create a multilayered potato cake that’s crisp on the outside and tender in the center. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 5 1¼ ½ Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Slice 5 lb. large Yukon gold potatoes (10–15), peeled, lengthwise on a mandoline set to 1-mm thickness. Step 2Brush a large high-sided skillet with some of 1¼ cups clarified butter to coat. Cut a round of parchment paper to fit bottom of pan and place in pan. Brush parchment with more clarified butter. Using cutter and working with a few slices stacked together at a time, punch out enough rounds to fill bottom of pan. Arrange slices around sides of pan, overlapping slightly, to create a circle (make sure slices are compact and tight). Repeat process, creating concentric circles, until you have an even layer covering entire bottom of pan. Drizzle with some clarified butter and generously season with kosher salt. Repeat process (no need to cut potatoes into rounds), creating more layers, until all of the potatoes slices and clarified butter have been used. Dot ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, sliced, over final layer of potatoes. Step 3Cover pan with a lid or foil and bake potatoes until tender, 50–55 minutes. Uncover and bake until deep golden brown in spots, 45–55 minutes more. Let cool slightly, then place a plate upside down over pan. Holding plate and pan together, carefully turn over in one swift motion to invert pommes Anna onto plate. Remove pan.

item.title: Pommes Dauphine
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.03
Pommes dauphine (classic French potato puffs) are part of the vast lexicon of potato dishes rarely seen outside of the country. Think of the bite-size clouds as fried mashed potatoes, only lighter and more magical. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City sticks to the traditional method, mixing equal parts pâte à choux with a purée of roasted potatoes. You’ll spoon the mixture into hot oil to create golden, crisp yet airy puffs. Serve as a chic appetizer or party snack paired with aioli or whatever dipping sauce your heart desires—or, in true French fashion, alongside a hearty steak or roast chicken as an impressive side. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; Ratatouille; and Dover Sole Meunière. Ingredients 1 4 1 ⅔ 2–3 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Sprinkle coarse salt over a rimmed baking sheet to cover (aim for a ¼"–½" thick layer). Nestle 1 lb. large Yukon Gold potatoes (2–3) into the salt and roast in oven until a knife pierces through flesh with little resistance, about 30 minutes. Step 2Remove from oven and, working quickly so potatoes remain hot, peel with a paring knife and halve. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl; set aside. Step 3Bring 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ⅔ cup water to a simmer in a medium saucepan over high heat, stirring with a stiff heatproof spatula or sturdy rubber spatula to help melt butter and dissolve salt. Immediately reduce heat to medium; add ⅔ cup all-purpose flour all at once and stir quickly until most of the flour is absorbed. Cook, stirring vigorously and breaking up pockets of flour as needed, until a thin film forms on bottom and sides of pan and dough comes together into a single mass, 2–3 minutes. (It should look glossy and feel buttery and smooth.) Remove from heat and let sit in pan until no longer hot but still warm, about 3 minutes. Step 4Add 2 large eggs to mixture one at a time, mixing until incorporated after each addition. Pâte à choux should be thick, glossy, and fall off spatula in a V-shape. If it’s too thick, stir in another 1 large egg. Add dough to reserved potatoes and stir to combine; season with kosher salt. Step 5Pour peanut oil into a medium Dutch oven or large heavy saucepan fitted with thermometer to come 3" up sides (about 8 cups). Heat over medium-high until thermometer registers 360°. Reduce heat to medium (you want to maintain the temperature). Using a spoon lightly coated in oil and working in batches of 6–8, spoon irregular amounts of batter into pot. Fry, turning often, until golden brown all over, about 4 minutes. Using a spider or slotted spoon, transfer to a rimmed baking sheet lined with paper towels to drain and immediately season with kosher salt. Repeat process with remaining batter, adjusting heat as needed to maintain temperature. Transfer pommes dauphine to a platter to serve.

item.title: Cheesy Apple Omelet
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.89
Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to. When I’m left to my own devices for dinner, there’s really only one thing I care to make: an omelet. Perhaps you’re more familiar with ordering them alongside bacon and hash browns for brunch, but the omelet is in fact ideal at the end of the day, ideally for just you. Manageably, omelets are best prepared one at a time, and ideally eaten immediately. I take a cue from diner-style omelets by using heavier fillings—this is dinner, after all!—and simply folding the set eggs in half (no need to mess around with a delicately rolled version after a long day of work.) If you have a well-seasoned carbon steel pan, this is the time to use it. Properly heated, its surface is totally nonstick, and you can use metal tools to maneuver the eggs without risk of scratching the pan. That said, nonstick works just as well. I like to use a 10” pan for a 3-egg omelet; if you only have a larger pan, it will cook more quickly (or add a fourth egg and a little extra cheese and this could easily be a meal for two.) If I feel like rounding out the meal with proper side dishes, I’ll throw together a quick green salad and maybe heat up frozen sweet potato fries in the toaster oven; but more often than not, I just slide the omelet onto a plate, swipe it with mustard, and call it a night. Read More: All I Want for Solo Dinner Is an Omelet Recipe information - Total Time 15 minutes - Yield 1 serving Ingredients 1 2 ¼ 3 ¼ ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat a 10" carbon steel pan over medium-high 1 minute. (Add a flick of water: If the droplets bead and slide around surface before evaporating, the pan is ready; if they sizzle and immediately evaporate, heat another 30 seconds and try again.) Reduce heat to medium. (Alternatively, heat a 10" nonstick pan over medium.) Cook 1 large shallot, thinly sliced, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ tsp. freshly ground pepper, and a pinch of kosher salt in pan, stirring often with a heatproof rubber spatula, until shallots are softened and deeply golden in spots and almost charred in others, 8–10 minutes. Scrape shallot onto a plate and wipe out any solids from pan. Step 2Meanwhile, beat 3 large eggs and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Step 3Add remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to same pan and swirl to coat. Add eggs and immediately stir around with spatula, tilting pan to fill empty areas, 30 seconds. (If cooking in a carbon steel pan, you can use the same whisk or fork you used to beat the eggs if you’d like.) Continue to cook, agitating eggs and occasionally shaking pan and running spatula underneath to ensure eggs aren’t sticking, until surface of eggs looks somewhat set but still slightly shiny, about 30 seconds more. Lightly season with more pepper, then sprinkle ¼ cup coarsely grated Fontina cheese or sharp white cheddar over half of surface. Shingle ½ small crisp apple (such as Fuji or Gala), very thinly sliced, over cheese, then top with shallots. Gently run spatula underneath eggs and shake pan a bit to release, then fold empty side of eggs up and over filled side (use a larger flat spatula if you’re having trouble maneuvering omelet; it’s okay if filling isn’t completely covered). Remove pan from heat and let omelet sit 30 seconds to continue to set. Step 4Slide omelet out onto a plate and serve with Dijon mustard if desired.

item.title: Best Dutch Ovens for Braising, Baking, and Beyond (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.38
Over the past few decades, I'd argue that the Dutch oven has eclipsed the stand mixer as the most crucial piece of kitchen equipment for making a kitchen feel like a home kitchen. Is it because they're heavy and expensive? It it because couples always put them on their wedding registries? Is it because you can make soup in them and soup is comforting and feels homey and there's something to that? Not entirely sure. I can say though, that setting down one of these colorful, enameled hunks of cast iron onto a stove is akin to dropping an anchor. By committing to making a Sunday braise in a Dutch oven you're saying, “ This is my home, and because it's my home, I'm gonna make the entire place, and my clothes, smell like ragú.” But which to buy? I've spent years and years thinking about this, because the question of what the best Dutch oven is, is a question that requires a lot of caveats and asterisks. Yes, there are certainly some design and quality metrics that help distinguish the Staubs and Le Creusets from Amazon Basics, but the bottom line is: Every Dutch oven on the market will deliver an extremely similar cooking performance. What it all comes down to is quality and design. Our top picks - The best Dutch oven overall: Le Creuset Signature Round 5.5-Quart Dutch Oven - The other best Dutch oven: Staub 5.5-Quart Cocotte - The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Cheap Dutch ovens work just fine, but their affordability comes at the cost of quality control. Budget Dutch ovens consistently feature manufacturer defects, chipping, and thinner enamel layers that can lead to accelerated wear and rusting. As for design, while there are some practical advantages that some have over others, a lot of it comes down to subjective preferences. There are two people who have worked on this test over the years and we have vehemently disagreed with each other over the top spot, though, to be clear both of our choices are great Dutch ovens. I'll get more into the two that always tussle for the top spot, as well as the most well-designed budget picks that also come with lifetime warranties. Keep reading to learn about how I and my team have tested Dutch ovens over the years, how to keep the enamel in tip-top shape, and which brands didn’t make the short list. New in this update: I added reviews for the Crockpot, Goldilocks, and Müeller Dutch ovens, and moved Le Creuset into a clear top spot. A Beautiful, easy-to-handle Dutch oven with a light interior: Le Creuset Signature Enameled Cast-Iron 5.5-Quart Round Dutch Oven Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Relatively lightweight - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Light interior enamel will show wear more readily than dark enamel Specs Interior enamel: Light and smooth Available sizes: 2-qt., 4.5-qt., 5.5-qt., 7.25-qt., 9-qt., 13.75-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 11.6 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: We’ve been recommending Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens for as long as we’ve been recommending Dutch ovens. So if you have your heart set on one of these iconic pieces and you’re wondering whether it’s still a wise investment, the answer is a resounding yes. Le Creuset’s smooth, sand-colored interior enamel produced a beautiful, even sear—and the light enamel makes it easy to keep an eye on browning and fond development. Le Creuset’s 5.5-quart Dutch oven also weighs about a pound less than Staub’s with thin loop handles that are easy to grip with or without oven mitts. The lighter weight comes courtesy of noticeably thinner cast iron, but it’s still thick enough to offer wonderful heat retention. Le Creuset Dutch ovens typically have a wider cooking surface and lower sides. This means more space for searing meats for braising—an essential Dutch oven task. A few years ago Le Creuset began offering metal knobs on its Dutch ovens, which was a meaningful upgrade as the old phenolic knobs could melt if you tried to do something like use your Dutch oven to bake bread at 450℉, it would melt. Then there is the manufacturing quality. Le Creuset is a century-old French brand, and though some of its cookware and tableware is now made in other countries, all of the enameled cast-iron cookware—including the Dutch ovens—is still made in the original manufacturing facility in Fresnoy-le-Grand, France. And while we know from experience with inherited pieces that the chip-resistant enamel can last a lifetime (with proper care, of course), Le Creuset Dutch ovens do come with a limited lifetime warranty. What I’d leave: When covered at a boil, the Le Creuset may sputter at the edges a little. If you choose a Dutch oven with light-colored interior enamel, and cook in it often, you should expect some gradual discoloration. If you’re intent on keeping it pristine, you may jeopardize the lifespan of the enamel. Abrasive cleaners can wear the seal off of it and lead to even more staining. A gorgeous, top-notch Dutch oven with a dark interior: Staub Round Cocotte Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Dark, textured cooking surface browns quicker and hides stains - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Lint from some dish towels can catch on interior enamel Specs Interior enamel: Dark and textured Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 12.57 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: In terms of craftsmanship and price, Staub’s Dutch oven, which the brand calls a “cocotte,” is in no ways inferior to the Le Creuset. Both are premium enameled cast-iron round Dutch ovens with high-quality chip-resistant enamel, and both heat and sear evenly. Interior enamel is a matter of preference, and the Bon Appétit staff is divided on this matter. The Staub's dark, textured enamel interior does absorb more thermal energy which is helpful for producing an intense sear. The enamel also also has a rougher surface texture, which Staub claims helps distribute fat beneath ingredients to encourage browning and an easier release. While there is some truth to this, the relationship between surface texture and food sticking isn't cut and dry. Many other variables, such as temperature, time, fat volume, technique, and the type of food, have an impact as well. As Robert J. Macfarlane, a materials scientist at MIT pointed out to me, surface texture can increase surface area, which combined with poor technique and inadequate oil can actually make sticking worse. All of that to say: This Dutch oven produces a great sear, but the added benefits of Staub's dark textured enamel aren't significant enough to champion over classic light enamel. One thing that is for sure though—the dark interior won’t show discoloration like a light one will. Looking beyond the enamel, the Staub's lid is well-designed, preventing liquid sputters when shut at a boil. The bumps underneath are supposed to distribute condensation, though we've never observed a difference in the end product between Dutch ovens with bumpy lids and Dutch ovens without. I prefer the flat lid over a curved one, as you can invert the lid and stack the Dutch oven for easy storage. Yes, it’s pricey, but with proper care it will be something your kids fight over once you're gone. Like Le Creuset, Staub is a French cookware brand (now owned by Zwilling), its Dutch ovens are still manufactured in France, and they maintain an exceedingly high bar for what ends up on store shelves. One of the big reasons for the price is the high volume of units they reject along the assembly line (cast-iron is a material that evades easy refinement). This scrutiny means that your Dutch oven will almost certainly be free of surface defects and chips. If you do find any, definitely reach out to them, as Staub also offers a limited lifetime warranty on its enameled cast iron. What I'd leave: The dark enamel makes it a bit harder to monitor browning, which might be intimidating for greener cooks. Also, the Staub is heavier than the Le Creuset and the handles are slightly smaller, but it's a pretty negligible distinction if you're trying to champion one excellent product over the other. The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Pros and cons Pros: - Generous surface area - Large handles - Affordable - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Too young a brand to judge longevity Specs Interior enamel: White Available sizes: 6 qt Weight (5.5-qt. size): 13.7 lb. Multiple color options: Blue, red, green. Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Lifetime warranty What I loved: As a relative newcomer to the cookware space, Goldilocks has consistently produced well-made, affordable cookware.
