It's clear that they pay attention to design, and that is evident in their Dutch oven. This Dutch oven was a pleasure to cook with, and had no apparent defects in design or performance. The design prioritizes width over height, something we appreciate for searing and browning meat before a braise. In fact is one of the widest round Dutch ovens relative to its height and volume. But rest assured it fits fine over standard burners. Its handles are also nice and large, making them easy to grab and maneuver, even with thick oven mitts on. It is still more expensive than some of the better known and more popular cheaper models made by Amazon and Lodge, and we can't yet speak to the longterm longevity of the enamel coating since this is still a newer product. However, I'd argue that the physical dimensions themselves also make this a superior choice to previous budget picks. What I'd leave: Again, I can't yet speak toward longevity yet so we will update this test in the future. Beyond that, it is slightly heavier than the winners, and also is extremely limited in size and color offerings. However, 6 quarts is the median ideal size for a Dutch oven. How we tested Dutch ovens Steam test We also tested the lids by conducting steam tests and filling each one about halfway with water that we brought to a rolling boil in order to see if the lid would prevent spattering. Ideally, the lid will release some steam at such high temperatures, but contain water in its scalding, liquid form. Form evaluation Most importantly, we evaluated the physical dimensions of each Dutch oven: how much they weigh relative to their size, how large their handles are, and their height-to-width ratio. We also do longterm testing on winning models to evaluate issues with wear and longevity. Both the Test Kitchen team and the product reviews team use Dutch ovens on a regular basis, which helps inform our testing as well. What we looked for in a Dutch oven Durable enamel Without the kind of serious long-term testing we’re able to do with the Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens many of us have owned for years, it’s hard to tell just how durable a Dutch oven’s porcelain enamel will be. But sometimes really cheap enamel will have small chips or pinholes right out of the box. You can also look at customer reviews; most will have at least a few reporting enamel damage. If it’s a small percentage of reviews, it’s likely a manufacturing defect, but if a disproportionate amount of reviewers complain about chipped or damaged enamel, it’s likely a durability issue. Comfortable handles Even when they’re empty, Dutch ovens are pretty heavy—hell, the lids alone are heavy—so the handles should be comfortable to hold with your bare hands. They should also be easy enough to hold or grip while wearing oven mitts. Large surface area A larger cooking surface relative to the total liquid volume means more space for browning meat and other ingredients with less risk of crowding, which can cause things to steam rather than brown. If you remember Julia Child's advice for making boeuf bourguignon, do not crowd the meat! A tight-fitting lid A Dutch oven’s lid should fit snugly on the pot and not rattle around when you’re carrying it or boiling water in it. That said, it’s normal for some steam to escape from even a heavy tight-fitting lid when water inside is at a rolling boil. A long warranty Enameled cast iron, in theory, is very durable, and the very best Dutch ovens are heirloom-quality pieces that will last at least a lifetime with proper care. If a manufacturer offers a very short warranty on their enameled cast-iron cookware, it could (though may not always) indicate a lower-quality product. Other Dutch ovens we liked Made In fits in the middle tier here, as it is a great Dutch oven made with a higher standard of quality than budget models. It is heavier than both Staub and Le Creuset, and the handles are divisive among staff. Some like the wide flat handles for holding when full, while others find there to be not as much knuckle clearance, making them more challenging to grasp completely with oven mitts on. This is a good Dutch oven that had a brief run as our budget pick (before Goldilocks became available), as it comes with a limited lifetime warranty not typical for budget Dutch ovens. It performs well, and was lighter than other budget Dutch ovens. The drawback is that the handles are slimmer than I'd like for easy gripping. Amazon Basics’ kitchen gear is really hit or miss, but the Amazon Basics Dutch oven is surprisingly good—especially for something with such an accessible price tag. This was also a former budget pick. Performance wise it gets the job done. Like the Zulay, it has narrow handles. It’s a good option for home cooks on a budget. However, unlike the Zulay Dutch oven, which has a lifetime warranty, this one comes with a one-year warranty, so inspect it for defects as soon as its out of the box. Overall, our testers were impressed with this sleek, stylish 5.5-quart dutch oven from DTC lifestyle brand Kana. The smooth, light interior enamel produced an even sear on both meat and vegetables, and we didn’t experience any cold spots or notice any chips in the enamel out of the box (some customer reviews have complained of chipped enamel). It’s about a pound lighter than the comparably sized Le Creuset, which means it can heat up and cool down a bit quicker, but the thinner cast iron won't retain heat quite as well. If you want a budget pot and like the modern look (or you really want a moderately priced Dutch oven with a gold-toned knob), the Milo by Kana is a good choice. Dutch ovens we don’t recommend This large, oval Dutch oven from Great Jones is gorgeous. We love the color options, and for a 6.75-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven from a popular brand, the sub-$200 price tag is nice too. But, with only one rather large size and the oval shape, it’s not the best option for everyday use—or for induction cooktops with round “burners.” But it’s the perfect size for roasting a whole chicken and large cuts of meat, and the large loop handles are easy to grab with or without oven mitts. Great Jones does offer a smaller round Dutch oven, the Dutch Baby but at 3.5 quarts it’s on the small side of the Dutch oven sweet spot. Tramontina’s relatively affordable stainless-steel cookware is often compared to All-Clad, so we had high hopes for the Brazilian brand’s 5.5-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven too. Out of the box, we liked the tall sides (great for deep-frying), but unfortunately it just didn't perform well in our testing. Our testers noticed a persistent cold spot that resulted in uneven cooking—and food sticking to the smooth, light interior enamel. We like Cuisinart’s enameled cast-iron skillet, but the Dutch oven is disappointing. Unlike the skillet, which has a dark, textured interior enamel, the Dutch oven has a smooth, light interior that didn’t perform well in our sear test. We also found multiple cold spots even when it was fully preheated, which produced pork that was unevenly cooked. In addition to its popular pottery and ceramic tableware, English brand Denby offers a small selection of enameled cast-iron cookware, including several Dutch ovens—which it calls “casseroles.” They’re moderately priced compared to similarly sized Dutch ovens from other well-known brands. When we tested the round 5.5-quart (listed as a 26-cm size) the performance was adequate, but the handles were small and hard to grab, especially when it was hot. And overall, nothing about it wowed us. But if you like the look and it’s within your budget—and you don’t mind the small handles—you may be happy with the Denby Dutch oven. We love a lot of KitchenAid gear (hello, gorgeous stand mixer!) but in general, we haven’t been that impressed with the brand’s cookware, and that trend continued with the enameled cast-iron Dutch oven didn’t impress us—though we were certainly impressed with its heft. The 6-quart Dutch oven weighs 20 pounds, empty! That’s the only size available, and it only comes in two colors too. The first time we tested Misen’s Dutch oven, we really liked it. It’s large and deep, which is great for deep-frying, and it made a pretty good stockpot too. But then Misen changed some design elements—most notably it did away with the traditional Dutch oven lid and instead offers the choice of either a silicone option or an enameled cast-iron grill pan that can double as a lid (a traditional lid is available on the larger 7-quart model, which, as we've said, is bigger than most people need). Both lid alternatives made this less functional and appealing than it was when it had a traditional enameled cast-iron lid with a metal knob. Also: Our testers have experienced some minimal enamel chipping with long-term use. This 4-quart Dutch oven from Vermicular comes as-is or alongside Vermicular’s Musui-Kamado, a stand-alone induction heating element that holds the pot, sort of like a very high-end, precise slow cooker. The interior enamel is an off-white color and minimally textured, though not as textured as the dark interior enamel of the Staub. The rim is unfinished to provide a “precision seal.” However, this makes it susceptible to rust, and during testing, did not do a better job at sealing in moisture than the Le Creuset or Staub, which do have an enamel coating around the rim. The side handles on the lid were also unnecessary, and made it difficult to grab, especially when removing it from the oven. This is one of the few cast-iron Dutch ovens we've tried without an enamel coating. While this is a beautiful piece of cookware, it’s the sort of thing that only really makes sense for dedicated cast-iron enthusiasts who love to care for and maintenance their cookware. We’ve found that developing a seasoning on this is quite challenging, and that the type of cooking we generally employ our Dutch ovens for (soups, braises, stews) tends to hinder the process. Smithey recommends a just-cook-with-it method for developing the seasoning, and the brand also claims that it’s fine to use when making soups or acidic braises. However, we found that tomato sauce stripped the seasoning and developed a metallic taste. A really robust seasoning would potentially withstand this, but you’d need to do several rounds of seasoning on your own, and with a big pot like this, that isn’t an easy task. We also found that the cast-iron lid is prone to rust spots. This is because (if you’re primarily cooking on the stovetop with your Dutch oven) the lid never gets hot enough as has no direct contact with fat, which means that it will not develop a seasoning as you cook with it. This is a problem especially because moisture condenses on the interior of the lid while cooking. All in all, having an uncoated Dutch oven is a labor of love. If you do a lot of deep-frying, or cooking on open fires, or you just really like to season cast iron as a hobby, you might be able to tame this beast. If you’re just looking for a regular-shmegular Dutch oven, we’d advise against it. Over the years, we've have tested both Lodge Essentials Dutch ovens and Lodge USA Enamel Dutch ovens, the latter of which is made in a newer manufacturing facility in North America. Unfortunately, not all Lodge cookware is created equally, and even though the USA Enamel line is clearly a much higher quality than the Lodge Essentials enameled cast iron, customers have complained about chipping with both. On the other hand, a colleague has been using a Dutch oven from the USA Enamel line for more than a year and hasn’t experienced any chipping. The issue here seems to be inconsistency in quality, but we’ll continue to use these Dutch ovens to see if the newer lines prove to be more durable. FAQ What size Dutch oven should I get? The size you get really depends on what you’ll use it for—if you’re cooking every night for a family of six, a 7-quart Dutch oven will make sense. But for most home cooks (and anyone with four or fewer people in their house), the Dutch oven sweet spot size is 5.5 or 6 quarts. It’s big enough to accommodate a pot roast or a whole chicken, but not too big for a loaf of sourdough if you’re the bread-baking type. It’s also a good size for deep-frying and gives you plenty of room for tossing four servings of pasta without overcrowding the pan. What material is a Dutch oven made of? Dutch ovens can be made of various types of metal or ceramic, and they can be enamel-coated or uncoated. For example, Emile Henry makes an enameled clay ceramic Dutch oven and Dansk makes an enameled carbon-steel Dutch oven (er, “casserole”). You can even get high-quality raw cast-iron Dutch ovens from brands like Smithey and Lancaster, but they require seasoning and more maintenance than enameled cast iron. However, its enameled cast-iron Dutch ovens that are ubiquitous. The cast iron offers incredible heat retention and is compatible with gas, electric, and induction cooktops while the durable porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion caused by water as well as acidic foods like tomatoes. The enamel also eliminates the need for seasoning. Are Dutch ovens nonstick? One of the biggest misconceptions about this kind of cookware is that the cooking surface is supposed to be nonstick. It’s not. Porcelain enamel may look like a ceramic nonstick coating, and it’s far easier to clean and care for than raw cast iron, but it is not a nonstick surface. Its purpose is to protect the cast iron underneath. That said, with the right temperature and enough butter or oil, food releases from enamel pretty easily. How do I protect my Dutch oven from damage? Enameled cast iron can withstand high heat as well as freezing temperatures, but you do want to avoid thermal shock to your Dutch oven. For example: Don’t take it from the fridge and put it straight over high heat on your stovetop. And when you’re preheating it, do it slowly over low to medium heat. Sudden temperature changes can cause the enamel to chip and in some cases damage the cast iron itself (up to and including actually cracking it), and this kind of damage will often be grounds for the manufacturer to void the warranty. Why shouldn’t I use metal utensils in my Dutch oven? Though some user manuals say metal utensils are fine in their enameled cast-iron cookware, it’s best to use wood or silicone. Metal utensils can, over time, damage the protective enamel, especially if you use them in a hot pot. Even minor, cosmetic scratch marks from metal utensils can be an issue because you may be tempted to buff them out with an abrasive cleaner. Doing that once or twice might not cause any major damage, but repeated use of abrasive cleaners will absolutely erode the top layer of the porcelain enamel and eventually make it porous and prone to much worse staining. What’s the deal with braising divots? Many Dutch oven lids are pocked with divots, which supposedly help to evenly distribute moisture when braising—in theory, kind of basting the meat inside the closed pot. That said, in many years of testing, we haven’t seen any clear evidence of this actually happening. How should I clean a Dutch oven? Enameled cast-iron cookware is incredibly durable because the porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion. And unlike traditional and ceramic nonstick cookware, a high-quality enamel coating can last forever if you take good care of it—which, sorry to say, means never putting it in the dishwasher. While it’s true that some enameled cast-iron pieces, including Le Creuset’s colorful Dutch ovens, are marketed as dishwasher-safe, if you read the manual, you’ll learn that most manufacturers generally recommend hand-washing. That’s because over time, harsh dishwasher detergents can erode the enamel, making it more porous, which can lead to staining and stuck-on food.

item.title: Where to Stay in Great Smoky Mountains National Park for Mountain Views and Fall Foliage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.17
Frequently named the most visited national park in the US, Great Smoky Mountains have universal appeal—travelers come from all over the country (and the world) to enjoy the natural beauty of this part of North Carolina and Tennessee. Hikers, anglers, photographers, road-trippers, birders, families, and thrill-seekers can all find reasons to make the trek. Whether you want to see the namesake fog blanketing the peaks—many of which tower well over 6,000 feet—breathe in the crisp air, or glimpse the famous wildflowers and fall foliage, there’s plenty to do, and some excellent places to spend the night once you get here. From the historic LeConte Lodge—the only lodging within the park’s boundaries—with its hard-to-come-by reservations and hike-in access to some of the South’s most luxurious hotels—Blackberry Farm and The Swag are legendary in the hospitality world—there’s something for every type of traveler. Whether it’s your first time exploring the park or you’re planning a return trip, you have options for where to set up your base camp. You can opt for a rustic cabin rental, a kid-friendly resort, or a stylish glamping site depending on your mood. Read on for some of the best places to stay near Great Smoky Mountains National Park for your next nature-filled adventure. How to plan a trip to Great Smoky Mountains National Park How do you get to Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Great Smoky Mountains National Park sits along the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. If you’re flying into the area, McGhee Tyson Airport (TYS) in Knoxville, Tennessee, and Asheville Regional Airport (AVL) are among the most convenient options. From TYS, it’s a 30- and 60-minute drive, respectively, to the park’s main entrances in Townsend and Gatlinburg, Tennessee. The drive from AVL to the entrance in Cherokee, North Carolina, will take you a little over an hour. When is the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Undoubtedly, the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park is in the fall. If you time it right—keep an eye on the foliage reports—you’ll witness the splendor of all the reds, oranges, and yellows. The changing colors typically start to appear in late September, and they peak between mid-October and mid-to-early November, depending on the weather and elevation. This time of year also tends to be the busiest season in the park, so keep that in mind when you’re planning a trip (book early and visit mid-week if possible). How long should you visit the Great Smoky Mountains? Because of the size and plethora of things to do within the park, you’ll want to plan for multiple days of exploration—I’d recommend at least three. That way, you can drive the scenic loops, complete a few hikes, and check off all the major sites without rushing. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

To the chagrin of budget travelers everywhere, airfares have continued to climb to new highs throughout 2026. In July 2026, for example, average airfares were nearly 26% more expensive than in July 2025, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics—a significant hit to travelers’ wallets. And unfortunately, due to a complex web of geopolitical and economic factors, prices aren’t expected to drop anytime soon. Historically, fall is the time of year when airfares cool off, but this year, shoulder season deals are harder than ever to find. In fact, airfares for fall are trending about 2% higher compared to summer prices, according to Expedia. Average airfares this autumn for domestic flights range from about $150 to $400 roundtrip, according to data emailed from Going. On international routes, flights to Europe are as high as $800 roundtrip, and airfares to the Caribbean are reaching up to $500. However, while it might sound hopeless to try to scour booking sites for a good deal, rest assured there are tried-and-true strategies that travelers can use for finding reasonably priced fares through the end of the year. “Flexibility is key—both with dates and destination—to find affordable flights this fall,” says Jennifer Yellin, managing editor of Points Path, which shows travelers flight search results priced in points and miles. Here are our top tips for unlocking affordable airfares through the end of the year. Target an airline and airport known for deals Your choice of carrier, airport of origin, and destination can all play a major part in the final cost of your airfare. Aim to fly into or out of an airport that has a strong track record of offering affordable flights. Going analyzed its 2026 flight deal data to find the US airports that have offered the most affordable departing flights so far in 2026. It found the best airports for cheap domestic flights were Denver (DEN), with 150 departing flight deals that cost an average of $219; New Orleans (MSY), which had 166 deals that were about $228; and Orlando (MCO), which offered 146 deals at an average of $211. Other top airports for domestic deals were Fort-Lauderdale (FLL), Los Angeles (LAX), Charleston (CHS), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Tampa (TPA), Portland (PDX), and Las Vegas (LAS). The best US airports for international flight deals were Boston (BOS), with 415 deals at about $451 roundtrip; New York (JFK), which has seen 404 international deals so far this year at an average of $445; and Newark (EWR), which has had 333 international deals for about $450 each. Other top airports for international deals included Chicago (ORD), Los Angeles (LAX), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Orlando (MCO), Miami (MIA), Washington Dulles (IAD), and Austin (AUS). Departing from one of these airports can add up to significant savings. If it’s feasible, consider driving or taking a train to one of these to score discounted airfare for your next big trip. Some airlines offer a greater number of deals, too. Going found that American Airlines offers the most domestic deals (646 so far in 2026), and United offers the most international deals (1,850 and counting this year). Looking to these carriers first could help uncover the most affordable fare quickly. Carefully time your trip The timing of your vacation can make all the difference in finding affordable airfare. Shoulder season is traditionally an off-peak stretch with added savings for travelers, but with off-season deals shrinking, fliers need to get even more specific with timing. Specifically, consider pushing back your fall getaway as late on the calendar as possible, and just before hitting the start of the winter holidays. “Summer demand has spilled into fall,” according to Expedia’s fall travel outlook report. Pushing trips later into October or the first week of November could be a sweet spot for fare savings. In most years, the week of Thanksgiving is usually a guaranteed window for international flight deals from the US because domestic travel soars at this time. But 2026 has put a bit of wrench in that convention, too. International flights around Thanksgiving this year are averaging $1,096 roundtrip, according to Going. It’s still the more affordable window compared to December, when the average international fare swells up to $1,695. Travelers on the hunt for an international deal should plan to fly on the Thanksgiving holiday itself to save up to 25% and plan to book their flights by early October, per Going’s guidance. Using search tools that allow you to look over a stretch of several days to find the cheapest fare, like Google Flights, also helps. “You might find shifting your dates by a date or two in either direction can save you a significant amount of money,” Yellin says. As a general rule of thumb, Saturdays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays tend to be the most affordable days of the week to fly, according to data from Expedia and Going. Leverage your points and miles Put those hard-earned frequent flier miles and credit card points to work for you to unlock airfares. It’s possible to compare the best airfare deal across credit cards and loyalty programs if you use the right search tool. Points Path, for one, plugs into Google Flights to help travelers compare prices. The tool will “tell you if using cash or points is a better deal, without having to search multiple airline websites individually,” Yellin says. Target your flight search to departure airports that regularly offer the greatest number of points and miles deals. In the US those include: New York (JFK), Boston (BOS), Los Angeles (LAX), Chicago (ORD), Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), Going says. Where to find specific deals this shoulder season Going’s intel shows that a handful of destinations have a better chance of offering flight deals this fall. For international trips “Portugal, Spain, Italy, Greece, the ABC islands, and Scandinavia are seeing nice shoulder season fare dips,” according to Anna LaBrie, Going’s senior PR manager. “Japan and Southeast Asia are worth watching too, along with Mexico, outside of Día de Muertos.” On the domestic side, “Hawaii, Florida, Phoenix, the Pacific Northwest, Atlanta, the Carolinas, and San Diego are showing softer prices this fall," LaBrie says, noting that travelers should avoid ski towns like Jackson Hole and Aspen, where airfares are beginning to spike. Recent fall fare deals from Going include Boston to Madrid for $517 roundtrip—a 49% discount—and Los Angeles to Tokyo for $613 roundtrip, which is 48% cheaper than average. That’s encouraging evidence that there are good flight deals to uncover this fall, if you know the right tactics for finding them.

item.title: The Best Beaches in Miami, From Nature Reserves to Sceney Beach Clubs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.21
Miami has always known how to turn a day at the beach into a scene. This rings especially true along the sandy patches belonging to Miami Beach’s top hotels, which have been upping the stakes with cushy amenities and experiences designed to warrant hefty membership fees for locals—and generate enough revenue to keep their beach clubs at the top of their game. The good news for travelers? Book a room at such hotels—think CNT Triple Crown Winners 1 Hotel South Beach and Faena Miami Beach or the new and improved Delano Miami Beach—and many of those same privileges typically extend to hotel guests, no membership required (though nightly rates will cost ya!). Of course, you don’t need a hotel key, annual dues, or an impending inheritance to experience Miami’s best beaches. Miles of public shoreline remain gloriously democratic, whether you want to join the beautiful bodies and colorful lifeguard stands of South Beach, bike beneath the palms of Key Biscayne, kayak through mangroves at Oleta River State Park, or ditch your swimsuit altogether at liberating, clothing-optional Haulover Beach. Consider these 18 picks less a ranking of sand and more a guide to Miami’s many ways of doing the beach, popular year-round thanks to a balmy climate that makes summer feel seemingly endless. item.title: The Best Fall Foliage in the USA: A Guide to Where to Go This Autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.82
It’s a rare occasion that vast swaths of the United States experience a season in a similar way—but the sepia-toned mosaic of fall foliage soon to sprawl across the country in a few short weeks proves that fall is the one exception to that rule. Starting as early as late September and extending well into November, you can expect to find some combination of red, gold, yellow, and orange bathing the trees from coast to coast. But anyone well-versed in leaf-peeping—or the colloquial nickname given to any tourist with a proclivity for fall foliage gazing—knows that some states and regions have more colorful and sweeping offerings than others. So for any looking to leaf-peep-maxx this upcoming fall, we took the liberty of rounding up the states, parks, and areas from across the country where you can expect to find the most vibrant fall tableaus come this October. Blue Ridge Mountains, North Georgia Way down on the south of the eastern shore you’ll find a range of mountains absolutely awash for fall. The Blue Ridge Mountain region of North Georgia makes up a smaller enclave of the greater Appalachian Mountains—and though you can’t go wrong with any stop along the Appalachian Trail when it comes to fall foliage, this little corner right on the border between Georgia and Tennessee is especially ideal for the changing seasons. The Southern climate makes things a little milder, without having to sacrifice the fall grandeur. The area skews more towards nature aficionados, with plenty of nature paths and mountain trails to climb. One particular favorite includes Brasstown Bald, where you can catch the best view of the leaves in peak color. Where to stay in the Blue Ridge Mountains: - A charming Victorian B&B: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast - A peaceful mountain escape: The Copperhead Lodge The Berkshires, Massachusetts When it comes to the idyllic pastoral regions of New England, Massachusetts’s Berkshires are right up there with the likes of New York's Adirondacks. One look around and you can see exactly how the lush area inspired writers like Edith Wharton and artists like Norman Rockwell (and if you don’t, just take a quick trip to the Norman Rockwell Museum). Other highlights for our Berkshires guide includes shopping at stores like Fluff Alpaca, hiking up Monument Mountain’s three different trails, grabbing some coffee beans from West Stockbridge’s famous No. Six Depot, and ordering a bite off the farm-to-table menu at Prairie Whale. Pair all of that with the area’s bustling boutique hotel scene in Lenox, Massachusetts, and you’ve got one must-see stop on your Great American leaf-peeping tour. Where to stay in the Berkshires: - For an artistic flair: 33 Main - A motor-lodge-turned luxury hotel: Life House Stowe, Vermont Nestled in the embrace of Vermont’s Green Mountains, Stowe might be known for its slopes and skiing—but it’s also one of the best places to catch a verifiable sea of fall foliage come October and November. This is your quintessential idyllic northern New England escape. While it’s had its fair share of development, there are plenty of locals who reside in the town year-round. Pre-game leaf-peeping by exploring the microbrewing scene or shopping for some top-of-the-line maple products at Shaw’s General Store. It’s also something of a hikers paradise, with absolutely no small shortage of trails for the ambitious explorers and gentler strollers alike. No matter what you choose, there’s sure to be one fantastic view. Where to stay in Stowe, Vermont: - For a hygge vibe: Field Guide - A spa-retreat: AWOL Stowe - A traditionally intimate ski lodge: Edson Hill Great Smoky Mountains, Tennessee and North Carolina The Great Smoky Mountains that trail up the border between Tennessee and North Carolina earned their name from the natural, gauzy fog that often drapes across the region. It gives the area an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality during any time of year. Add in a mosaic of fall foliage and it's no wonder why this spot is home to some of the best fall foliage in the USA. See the sights from the famous Cades Cove loop or hike the Laurel Falls Trail or any of the many paths along the mountains. You’ll also find a range of different lodging options in the area—including glamping experiences, cabins, farms, and more. Where to stay in the Great Smoky Mountains: - An irreverent farm getaway: Blackberry Farm - A sprawling ranch: Cataloochee Ranch - A one-of-a-kind glamping stay: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains Aspen, Colorado Aspen is one of those cold weather destinations that’s spoken of with an undeniable air of prestige—the same way you would speak of Lake Como in the spring, or the French Riviera in summer. Like Stowe, it’s most famous for its skiing, but it’s got its fair share of foliage to show off around fall. Especially ideal for those who have a taste for the finer things in life, Aspen’s also a prime luxury shopping destination. Shop high end designer brands like Prada or Gucci, and grab a chic cowboy hat from Kemo Sabe. And you can’t forget the decadent fare available at eateries like Bosq, White House Tavern, Matsushia, and more. Where to stay in Aspen, Colorado: - An Aspen mainstay: Hotel Jerome Sun Valley, Idaho Another skiing staple, Sun Valley has long charmed celebrities and nature-lovers alike. It’s renowned for its skiing but offers golden escape during the shoulder season of fall. Sun Valley’s especially great for any leaf peepers who happen to also be fans of Ernest Hemingway. The famous Lost Generation author loved the region and even finished his book For Whom The Bell Tolls in the Sun Valley Resort’s suite 206. Hemingway’s admiration of and attachment to the area is immortalized with with a memorial and free audio walking tour. Where to stay in Sun Valley, Idaho: - A historic ski resort: Sun Valley Resort - For a laidback lodging: Limelight Ketchum North Cascades, Washington New England often takes the cake when it comes to fall foliage, but don’t write off the Pacific Northwest. One drive along the Cascade Loop will show that this craggy region has its own verdancy amid the snow dusted mountains. Often referred to as the American Alps, there are plenty of peaks and summits to see the leaves—such as the Washington Pass overlooking the Liberty Bell Mountain—while hiking trails like the Maple Pass Loop and Blue Lake offer some of the best opportunities for leaf-peeping. Where to stay in North Cascades, Washington: - A floating cabin: Ross Lake Resort Laurel Hill, Pennsylvania There are plenty of trails and state parks you can take advantage of to gaze at the Pennsylvania foliage. There’s Mount Davis, Ohiopyle State Park, Laurel Hill state park, and so much more. You really can’t go wrong with any of them. But we’d recommend conducting your leaf peeping from inside, specifically inside one of famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s most well-known works. Dubbed Fallingwater, this quintessentially mid-century modern structure sits atop a waterfall and is entirely ensconced in a forest of trees—making its airy interiors the ideal framing for the lush colors of fall. Where to stay in Laurel Highlands Pennsylvania: - A sprawling estate: Nemacolin Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire Rounding off the New England stops, this nature reserve is nestled in the middle of New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest. Here, you’ll find parts of the larger Appalachian Trail, as well as hikes up well-known peaks like Artist Bluff—which afford panoramic views of the area’s famous Echo Lake. The body of water sits at the base of Cannon Mountain and perfectly reflects the prism of color around it, even more so when those colors are the rich reds, golds, yellows, and oranges of fall. Where to stay in Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire: - A mansion inn: The Franconia Inn Adirondacks, New York You just need to watch one episode of Gilmore Girls to know that New England is one of the top best places to see fall foliage, and the Adirondacks is one of the region’s best fall exports. Located just about four hours outside of New York City, this mountain area encompasses much of New York’s storied “upstate” region—where people escape from the city to ensconce themselves in the privacy of cozy cabins, lake houses, and more. Here, you’ll find over 3,000 lakes and ponds—such as the famous Lake Placid—and the Adirondack High Peaks. Grab a quick drink at Raquette River Brewing or fill up on French-Canadian comfort dishes at Woodshed on Park, before heading out to take in the vivid leaves. Where to stay in the Adirondacks: - For a luxurious lake island resort: The Sagamore Resort - A rustic log cabin experience: The Point - A Lake Placid classic: Great Adirondack Hotel Columbia River Gorge, Northern Oregon Just above California and below other fall foliage fave Washington, the Northern Oregon region similarly offers plenty of mystically foggy places to peep some leaves. What’s even better is you get the best of both worlds with forests and beaches colliding to make up this scenic coast. Travel through the Columbia River Gorge to see all the leaves, then take a road trip out to Cannon Beach to top the adventure off. Where to stay in Northern Oregon: - A water-front property: Cannery Pier Hotel & Spa Shenandoah National Park, Virginia Just off the Blue Ridge Parkway, and not too far from the border of West Virginia, Shenandoah National Park extends about 197,439 acres across Virginia’s Blue Ridge region. It’s got breathtaking views and nature, making it ideal to catch some of the best fall foliage in the USA. After all, there's a reason we named it one of the best national parks to enjoy during the fall. Shenandoah is mostly visited for hiking, with over 500 miles of trails—many of which you can find along the area’s Skyline Drive—that offer ample opportunity to take in nature, no matter the time of year.

item.title: The Most Beautiful Italian Coastal Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
Most first-time visitors to Italy tend to concentrate on cities like Rome, Florence, and Venice, but if you ask us, off-the-beaten-path Italian coastal towns are some of the most beautiful places in the country. After all, Italy has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, and some of the country’s coastal settlements predate the Roman Empire. From Liguria all the way down to Calabria, not to mention the Adriatic Coast and the islands, there are charming seaside villages that offer a wide variety of experiences. You might want the glamour of world-famous resort towns like Portofino, Capri, and Taormina, where your dolce vita fantasies can come to life. Or perhaps you’d prefer more under-the-radar towns like Maratea and Carloforte, where you can get an authentic taste of local life. In Italy, most coastal towns come alive in the summer, when visitors from around the world hit the beaches. If you want to avoid the crowds, plan to visit coastal towns in the off-season, but keep in mind that some of them all but shut down in the winter. Spring and fall are usually a good compromise. Read on to learn about 25 of the best Italian coastal towns, with Condé Nast Traveler-approved recommendations of where to stay. item.title: Asanas at Sea? The Best Places for Yoga Around the World Are Also the Most Unconventional
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
The best places for yoga are at once picturesque and contemplative, whether it be pranayama in Ladakh’s austere landscape, dhanurasana in the thick of Thailand’s jungles, or shavasana beside an Alpine lake in New Zealand. These experiences offer as much external peace as they do internal, and even long after the session and trip have ended, it's those stirring, outdoor moments that endure. They feel like they’ve stopped time and are worth going out of the way for—planned or spontaneous. And what's better than practicing your asanas in a phenomenal natural setting? With these 10 best places for yoga, grab your go-to mat and embrace your inner yogini. Lux* South Ari Atoll, Maldives The middle of the Indian Ocean is possibly the most unique spot one can find to do yoga. Practice asanas while sailing on a traditional wooden dhow at this Maldivian resort. Lux* South Ari Atoll organizes this cruise at golden hour with an instructor guiding you on Tibetan Sound Bowl therapy, breathwork, and yoga. Sip on a refreshing drink, inhale a mood-enhancing oil blend, and float on the waves as you meditate and feel your mind reset. The Kyagar, Nubra Valley, India This boutique hotel is located on the ancient Silk Route in Ladakh’s stunning but stark landscape. Sitting on the sandy banks of the Siachen River and surrounded by the icy Karakoram peaks, it has a very special location that owner Rinchen Kalon believes furthers your yoga practice. To that end, she hosts a retreat at the property every season, and when the weather permits, outdoor classes are held on a river trail surrounded by wildflowers and sea buckthorn bushes. The Kyagar's regular yoga classes are free of charge for guests and last 30 to 90 minutes. Haritha Villas and Spa, Sri Lanka This luxury villa property in Hikkaduwa has an open-air jungle yoga pavilion nestled amidst lush tropical greenery, overlooking the serene canopy of the surrounding forest. Haritha offers hour-long, private lessons in Hatha Yoga, which are apt for beginners. Guests love the serene jungle setting with sweet birdsong in the background and a gentle wind rustling through the trees. Many cite the yoga lesson as one of the most memorable parts of their stay here. Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar Resort, Oman This rocky mountain resort is one of the highest hotels in the world and has a spectacular deck which can be booked for a yoga session (based on weather and availability). Diana’s Point is a platform where Diana, Princess of Wales, once stood back in 1986 and has a breathtaking canyon view of the fabled Green Mountain. Anantara offers hatha, sarvanga, meditation, and monthly full-moon yoga classes, but this spot is not for the fainthearted, as it juts out into a valley with a steep drop-off. March to May is rose season in this region, and the entire valley below erupts into unbelievably fragrant Damask roses. The Kumaon, India The exquisitely-designed Kumaon is located in a remote part of the Himalayas, and its most magical setting for yoga is the rooftop terrace located at the highest point of the property. Views extend to the valley of the Kosi River on one side and the Binsar Forest on the other, all under the watchful gaze of the upper Himalayas, including the divine Nanda Devi peak. With reclaimed Himalayan slate as the cooling floor of the terrace, a wispy breeze scented with pine and carrying birdsong, Kumaon's yoga space feels magical. It offers traditional hatha yoga along with basic pranayama, and guests describe them as rejuvenating and peaceful. Qasr Al Sarab, Desert Resort by Anantara, Abu Dhabi Doing yoga surrounded by vast sand dunes is certainly an unusual proposition. The wellness and meditation center at Qasr Al Sarab by Anantara is nestled on the edge of the resort, a sanctuary that opens to an uninterrupted panorama of the golden Liwa Desert. Guests can practice in the midst of raw nature as the sun rises or sets; in the early morning, the desert sky turns pink and gold, while at twilight, it twinkles with stars. Yoga instruction is available year-round, and the resort also collaborates with yoga gurus specializing in yin yoga, immersive sound healing, and yoga nidra from October to April. Those looking for silence and stillness to escape a chaotic lifestyle will truly appreciate this setting. Keemala Resort and Spa, Thailand This luxury jungle resort in Phuket has a special focus on wellness with a tropical spa, healthy cuisine, and eco-friendly operations. Keemala has two outdoor yoga spaces, one intimate wedding venue nestled within the forest, and the other on a rooftop, offering scenic views. The forest yoga takes place amid lush foliage under a 300-year-old Takian tree; guests are encouraged to practice barefoot so that they can ground themselves directly to the earth for a soulful experience. The resort also has a meditation cave with a waterfall designed to help guests heighten their focus and fully immerse in the present moment. Group classes are complimentary, and private instruction is available at an additional charge. Aro Hā Wellness Retreat, New Zealand A world-famous retreat in the Southern Alps, Aro Hā is located on serene Lake Wakatipu, just 40 minutes from Queenstown. Its yoga classes take place in the Aro Hā Room, which is well known for its striking views of the alpine lake. It offers a range of hatha styles that cater to a wide range of skill level, and all classes are complimentary. Yoga is a key element of their larger program, which also includes subalpine hikes, daily massages and spa time, and a variety of wellness workshops. Jumeirah Olhahali Island, Maldives You may have done yoga on a beach, but have you ever done yoga on a private sandbank? Jumeirah Olhahali Island takes guests on a five-minute speedboat ride to reach a private sandbank at sunrise or sunset. Its Oceanic Balance Retreat is an all-encompassing yoga experience tailored to its surroundings, whether energizing at dawn or grounding at sunset. Pleasant ocean breezes, uninterrupted horizons, and the sense of pure seclusion create space for profound clarity and calm. Acro Suites, Greece Located on the cliffs of Crete, Acro Suites describes itself as a restorative retreat. Its asana wellness studios are sleekly designed with bamboo and local stone, overlooking the Aegean Sea and dramatic cliffs of Mononaftis Bay. The studios offer a variety of yoga styles, including hatha, vinyasa, yin, and yoga nidra, all guided by certified instructors. In addition to complimentary daily practices, guests can also partake in intimate couples sessions, healing circles, and sound healing journeys, each designed to deepen connection.
