item.title: In Guadalajara, Chasing Art, Fantastic Food, and the Love of a Good Time
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.91
The second day of my first trip to Guadalajara, a decade ago, began, like so many mornings in Mexico's second city do: with blazing sunshine and a blazing hangover. I'd spent the previous evening sipping agave distillates at Mezonte, a miniature plywood-clad tasting room that pours some of Mexico's most exciting spirits, and dancing clumsily at what may be the world's most perfectly named bar: Pare de Sufrir, or Stop Suffering. My inevitable headache required an antidote. And so, in the fine expiatory fashion of this famously Catholic, famously hedonistic metropolis of nearly six million, I chose sublimity. I remember heading east that morning from the café-studded streets of the Colonia Americana neighborhood, the epicenter of Guadalajara's buzzy restaurant and art scene, through the historic center, to the Hospicio Cabañas, an early-19th-century orphanage turned museum. From 1937 to 1939, the muralist José Clemente Orozco filled the Hospicio's central chapel with 57 frescoes that trace Mexico's history from colonial savagery through the brutalizing hope of industrialization. A Promethean prophet, the celebrated Man of Fire, strides across the central dome, ringed with allegorical representations of arts, crafts, and sciences: learning and labor as equal paths to enlightenment. I left reeling, almost in tears. I'd never encountered a more heartrending room. I still haven't. Since then I've returned to the city, and to Orozco's murals, at least a dozen times, and I always leave reluctantly. I've lived in Mexico City for 10 years, and while I adore my adopted home it's hard not to be seduced by Guadalajara's gorgeous weather and gorgeous people, its offhand elegance and easy pace, its languorous lunches and, perhaps above all, its commitment to the disciplines represented in Orozco's dome, which taken together are known as oficios. In actual usage, oficios, which translates to “vocations,” encompasses all the artisanal practices (ceramics and glassblowing, carpentry and bricklaying, painting and cooking) that make the city one of Latin America's most thrilling destinations. “If you want to find a particular oficio in Guadalajara, you'll find it,” said Oliver Pendragón, a young architect who I met up with on a bright Sunday in January at the entrance to the Mercado San Juan de Dios, a Brutalist public market a few steps from the Hospicio Cabañas. Immense and intimate, rigorous and rooted, with texture and drama to spare, San Juan de Dios has for years been my favorite building in Mexico, and I wanted to visit with someone who knew it well. Pendragón spent three years overseeing the restoration of a childcare center on the market's roof, part of the ambitious original 1957 design. Inside he led me past stalls packed with food, clothes, electronics, and leather goods. Dark, narrow aisles opened onto leafy patios and soaring atria crowned with voluptuous canopies of cast concrete. Founded in 1542 and morphing into a commercial capital for western Mexico, Guadalajara was, for much of its history, small in scale and spartan in its tastes. The relative lack of monumental architecture made it easy, as the city grew in the 1950s, to demolish huge swaths of the historic center in the name of modernization. That process yielded its share of masterworks, like the Mercado San Juan de Dios. But on the whole, Pendragón told me, “tearing down all of those historic properties was basically an atrocity. That's why we Tapatíos”—the peculiar demonym for Guadalajara's residents—“are so lacking in architectural memory.” This struck me as an odd contention in a city so enamored of its traditions. Mariachi, tequila, and the florid masculinity of charrería, Mexico's national equestrian sport, all originated in Jalisco, the state for which Guadalajara serves as capital. The muralist Orozco was born in Jalisco. So were architect Luis Barragán, the author Juan Rulfo (his novel Pedro Páramo is to Mexican literature what The Great Gatsby is to American), and Vicente Fernández, the singer and film star who for decades embodied a chivalric ideal of Mexican manhood. Still, Pendragón had a point. Compared with the stage set perfection of cities like Puebla and Oaxaca, Guadalajara's historic center is gleefully chaotic, with functionalist schools abutting neoclassical chapels and midcentury parking garages looming over the rudely dismembered remains of former convents. Yet, today, few cities in Latin America have a clearer architectural identity. The morning after my visit to San Juan de Dios, I met up with Francisco Chavarría, a young design researcher, for a guided walk around La Americana, where, he told me, “Guadalajara's modern architecture was born.” On a single block Chavarría pointed out a pair of eclectic Beaux Arts villas—survivors from the area's early days as a turn-of-the-century garden suburb; the more modest of the two was restored five years ago to become the 17-room Casa Bosque Eduviges, where I stayed. Across the street a functionalist school clad in clay tiles sits next to the half-moon arches of Barragán's Casa Clavijero. With its fountains and patios, its spare ornament and spatial poetry, Clavijero epitomizes the idiosyncratic regionalist style that flourished here in the 1920s. Even today Guadalajara's most forward-looking designers continue to experiment with these deeply rooted tropes, from the lyrical modulation of their city's radiant light to the proud application of local oficios. As we walked Chavarría identified not only the neighborhood's many significant modern buildings but also modest midcentury houses and apartment blocks dignified by their subtle use of the city's raw materials. Handmade earthenware brise-soleil (an external shading technique) turned otherwise bland boxes into undulant clay tapestries, while expanses of golden limestone linked functionalist schools and modernist churches to historic structures like the Hospicio Cabañas: architectural memory as free association. “Guadalajara has this long tradition of craft, so the integration of craft into our buildings is very Tapatío,” Chavarría said. “It's a matter of identity.” I spent the rest of that afternoon in La Americana, where I saw that Tapatío genius for craft in countless shops, showrooms, galleries, and cafés. At Plataforma, a two-year-old contemporary art space, the architect Sergio Ortiz, the designer behind Casa Bosque Eduviges, had stripped away the crumbling exterior walls of an abandoned funeral home and replaced them with glass blocks. Inside he'd removed false ceilings to reveal shallow brick barrel vaults—an artisanal colonial building technique still used today—and set a central staircase into a dark cedar chamber, like a wardrobe that transports you from one luminous floor to the next. Two years after its opening, Plataforma has become “a place where you can take the pulse of what's happening in the city,” said José Noé Suro, the space's cofounder and director of Cerámica Suro, a ceramics factory that produces work for artists and architects around the globe and a nodal hub for Guadalajara's design scene. After leaving Plataforma I stopped at the workshop of designer Alejandro Julián Núñez, where, left to my own devices, I scattered a dozen hand-embroidered guayaberas across a broad wood table, as though shopping for carpets in Istanbul. I browsed textiles and photographs at Albergue Transitorio before continuing on to Occidente, a sleek showroom that offers a panorama of the city's contemporary design scene. At Lofa Ceramics, ceramist Andrea Mantecón showed me her collection of sculptural wall tiles slicked in mineral glazes, while at newly opened Musgo I perused ceramics by artists transforming their city's traditions with Japanese-inspired glazes and 3D printing. Around the corner at Chamula Hecho a Mano, narrow shelves overflowed with objects from across central and western Mexico, including burnished jugs from Tonalá, 1 of 10 municipalities now absorbed into greater Guadalajara. More than anywhere else in Guadalajara, “Tonalá is the place where craft is actually made,” said Sofía Cruz del Río Castellanos, a former director of Jalisco's state agency for the development of craft, a government office dedicated to economic advancement for artisans, when we met the following morning. If the shops in La Americana offer a thrilling window to where Tapatío design is going, then Tonalá, a 30-minute drive from the city center, is the best place to understand where it comes from. In Tonalá's bustling center, Castellanos guided me among craft workshops tucked discreetly into private homes. We visited the Valdivia family, who've produced utilitarian red-clay ceramics for generations, and the Bernabes, who specialize in the exquisite cross-hatching technique known as petatillo, before ducking into the humble atelier of Ángel Ortiz, “one of the great masters in Tonalá,” Castellanos told me. Ortiz and his son worked in companionable silence inside their earth-colored studio illuminated by a narrow blade of light that cut through their open doorway. Ortiz, his rope-veined hands remarkably steady, traced elaborate webs of vines and flowers onto a large clay rooster, while his son used a small black stone, smooth as obsidian, to burnish the surface of a water jug, a process called bruñido. “If bruñido disappears, that's the end of Tonalá,” Ortiz said. “Bruñido is the mother of all crafts.” To my mind, the true mother of all crafts is cooking, particularly in Guadalajara, which is, beyond any doubt, among the best food cities in Mexico and, by extension, the hemisphere, if not the world. Any trip here should be organized, first and foremost, around what and where you eat. Options are endless. You might start your day with chilaquiles at Comala Café or with a gordita de chicharrón, a griddled masa casing folded around minced pork, at two-year-old Nejayote. Another morning, stroll among the modernist buildings around Parque Agua Azul before paying a visit to Tortas Ahogadas Don José el de la Bicicleta, one of countless stalls and storefronts dedicated to Guadalajara's most improbable culinary delight: the famous—and, to most nonlocals, preposterous—torta ahogada, or drowned sandwich. Made by stuffing braised pork onto crusty bread and dousing the whole thing in a tomatobased sauce, tortas ahogadas are impossible to miss and impossible to eat politely. At Kobuta Co, a sunny slip of a restaurant, husband-and-wife owners Ivan Salcedo and Yukari Tanaka serve a superlative katsu sando with a side of curry for dipping—a sly wink at the city's emblematic sauce-soaked dish. Guadalajara is fundamentally a lunch city. (This past January I spent eight full hours lunching at old-school power spot La Matera on chewy riojas and thick cuts of steak.) But for dinner you could hardly do better than Xokol, where chefs Oscar Segundo and Xrysw Ruelas turn out dishes as heady as they are satisfying. On my most recent visit, I devoured buttery slices of tongue served with deep-fried masa-wrapped marrow and marveled at a single perfect tortilla folded around field greens from Segundo's grandmother's farm. New bars, which seem to multiply by the second, are no less invigorating. Some favorite new additions include Fandango, which serves an excellent Negroni, and Mecenas, known for its brainy concoctions using house-made liquors and infusions. Happily, Guadalajara's bars and restaurants, even at their most cerebral, treat cooking as no more and no less than another revered oficio. “We want to make food that inspires nostalgia,” Segundo told me over a leisurely lunch early in my trip. “When we cook we're imagining how people will feel when they eat what we're making.” I'd met Segundo and Ruelas that afternoon at their favorite seafood joint, El Desconchadero de Caguamo, located in an open lot on the northern edge of town. As we crunched through bracingly acidic tostadas de aguachile, we were joined by the restaurant's owner, Juan José Padilla, known to everyone by his adolescent nickname, El Caguamo, the word used for liter-size bottles of beer. “That's how I used to greet people: ‘Take out the caguamas!’” he told me with a laugh. “Now even my nieces and nephews call me that.” Padilla started El Desconchadero during the pandemic to sling beer and ceviche for close friends under an open sky. Today it may be the city's worst-kept secret, as it fills every weekend with large groups that linger for hours, as is Tapatíos' wont, over eternally replenishing micheladas, mountains of raw oysters, and steaming platters of chargrilled shrimp. “This place is a total disconnect,” Segundo told me as empty beer bottles accumulated on our folding metal table. “It wasn't built to rake in cash or create an ‘experience.’ It was for friends to hang out and let life go by.” In Guadalajara there's no raw material more basic, and more sacrosanct, than time. Beauty and pleasure, as any Tapatío can tell you, don't rush. Sadly, I had to. I'd made plans for that afternoon (rookie mistake), which I already pushed back twice. When I announced my departure, scudding my chair over the concrete floor, Segundo poured a final caguama and, eyebrow cocked, slid my glass across the table. It was a classic Guadalajara goodbye, which is also always an invitation to stay. Stay With its 17 quiet rooms in a charming house and small modern tower in Colonia Americana, Casa Bosque Eduviges is about as quintessentially Tapatío as it gets. Set in a 1940s house in La Americana, Casa Habita has been the gold standard for design hotels in Guadalajara since its opening in 2015. Rentals we recommend: Eat and drink At Xokol, surprising, sophisticated cooking in a theatrical black box of a room is always rooted in the extraordinary diversity of Mexican ingredients and regional culinary traditions. La Panga del Impostor is a local favorite for seafood tostadas and fish tacos on a sunny terrace in La Americana; it's easily among the best places in town for a long, leisurely lunch. Traditional Mexican breakfast dishes like chilaquiles and eggs with beans are served on a long communal table in the entrance to Yunaites, one of the city's historic public markets. Lines form early on weekends. Mezonte is a minuscule tasting room pouring small-batch agave distillates sourced with care from across western Mexico, with particularly exciting options from Jalisco and neighboring Michoacán. The fragrant smoke from the grill will guide you to street stall Tacos Don José, at the edge of La Americana, famous for its tasty tacos de birria and enfrijoladas. Shop One of Mexico's most exquisite clothing stores, Alejandro Julián Núñez displays its hand-embroidered cotton shirts, each one uniquely beautiful, on a seemingly endless wall of open shelves. The recently opened design store Musgo places a special emphasis on contemporary crafts and homewares, particularly ceramics, made by young artists and designers in Guadalajara. The showroom for Joselo Maderista, one of the city's finest carpentry studios, shares a building with contemporary art space Plataforma, which is also a great place for a streetside coffee. Chamula Hecho a Mano is an overflowing wunderkammer of witty, whimsical crafts from western and central Mexico. A sunlit showroom shared by over 20 local makers as well as an exhibition space run by the nonprofit Foro de Arquitectura, or Architecture Forum, Occidente offers a fascinating panorama of the city's vibrant contemporary design scene. Explore If you'd like to go deeper into the city's architectural history, Francisco Chavarría organizes personalized walks for up to four guests starting at $100 an hour. Guadalajara is one of our Best Places to Go in 2026. Find the full list here. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: The 17 Most Beautiful National Parks in the World, From Yellowstone to the Serengeti
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.82
Some places are beautiful for one specific reason: a beach at sunset, a mountain perfectly reflected in a lake, a rainforest humming with wildlife. But national parks offer something broader. By definition, they protect entire landscapes and ecosystems—drawing a line around expanses we’ve collectively decided are too precious to lose. For travelers, having a list of designated wonders is also an easy way to know exactly where (and how) to see some of the world’s most incredible forces of nature. That could mean rafting under waterfalls in Argentina, ballooning over fairy chimneys in Türkiye, ice caving in Iceland, or hiking for three days to reach a wildflower-filled valley in India. There are many thousands of national parks around the world, so the trickiest part is narrowing down the list—but these 17, spanning six continents and encompassing an extraordinary range of scenery, are a good place to start. Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil At first glance, Lençóis Maranhenses looks like an enormous white desert—but this vast expanse contains multitudes. The park’s sand dunes are striped with turquoise and emerald lagoons (which accumulate during the rainy season), creating the effect of infinitely repeating oases. Book a five-hour bus ride from São Luís for a surreal swim break. Iguazú National Park, Argentina This park protects the Argentine side of the enormous Iguazú Falls (Iguaçu National Park is a hop over the border in Brazil), a system of some 275 roaring cascades deep in the rainforest. The bombastically—but fittingly—named Devil’s Throat is the standout waterfall here. Admire it from one of the walkways, or ride a speedboat right into the spray. Cabo Pulmo National Park, Mexico Who says national parks have to be in the mountains—or even on land at all? Located on the tip of Mexico’s Baja California Sur peninsula, Cabo Pulmo is a coastal wonderland of quiet beaches and rock formations—but its true appeal lies under the surface. Just offshore, the brilliant Pacific waters protect a vast coral reef system teeming with sea turtles and swirling schools of zooming jacks. Yellowstone National Park, United States Choosing just one US park is a near-impossible task, but Yellowstone takes the narrow lead. Not only was it the first designated national park in the country (and, by most accounts, the entire world), but its geological diversity can’t be beat—within its 2.2 million acres, you’ll find mountains, canyons, geysers, rainbow-gradient hot springs, and more. Banff National Park, Canada This one’s no surprise. Banff National Park is one of Canada’s shining stars, beloved for its staggering views of the Rockies and glacial, almost impossibly blue lakes. Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and Lake Minnewanka are all standouts, equally lovely when reflecting sunshine in summer and frozen over in winter. Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia Namib-Naukluft is the Namibia you came for: burnt-orange sand dunes, blindingly white salt pans, and the eerie skeleton trees of Deadvlei. It’s a little bit Mars, a little bit Fury Road, but an absolute original that has no peer. Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, Madagascar Madagascar is one of the world’s hardest-to-reach countries, which makes its landscapes feel even more immaculate. Case in point: the Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park. Famous for its forest of limestone needles jutting into the sky, the park is almost terrifying in its beauty—though lightened by the fact that the Malagasy word “tsingy” roughly translates to “where one cannot walk barefoot.” Noted! Serengeti National Park, Tanzania The Serengeti occupies an almost mythical space in our collective mind. The Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest move across the plains, is one of Earth’s greatest natural shows. But even in stillness, the region is magnificent—golden grasslands rolling beneath the open sky, with acacia trees punctuating the otherwise endless horizon. Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland Iceland is known as the land of fire and ice, and no place better encapsulates that dramatic epithet than Vatnajökull National Park. Its eponymous glacier and accompanying ice caves dominate the scene, but active volcanoes simmer beneath the freeze, and rivers of meltwater cut through the terrain. It’s a true study in contrasts, both elemental and chromatic—brilliant blue ice, inky black rocks. Las Salinas de Torrevieja National Park, Spain Yes, it really is that pink. Torrevieja’s salt lagoon gets its hue from microorganisms that release red pigments in saline conditions—an imperceptible process that yields magnificent results. It’s an Instagram darling, sure, but it’s also a place to appreciate nature’s inner workings and see the world through bubblegum-colored glasses. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia Plitvice Lakes National Park may not be hidden, but it sure is a gem. Sixteen interconnected lakes cascade through the forest, linked by a series of waterfalls and natural travertine barriers, and ranging in hue from brilliant turquoise to deep blue and green. Make your way through the selfie-snapping crowds, find an empty spot on one of the wooden walkways, and just stand in awe. Valley of Flowers National Park, India The name pretty much says it all: During the summer blooming season, Uttarakhand’s Valley of Flowers transforms into a huge natural garden, with wildflowers blanketing the alpine meadows in a riot of color. Getting here requires a lengthy trek (we’re talking several days) through the Himalayas, but the effort just makes the visual payoff that much sweeter. Göreme National Park, Türkiye Göreme is defined by Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, which are about as magical as they sound. The mushroom-shaped rock structures, carved over millennia by volcanic activity and erosion, are best viewed from above—namely in the basket of a hot-air balloon. Set your alarm and time your ride to sunrise, so you can be the first to watch the landscapes awaken for the day. Kelimutu National Park, Indonesia Three lakes, three wildly different colors. Kelimutu National Park’s bodies of water shift at the whims of the minerals and gases beneath the craters, so you never know exactly what shade you’ll see when you arrive—red, blue, green, or black. It’s as if Mother Nature is wearing a trio of mood rings. Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, China Located in China’s Wulingyuan Scenic Area, Zhangjiajie boasts thousands of jagged sandstone peaks that rise dramatically over lush treetops—and when mist shrouds the valley below, they almost seem to float above the clouds. (Look familiar? The park famously inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in Avatar.) Fiordland National Park, New Zealand Fiordland National Park showcases some of New Zealand’s most striking features, all in one space: mountains, rainforests, waterfalls, and deep glacial fjords. Many visitors zero in on Milford Sound, the undeniable star attraction; but there truly are no bad views here. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Australia Few landmarks are as recognizable as Uluṟu, a sandstone monolith rising from an otherwise flat and open desert. The rockface changes color depending on the sun’s position—ochre during the day, blazing orange and pink at sunset, and purple at twilight.

item.title: The Last-Chance Tourism of Iceland's Glacier Raves
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.76
Weaving through the crowd, I pause next to Kali Van Horn, a 30-year-old architect from Brooklyn with glitter dripping from her eyes like crystallized tears. We share the moment as strangers, pressing our backs against the frozen wall as two DJs spin house and techno tracks in the heart of Langjökull—Iceland’s second-largest glacier. “It’s healing,” Van Horn says, as rainbow lights illuminate the ice cave’s blue hues. Surrounding us are people wearing winter coats accessorized with light-up scarves, sparkly snowflake-shaped sunglasses, and hoods lined with lavender fur. This is part of Iceland Eclipse, a festival on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, offering late-night raves, cacao ceremonies, and lectures on whale communication to 3,333 total attendees. With an energy akin to Burning Man, the vibe is distinctly hippie; guests are gnawing to get into heady discussions. Most are here to extend their experience of the total solar eclipse two days prior, for which they’ve traveled great distances and invested even more grandly. This experience, an 11-hour, $600-price-tagged excursion called “Into the Glacier”, is perhaps the most exclusive event on the lineup. More than ever, rare natural wonders and phenomena are gaining top billing for luxury travel experiences—and this one, both in ambition and vibe, is a standout, drawing just 100 attendees to commune with this 395 square-mile mass of ice. As we drive from the festival grounds toward Langjökull, the stark landscape is punctuated by the occasional sprig of purple flowers. Spikes jut from the massive tires of our car—a vehicle bearing a Jägermeister sticker and the license plate JAGER (the owner just really likes Jager, he says)—which crunches over gravel as the Red Hot Chili Peppers blasts through the speakers, and ravers in the back seat discuss ketamine and the rise of AI. The cars climb higher on the glacier until they begin to get stuck. Then, when they inevitably do, drivers jump out and release air from the tires, redistributing weight so they can continue. The rocks around us fade into sheets of textured ice as we drive onto the glacier, streams of clear water rushing through jagged indentations. This glacier is thousands of years old, our driver explains, formed from layer after layer of snow compressing into ice. As we exit the vehicle, I notice a metal-wrapped entrance in the ice—a portal beckoning us to another dimension. We enter the passage, its walls carved entirely from the glacier. I’m still dangling my crampon—a spiked traction device for walking on slippery ice—in one hand when an Into the Glacier staff member swoops in, gliding it over my hiking shoe in a single fluid motion. “Cinderella treatment,” he says with a grin. I follow a faint beat as I meander through a 1,640-foot labyrinth—the largest manmade ice tunnel in the world—before stepping into a wider, taller space within the ice. It’s designed like a chapel, with wooden benches and faux flowers forming a heart on the wall. Near the exit stands a bearded Into the Glacier tour guide whose name is Hjalamroli Hjalmrsson, I learn, and who tells me his age is “young and old at the same time.” We’re lucky to be partying in the Icelandic Highlands, he impresses upon me: 1,300 meters above sea level, surrounded by “500 billion tons of snow, water, and ice.” The sound dances around us. “It's very echoey. You feel the bass is bouncing off the icy walls,” Hjalmrsson says. “The sound kind of drowns, but that's interesting. It's something that you can compare to a big warehouse.” Just two days ago, when I met with Iceland Eclipse’s co-producer Fridrik Olafsson, 41, he told me that he chose not to haul up large amounts of audio or lighting equipment for the event—“the setting itself does the trick,” he said, spreading his hands on the table. His wife was stenciling a drawing of a moon embracing the sun on his thumbnail. On his other hand, a crescent moon with a face howled. Olfasson took a phone call four minutes into our interview, speaking in terse Icelandic, before telling me that three days of storms had ravaged the festival, damaging three main-stage tents, and ruining 50 glamping tents. He described roaring gusts of nearly 70 miles per hour, desperately tying down tents with heavy machinery, and crew members working for 24 hours to make repairs. “Us Icelanders would call it a windy day, but our foreign counterparts were absolutely shocked,” Olfasson said. Olfasson received permission from local authorities and the mayor for Iceland Eclipse excursions. He had previously collaborated with Into the Glacier—which offers daily tours inside Langjökull—while organizing a music event for Secret Solstice, an Icelandic festival he founded that ran from 2014 to 2019 and offered $1 million ticket packages for groups of six guests, including private jet rides and a personal chef. This post-eclipse event is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to upscale glacial experiences. Inside Langjökull, I follow the steady pulse of music to a mass of 100 people swaying in a hypnotic trance. Hólmar Thor Filipsson, 52, an Icelandic DJ known as Hólmar (Acid Tourist), is playing back-to-back with Margeir Steinar Ingólfsson, 51, an Icelandic DJ known as Margeir. “Everyone there was experiencing something for the first time ever,” Thor Filipsson tells me, later, back at the camp. “It was like the eclipse in a way, but more concentrated, and it felt a little bit sci-fi.” Ingólfsson operates on the same wavelength. “I even came with a special gift for the glacier from my friend, who is a glacier specialist,” Ingólfsson, 51, says. His friend has collected water from glaciers around the world, and Ingólfsson placed a few drops near the DJ booth. When I ask about the night's song selection, Ingólfsson says they took their cue from the glacier itself. Was the glacier in the mood for house and techno, I ask? “Yes,” Ingólfsson replies. “That was the vibe that the glacier wanted at this time.” As the rave beats on, cans of pink vodka cocktails appear in our gloved hands. The beverage packaging suggests that “Flamingo” is an adequate description for a flavor—apparently, that means something like the nostalgic taste of liquified pink Starbursts. Iceland Eclipse staff members are on task with collecting trash in plastic bags, the goal being to leave the glacier just as it was found. Hours later, our two-drink-maximums met, we exit the glacier and totter down to the Into the Glacier Klaki Base Camp, about 10 minutes from the ice cave’s entrance. I meet Lyndsay Klebba, a 36-year-old writer from Chicago, who is wearing a fluffy yellow hat and a pashmina decorated with spotted mushrooms. She decided to visit Iceland after a 23andMe test revealed her Viking heritage: “To be surrounded by ancient ice and listening to New Age music—it's just a clash of titans,” she says. She spent most of the party tucked behind the DJ booth, her heart against the ice to feel the bass. She also wandered into an icy alcove and stuck out her tongue to catch droplets trickled from the ceiling. “The freshest water I ever tasted.” Klebba is the exact audience that Iceland Eclipse is after—those moved by the specialness of the glacier as a setting. “Ice holds a lot of history,” says Mitch Morales, CEO of IMXP and founder of Iceland Eclipse. “The ice in the glacier is thousands of years old–I think about what was happening in the world when this ice was frozen, all the memory, and thinking about this as being a temple in the same way." Morales, 41, is planning IMXP’s “Eclipse Trilogy” of annual totality events. Just this month, he was scouting for the ideal 2027 Luxor site; he is considering Australia or New Zealand for 2028. His ambitions extend even further, though, he says: He eventually wants to host an eclipse viewing on the moon. “In Egypt, there are stone temples that are dedicated to the things that came before them. In a way, I think that a glacier party is similar to that,” Morales says. Gazing out the window as the car crept down the glacier, Klebba observes small signs showing how far Langjökull’s ice once extended. The glacier has lost an estimated 29 percent of its mass between 1890 and 2019, according to a 2020 study published in Frontiers in Earth Science. “Where we were right now would have been glacier probably 40 years ago,” Klebba says. “The fact that we had to drive up several miles just to get to it makes you think about what's going on today.” Some travelers seek out landscapes threatened by global warming, a phenomenon known as “last-chance tourism.” Langjökull has already outlived nearby Okjökull, which became Iceland’s first glacier lost to climate change in 2014. Its name was shortened to Ok, dropping jökull—Icelandic for glacier. “Knowing that this was the last chance to party inside a glacier because of climate change was a big factor in me deciding to attend,” says Hayley Sharkey, 27, as our car jostles away from the ice. Sharkey is a Miami public relations coordinator who has adorned her blue snow jacket with faux-fur cuffs. “Future generations will not be able to understand how it felt to be inside a glacier. The feeling of natural ice surrounding you will be seen as a myth.”

item.title: 7 Famous Homes From Movies and TV Shows You Can Actually Rent, Including Harry Potter’s Childhood Home and the 'Bachelor' Mansion
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.44
If you’ve ever dreamed of waking up in Bella Swan’s moody Forks home, where a vampire might pop in to say hello at any moment, or planning a Girls-style weekend trip out to Long Island’s North Fork, there’s a world of movie-famous rentals out there for turning your fictional fantasies into a reality. The seven properties on this list span famous homes from film and television, from Harry Potter’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow to the Bachelor mansion in Agoura Hills. Whether you’re looking to relive your favorite series or cosplay as a main character, these rentals have a certain star quality—after all, it took many professional location scouts to find them. From whimsical lofts in Tokyo fit for solo travelers to Cornwall, England, mansions that double as wedding venues, there’s a recognizable rental below for every kind of travel scenario. Just be sure to book ahead; these famous sets fill up fast. Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, shared bathroom Why we love it: Courtyard view, wood-burning fireplace, backyard Featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part One, the Vere House serves as Harry’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow. But its history can be traced back to the 15th century, when the De Vere family built it as a hunting lodge; the front door, with its medieval wooden carvings, is one of the most photographed sites in Lavenham, a village in Suffolk. The house features four en suite bedrooms (another is available to rent here), with access to the shared sitting room, where guests can gather and enjoy a roaring fire (and some crumpets, marshmallows, and sweet chestnuts in the winter months), or the courtyard when the weather’s nice. You’ll also have the option to order a full English breakfast, enjoyed in the communal dining room surrounded by centuries-old objects and artwork. Location: Lavenham, England Things to do nearby: The Crooked House, Six Bells Preston, Great Cornard Country Park Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 baths Why we love it: Proximity to riverfront, film memorabilia, patio While it’s booked out for months, Bella Swan’s home from Twilight is out there—not in Forks, but St. Helens, Oregon. And it never left 2008: The home is remarkably similar to the way it appears in the film, down to Bella’s purple floral bedspread (while not available for use, it is on display). Though the movie makes it seem like close quarters between Bella and Charlie, the house actually contains five bedrooms for you and your seven closest Twihards to spread out across. One reviewer wrote, “Watching the Twilight movies while staying in the house is every teenage girl's dream, and I can't believe it happened to me!” Location: St. Helens, Oregon Things to do nearby: St. Helens Historic Riverfront District, Historic Columbia Theatre, Crooked Creek Brewery Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, 1 bath Why we love it: Quirky architecture, indoor fireplace, in-unit washer/dryer Season five, episode three of Girls, simply titled “Japan,” is a world unto itself, and Shoshanna’s cartoon-like home away from home is no different. A jungle gym of sorts, the loft is decked out in primary colors, with bulbous fixtures and a wraparound layout. The bathroom, for instance, is housed in its own circular pod, while the kitchen sits in a central pit. This is a personal unit within a shared residential building, so guests might run into each other along common walkways and staircases. Quirky design lovers, this one’s for you. Location: Tokyo, Japan Things to do nearby: Nogawa Park, Ghibli Museum, Fuchu Art Museum Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 4 baths Why we love it: Beach access, pet-friendly, private pool Of the North Fork, Marnie from Girls says, “It’s for people who think the Hamptons are tacky and don’t want to be on a beach that’s near a J.Crew.” Once a Coast Guard lifesaving station built in 1893, the East Marion home that fueled one of the most iconic episodes in the show’s history is available to rent. But that’s not the property’s only claim to fame; the home also appeared in The Undoing, when Grace (played by Nicole Kidman) flees to the beach after her husband (Hugh Grant) goes missing. Right on the Long Island Sound with its own private slice of sand, this spacious home has enough room for up to 13 guests (hopefully your bachelorette weekend is more synchronized dance, less fighting). Location: East Marion, New York Things to do nearby: Orient State Park, Kontokosta Winery, town of Greenport Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Private pool, hot tub, mountain view Bachelor fans will revel in a stay at Villa de la Vina, the 10,000-square-foot Mediterranean-style mansion nestled within the Santa Monica Mountains of Malibu. You and 12 other guests can spread out across seven bedrooms and get a real-life glimpse of your favorite moments from the show. Whether you compete for love is up to you (may we suggest a bachelorette weekend instead?), but the romantic archways, infinity pool, and Agoura Hills views are sure to make you feel like you’re on a reality TV show. Bonus: Chef-prepared meals, airport transfers, and a chauffeur service are all available upon request. Location: Agoura Hills, California Things to do nearby: Liberty Lane Farms, Ladyface Trailhead, Malibu Wine Hikes Number of guests: 4–6 Bed and bath: 2–4 beds, 1–2 baths Why we love it: Film memorabilia, guided tours, gift shop While the house from A Christmas Story is available for daily tours in Cleveland, real fans of the beloved holiday classic will want to stay overnight in suites styled after the film, including the main house (lovingly restored) or the neighboring Bumpus House. All rooms are decked out in 1940s “hillbilly chic” interiors, and the loft, located in the main house, is where two lucky guests can sleep in Ralphie and Randy’s beds. Be sure to plan ahead, as these coveted rentals get booked up quickly around the holidays, and don’t leave without buying a pair of pink bunny pajamas in the gift shop. Location: Cleveland, Ohio Things to do nearby: Rowley Inn gastropub, Hooper Farm, Lincoln Park Number of guests: 21 Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Seaview rooms, proximity to beach, grand piano, game room Ideal for an English seaside wedding, the Porthpean House is as romantic as it gets, not least because it was featured in the cult-favorite 2013 film About Time. Overlooking Porthpean Beach, the salt-sprayed home was originally built in 1793 and has belonged to the Petherick family for five generations before becoming a dreamy vacation rental. Sleeping up to 21 guests, it houses several historic rooms, including a drawing room, gaming room, dining room, multiple kitchens, and an office, as well as acres of fresh lawn to frolic around. Location: Cornwall, England Things to do nearby: Porthpean Beach, Porthpean Golf Club, RAF Quadrant Tower

item.title: What does the EU's new hand luggage rule mean for travellers? Here’s everything you need to know about the updated air passenger rights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.21
On Tuesday 1 September, Members of the European Parliament confirmed changes to air passenger rights that were first reported earlier in 2026. These rules have been in place for more than 20 years, since 2004, and aim to protect passengers against disruption to their travels. While many of our rights, such as compensation if flights are delayed by a certain number of hours, will simply be upheld by the latest vote, there are some changes due to come into effect, too. Extra costs for hand luggage have been something that’s plagued travellers for decades, but new regulations are set to change that. After more than a decade of negotiations between the Council of the EU and the European Parliament, a landmark agreement has been reached. What is the new rule for hand luggage? New rules will include the right for passengers to carry one personal item such as a small bag or backpack with them onboard without incurring an extra cost. Airlines will also be required by law to display air fares that include carry-on luggage while booking to improve transparency and comparability between airlines and tickets. Airlines may still offer cheaper tickets who travel without hand luggage, MEPs say. A small catch to be aware of, however, is that this regulation applies to EU airlines only. This means that on non-EU airlines, like easyJet and Jet2, passengers may still be bound to the old regulations – except on flights returning to the UK from an EU country. Which other rights have been introduced? Several new rights are set to improve passenger safety and protection. These include rules to make it easier for passengers to claim compensation and access assistance in case of delay or cancellation, as well as new regulations reinforcing rights for persons with specific needs, such as persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and pregnant passengers. Air passenger rights changes to know - The right to carry on board, without extra cost, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack - Passengers will no longer be charged for correcting spelling errors or for a printed version of a boarding pass if they have already checked in - Passengers will be able to take the return flight of a two-way ticket even if they did not use the first flight - Clearer and quicker reimbursement for flight disruption and travel delays - Passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility will have the right to compensation, rerouting and assistance if they miss a flight due to the airport’s failure to help them reach the gate on time - Any person accompanying a child below the age of 14 will be entitled to an adjacent seat without paying extra. The same right will apply to passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility, and to pregnant women. “I’m proud that, after 13 years of negotiations, we reached a landmark agreement to strengthen EU air passenger rights,” announced Alexis Vafeades, minister of transport, communications and works of the Republic of Cyprus. “This modernised framework will deliver certainty, fairness and stronger protection for millions of European air passengers. The agreement strikes a fair balance for our airlines, helping preserve connectivity that is vital to the EU’s internal market and its citizens.”

item.title: Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The sophomore season expands beyond English country piles to Mafia-held Italian palazzos
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.81
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions were something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveller, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’s filming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: Flying with children is about to get cheaper and easier thanks to new EU rules – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.45
Ever found yourself fuming that in order to ensure you get a seat next to your child on the way to your family holiday, you have to pay extra for a seat for each of you – on top of what's probably an already hefty ticket price? You're not alone. But changes to EU air passenger rights will make this annoyance a thing of the past, as the right for children under the age of 14 to sit next to an accompanying adult free of charge will be protected. In September 2026, Members of the European Parliament approved changes to rules on air passenger rights that have been protected since 2004. There's a slate of changes due to come into force, but the parents among the Condé Nast Traveller team were particularly intrigued by the promise that a free adjacent seat will be guaranteed for a child under the age of 14 and the adult accompanying them. That means airlines cannot split up families at seat allocation, and cannot charge you extra to sit together. Why under the age of 14? For most airlines, children under 14 cannot travel without an accompanying adult on the same flight. The change means that adding extra fees to allow parents and children to sit together – which can quickly add up as they're charged per person – will be a thing of the past. The rules come into effect 12 months and 20 days after their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union – around August 2027, just in time for any end-of-summer holidays. Other rights that will come into practice next August thanks to these include: - Making it easier to claim compensation if your flight is delayed or cancelled - Transparent pricing that displays ticket prices including cabin baggage by default - Personal items stored under the seat should be free of charge

item.title: The UK’s oldest recorded town has more than 2,000 years of history – and where it is may surprise you
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.33
When I found out where the UK’s oldest town was, I wasn't expecting it to be a place I've passed through quite so frequently, or one still thriving today. I’ve been lucky enough to travel the breadth of Britain over my 31 years, from tiny hamlets in the Scottish Highlands to artsy towns in Cornwall. I’ve spent half my life calling London home and the other half in East Anglia; holidayed in Wales, visiting beaches accessible only by wooden swing; slept in cabins in the Cotswolds; road-tripped through Northern Ireland; and spent years studying in Newcastle. All of which is to say, if you’d asked me to guess where it was, I’d have imagined a barely-there archaeological site somewhere in rural Northumberland, rather than a thriving modern city in Essex, close to the Suffolk border and just 60 miles northeast of London. I’m talking, of course, about Colchester. Today, the city is popular for its fast commuter trains into the capital, relatively affordable housing, open green spaces and, of course, its rich history. But in around AD 43, it was known as Camulodunum: the first major Roman city and the initial capital of Roman Britain, before it was destroyed during Boudica’s rebellion in AD 61. The story of the Roman settlement didn’t end there, however, and Colchester was rebuilt in the years that followed. During the Anglo-Saxon era, the city was largely neglected before later falling under Viking control. In AD 917, Edward the Elder drove the Vikings out, and Colchester began to regain its former stature. Following the Norman Conquest, Colchester Castle was built in 1066 over the ruins of an earlier Roman temple. Dating to the 1070s, it became the first and largest of the Normans’ great keeps, cementing Colchester’s importance as one of England’s key centres. But the city’s history stretches back even further than the Roman conquest. Colchester began as an Iron Age settlement, ruled by Cunobelin, known as the ‘King of the Britons’. Evidence of this early history can still be found in the city today, including a collection of Iron Age and Roman artefacts at Colchester & Ipswich Museums. There’s something slightly confusing about calling Colchester the oldest town in the UK, given that it is also one of the country’s newest cities. It gained city status in November 2022 as part of the late Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours, one of eight towns to receive the upgrade. It joined Doncaster, Milton Keynes, Dunfermline, Bangor, Wrexham, Douglas and Stanley. Of course, when compared with some of the world’s oldest cities, Colchester is relatively young in the grand scheme of human history. Jericho, on the West Bank near the Jordan River, is thought to have been inhabited as early as 9000 BCE, and is often described as the world’s oldest known walled city. Across Britain, several places lay claim to the title of oldest town, from Thetford in Norfolk and Ipswich in Suffolk to Amesbury, near Stonehenge, where evidence of settlement dates back as far as 8820 BC. Colchester’s claim rests on a specific point of difference: it is officially recognised as the UK's oldest town on record, based on a reference to the settlement by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder.

In your phone’s settings, you’ll be able to toggle between your existing physical sim card and the eSim, even being able to use both simultaneously, such as using one for mobile data and the other for calls and texts. It means that, if you download and install the eSim before you head off, you can activate it in the airport when you land and beat pricey roaming charges forevermore. The setup is simple. After registering online, all it takes is a quick scan of a QR code and you’re good to go. If you run out of data, you don’t need to download a new one – just top up your existing plan. Each eSIM has its own inclusions, from calls, texts, and internet streaming, to exclusive access to essential apps like Google Maps, so make sure to check in advance which plan best suits your needs. If that’s not enough to convince you, the entirely virtual setup means that they are also kinder to the planet than the plastic chips of traditional SIMs. Is my phone eSim compatible? Most Apple iPhone, Google Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy models released in the UK since 2018 are eSIM compatible. For other smartphones, the quickest way to check eSIM compatibility is by dialing *#06# on your phone's keypad – a screen pop-up including an EID number indicates your device is eSIM-friendly. You will also need to make sure that your device is not locked to a single network. If this is the case, provided you’ve reached the end of your original contract, you can ask your provider to unlock it for free by requesting a Network Unlock Code (NUC). Do I need a different eSIM for each country I visit? No. All eSIMs are suitable for use worldwide, so you’ll only need to install one eSIM. Do check, however, that the eSim provider you select has data plans available for the country you want to visit – all of the brands below have hundreds of countries available, so this shouldn’t be a problem in the vast majority of instances. Some plans are suitable for use in multiple countries, too, which is good if you’re taking a longer trip hopping from place to place – like if taking a cruise, for example. Airalo, for instance, has packages valid for use in up to 137 countries, from Jamaica to Japan.

item.title: 12 authors on the books that inspired them to travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.88
Reading a good book can be a way to unwind after a stressful week at work, a way to escape reality for a little while, and a way to learn more about the world around us. However, books can also serve as some indirect inspiration for travel too – especially when a writer has transported you to a particular place or environment. I had this very experience recently whilst reading Carley Fortune’s latest romance novel, Our Perfect Storm. She’s an author who uses location as a character in itself and writes about it so beautifully, and this book has made me want to visit Tofino in Canada. And I’m not the only one who has been inspired by reading to plan or visit a new destination. To aid with your holiday planning, we asked a group of authors to tell us about the books that inspired them to travel to somewhere new and why. Dalia Al-Dujaili recommends Little Women by Louisa May Alcott When I was in New York alone for the first time in 2023, I decided to spend a few days exploring Boston and New England. I had romanticised ideas of the East Coast from my American Literature degree – The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, Little Women, and the poetry of Robert Frost and Mary Oliver. So I boarded a 6am Greyhound to Boston – very main character! – with no money and barely anything to eat except nuts and American trail mix. Five hours later, I checked into a random hostel, completely unprepared but enjoying the spontaneity. The next day, I had planned to take a ferry to Provincetown, where Mary Oliver lived, but a storm cancelled the ferries. Instead, I took the train to Salem. It was late October, so the town was full of pumpkins and candlelit New England houses. I spent the next few days exploring forests, visiting Louisa May Alcott’s house, browsing vintage bookshops, and eating lobster rolls. It was one of the best trips I’ve ever taken alone! Dalia Al-Dujaili is the author of Babylon, Albion Julia Armfield recommends Solo Faces by James Salter Solo Faces is perhaps one of the most compelling novels I've ever read about the combined ugliness and beauty of climbing. His passages about the cruelty and yet astonishing grace to be found in the Alps are just incredible and made it more or less imperative for me to visit the Swiss Alps myself. Travelling entirely by train from London enables you to witness an outrageous cross-section of landscapes and really adds to the sense that you are growing incrementally further and further away from reality, the higher up you get. Julia Armfield is the author of Our Wives Under The Sea and Up To The Light Sian Meades-Williams recommends The Stone Boudoir by Teri Maggio I bought this book on a slight whim from a bookshop in Greenwich, where the author visited because her grandmother said there was ‘nothing there’, and I not only completely fell in love with Sicily but wanted to see it for myself. It was incredible; I’ve been back a few times since my first trip and my partner and I even got engaged in that tiny town with ‘nothing to see’. Sian Meades-Williams is the author of The Pyjama Myth Beth Ashley recommends Fault Lines by Emily Itami The writing is so beautiful in the way it describes the environment of Tokyo you honestly feel like you can see it. Itami is so descriptive and romantic in her prose, and having the main character have a job where she shows people around is such a brilliant narrative device, also showcasing Tokyo to the reader. And when I finally took a trip to Tokyo, I ended up re-reading Fault Lines. Beth Ashley is the author of Sluts Tahmina Begum recommends Without Reservations by Alice Steinbach Without Reservations is a memoir by a Pulitzer-winning journalist and single working mother. At the time of writing, Steinbach’s children had grown up, her nest empty and there is a level of contentment with her career, while a level of discontentment with her life. The date marked in the library stamp at the front says I took this out on 3 April 2018. I would have been 23. Although Steinbach was writing on the other side of life, I vividly remember the impact this book had on me. My own version of Eat, Pray, Love. In fact, my first solo trip to Malta came shortly after this. I may not have lived as long as Steinbach when reading Without Reservations, but I had at that point been interning and working a few writing jobs in newsrooms, all at the same time, for already five years by then. I was similarly becoming more content in my career decisions while feeling, as though I was not living enough. So I did what many South Asian Muslim women are not asked to do that Steinbach was also seeking: joyful memories that were just for herself. Tahmina Begum is the author of Womanhood Rioghnach Robinson recommends Outline by Rachel Cusk It's been five years since I visited Greece, and longer since I first read Rachel Cusk's Outline, so I can't remember whether the book's diamond-cut Mediterranean descriptions really did drive me to Athens. But I do remember landing in 115-degree heat as that summer's wildfires bore down on the city, and the tinkling music in the sprawling, deserted restaurants near the scorching beach, and a long, one-sided conversation with a stranger about the organisation of Greek transit. So: Rachel Cusk clearly made Athens feel like Outline to me, and now, when I reread, Outline feels like that summer's Athens. Rioghnach Robinson is the author of Bad Words Stephanie Wrobel recommends Misery by Stephen King Misery inspired me to write my own cat-and-mouse thriller set in the publishing industry, but instead of an author held captive by his number-one fan, Revenge Plot pits a literary agent against an unhinged aspiring writer. I knew I needed somewhere suitably remote to trap them together, which led me to an Airbnb treehouse in the Catskill Mountains in New York and eventually to spending a few nights there alone for research. The reality was more unsettling than I’d anticipated. The treehouse had no cell service, and its walls were made of glass. It was beautiful during the day; after dark, all I could think about was how easily someone could be standing among the trees, watching me. Needless to say, plenty of that unease found its way into the book. Stephanie Wrobel is the author of Revenge Plot Fiona Valpy recommends The Weight Of Water by Anita Shreve I love Anita Shreve’s books set along the New England coastline. The Weight of Water is a dual-timeline novel about a historical murder and a contemporary relationship in freefall on the mysterious Isles of Shoals in the Gulf of Maine. I’m planning a trip there next year to explore more of the coast, and to visit Celia Thaxter’s beautiful garden. She was a poet who made her summer home on one of the rocky and inhospitable islands, planting a garden that inspired some of the paintings by the American Impressionist painter Childe Hassam. Fiona Valpy is the author of Sisters of the Midnight Sun Meg Charlton recommends Weetzie Bat by Francesca Lia Block If I said I moved to Los Angeles because of Weetzie Bat, I would not be alone. This is, apparently, a common reaction to reading Francesca Lia Block’s psychedelically overstuffed ode to the city. Block's LA is a smoggy, fizzy heaven for freaks and rebels, the young and young at heart, anyone willing to see the beauty glinting out between the strip malls and dying palms. A YA novel that flutters into magical realism might feel a tad overheated for some adult readers. But then again, LA can feel like that itself: Too big, too much. Sprawling and tacky and totally, utterly sublime. Meg Charlton is the author of Voyagers Charles Cumming recommends the James Bond series by Ian Fleming In the 1980s, as a pupil at the sort of cloistered boarding school with which Ian Fleming would have been familiar, I read every James Bond book going. 007 travelled far and wide – to the Bahamas and Japan, to Paris and Berlin – but it was the Istanbul of From Russia With Love that I longed to visit. Years later, researching a spy novel of my own, I finally came face-to-face with the crumbling Ottoman buildings, subterranean passages and magnificent mosques so vividly depicted in Fleming’s classic. Istanbul was crowded and sensual, a hub of skulduggery and corruption, still the perfect setting for a story of espionage. Charles Cumming is the author of ICARUS 17 Anna Deacon recommends The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd I've always been inspired by great travel writing, and my bookshelves are full of dog-eared Lonely Planet books that have travelled with me in a backpack to many far-flung places, but one book I return to time and time again is The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd. Even though I've spent a great deal of my life in the Cairngorms in Scotland and know the area really well, this book offers a whole different view of this rugged, wild landscape. Nan's writing is so visceral and descriptive, and her adventures inspire the reader to explore, not only these wild places, but themselves too. I've taken this book on so many adventures and it never stops inspiring me to plunge in icy river pools, quietly observe nature, and walk until I find myself. Anna Deacon is the author of The Wild Fix Scotland C.J. Tudor recommends The Shining by Stephen King The Shining is one of my favourite books and I’ve always wanted to visit the creepy Overlook Hotel featured in the film. In 2023, I travelled to Alaska to research my novel, The Gathering, and booked an isolated lodge in the mountains: Talkeetna Lodge. Everything about it, from the snowy mountain views to the huge lounge with its high vaulted ceiling, reminded me of the Overlook. It had only just opened for the season, so it was almost deserted, adding to the eerie feel, although disappointingly, the bartender was not called Lloyd! C.J. Tudor is the author of Serenity Falls
