item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.44
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in September 2026 Bar Blondie, Queen's Park Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Address: 19-21 Lonsdale Road, NW6 6RA Website: barblondie.co.uk Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Oudh 1772, Borough Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry. Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Website: oudh1722.com Kismet, Borough Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening. The menu follows Turkish meyhane cooking, so come prepared to share. Start with Atom, a thick buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter; cool and tangy against the gentle heat, it is particularly good scooped up with bread or piled onto Sigara Böreği, a crisp pastry filled with salty white cheese. From the charcoal grill comes Tavuk Şiş, smoky chicken thigh with red pepper, alongside Patates Kizartmasi, fried Cyprus potatoes. Wash it all down with Basketcase, a bottled lager brewed in partnership with Coalition Brewery, or, my personal favourite, a glass of raki. The Turkish anise-flavoured spirit is made for sipping alongside food, its clean, herbal finish acting as a refreshing palate cleanser between bites. The final flourish comes with dessert, when waiters glide between tables carrying silver trays above their heads. Lowered on request, they reveal rows of Turkish tea in delicate tulip-shaped glasses and slices of pistachio baklava drowned in syrup. Kismet is only a year-long residency in the space, so visit while you can. Amelia Dhuga Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Website: kismet.london Cue Point, Latimer Road Cue Point is determinedly not a newcomer to the London restaurant scene. For a decade, the hybrid Afghan-Texas BBQ of Kabul-born chef Mursal Saiq and head chef Joshua Moroney has been making a name for itself through pop-ups, residencies and stints at breweries. This summer, they've finally found a permanent home for their low-n-slow, fired-up cooking. Cue Point at The Garden Bar is set inside an unchic West London boozer with, as the name hints, a truly enormous garden out back. Here, meat – Wagyu brisket, oak-smoked lamb shank, black lime pepper chicken bites – is smoked to meltiness, or else cooked over licking flames. Saiq's immaculate Afghan flavours are anything but shy and retiring, and a perfect match for Moroney's expert BBQ techniques. Those chicken bites' gnarly exteriors give way to soft meat – we boldly paired ours with the smoked pimento garlic chilli cheese flatbread to start. Wagyu brisket steak served with fluffy Texas naan and cowboy butter is a non-negotiable, although we'd also recommend ordering the flaky chilli-citrus seabass for something a little (emphasis on the word) lighter. The sticky toffee pudding with Bertotti kulfi was a surprise standout: moreish and sweet, Saiq works with West London gelataria Bertotti to perfect the kulfi. The team serve a special menu on Sundays, when Saiq tells me that people try to sneak in the door; advance reservations are so hard to get. This is West London's opening of the summer, and a must-book for anyone seeking serious flavour. Sarah James Address: Garden Bar Grill & Smokehouse at 41 Bramley Road, Notting Hill, London, W10 6SZ Website: cue-point.co.uk Rosina, Wandsworth It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite – its signature beef tartare is still one of the best dishes I’ve ever had, and I don’t even like beef tartare. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Antipasti comes to the table with a vibrant flurry – crimson tuna crudo, smoked sardines on toast, and a heavenly bowl of rainbow Datterini tomatoes with basil, nectarine and buffalo mozzarella. This is the kind of place where everything is confidently simple, and the bread basket is put to good use mopping up every sauce and vinaigrette. For mains, a pillowy turbot is roasted on the bone and swimming in lemon, capers, parsley and wilted spinach. The intriguingly named ‘post-service pasta’ was my favourite; an understated yet masterful bowl of spaghetti with anchovy, chilli, garlic and parsley, essentially the dish Byatt likes to make for himself after a shift in the kitchen. Wonderfully oily and crunchy in equal measure, I ate every tiny crumb and noodle. Pudding is served from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, with tiramisu rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. If there’s room to try two, the not-too-sweet but cheese-heavy Rosina's torte is a worthy option; the torte and the restaurant are named after Byatt’s daughter Rosie, who also works in the kitchen. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF Website: rosinarestaurant.co.uk All Roads, Brixton I visited All Roads during one of London's many 2026 heatwaves, so it says something about how delicious the food is that I wasn't remotely overwhelmed by the plates of mac and cheese, lamb from the house pot or fried wings that were placed in front of me on one of the hottest days of the year. While the rest of London was digging into light salads, or maybe a barbecue, I was more than happy to get stuck into the hearty dishes from chefs and partners Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, who have finally put down roots in Brixton following three years of sold-out supper clubs. The menu blends Caribbean cuisine with British, European and Southern American influences, resulting in a list of dishes that are hearty, moreish and full of flavour. Split into snacks, smalls, grill and plates (with just two or three dishes to each), it's tempting to order the whole menu – take three friends, and you probably could. Unfortunately for me, I was with just one friend, so we had to be discerning (albeit still rather greedy). Having tried over half of the menu, I truly think it would be difficult to order badly here, but my favourites were undoubtedly the chilli parm clams, served in a sweet and salty tomatoey-soy sauce, with crispy pancetta and topped with parmesan, or the impossibly cheesy baked mac and cheese. We ordered a fresh tomato salad to break up the dishes, and ended with homemade sorrel cheesecake ice cream. In the end, despite the heat, there's nowhere I'd rather have been on a Wednesday evening than here in Brixton Village, soaking up the vibe, flavours and fun of this memorable new spot. Abigail Malbon Address: 44 Atlantic Road, London SW9 8JN Website: allroadsldn.com Hon’s BBQ, Hackney Wick After earning a fiercely loyal following during his two-year residency at All My Friends, chef Man Hon Luk's first bricks-and-mortar restaurant – in the spot formerly occupied by Silo above Crate Brewery – was a natural next step. I never made it to the pop-up, but just knowing that Hon perfected his craft at world-renowned, Michelin-starred Interstellar BBQ was reason enough to clear the diary, hotfoot it over to Hackney Wick and see what all the fuss was about. The space is cool, casual and buzzing – high ceilings, whitewashed walls and simple red wooden tables and chairs let the food do the talking. Hon’s cooking is clearly shaped by his time in Texas, but what lands in front of us is something entirely his own: smoky, low-and-slow meats elevated with Chinese flavours and techniques. Every bite melts in your mouth, with just the right hit of spice and sweetness and the kind of deep caramelised crispy bits you’d fight your fellow diner for. The beef short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce are the star of the show (tender, peppery and sticky) but don’t sleep on the sides; perfectly crunchy green beans with an umami-rich glaze, and a silky mac and cheese with a tangy mustard-laced sauce. Our only regret? Opting to share a bowl of the creamy mango coconut pudding – one each is a must. Sarah Allard Address: First floor, Unit 7, The White Building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN Website: honsbbq.com Best new London restaurants in July 2026 Vesper, Exmouth Market When Jackson Boxer opens a new London restaurant, it’s safe to assume it’ll be a smash hit. The chef and restaurateur behind buzzy Brunswick House, Dove and Henri has just opened a new neighbourhood spot on Exmouth Market. Interiors are industrial, with bare brick walls, a metal bar in the centre and curtains hiding candle-lit tables in intimate corners. There’s also plenty of tables that spill onto the sun-drenched street. We dined at Vesper a full month after opening, as tables really are that hard to come by. We made sure to book an early 6pm reservation, as the infamous burger you may have seen plastered all over your Instagram, often quoted as one of the best burgers in London, is ordered off-menu to 10 lucky customers on a first-come, first-served basis. We secured the fourth burger of the evening. The bun is covered in sweet glaze, hugging a hefty slab of seared and torched beef with a rare centre, layered with caramelised onions and oozing gorgonzola sauce. We’d recommend sharing, or you’ll be rolling home without a chance to try any of the other delicious plates. Our favourite dish of the night was the fried potato pizzette: a little circular pizza bread topped with pineapple, stringy stracciatella cheese and mortadella. Other highlights include the green bean salad coated in goat's cheese and gooseberry tahini, the chicken agnolotti – al dente pasta pockets bursting with fragrant chicken liver in a madeira jus. For pudding, order the punchy poached apricot flavoured with ginger and amaretto. Plates were scraped clean, as were our little gimlets, previously filled with the Vesper martini finished with a little squirt of citrus oil. Sophie Knight Address: 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA Website: vesper.restaurant Langosteria, Whitehall Italian seafood restaurant group Langosteria has a knack for attaching itself to smart addresses in glamorous European locations, from Milan's Design District to St Moritz and the waves at Paraggi near Portofino. So it’s no surprise that the Milanese group’s first UK outpost has made a beeline for Raffles London at The OWO. Whitehall's neoclassical Portland stone grandeur doesn't quite evoke the summery spirit of the Ligurian Riviera, but once you pass through its doors, you're transported to that familiar Langosteria world, with its signature animated wallpaper and matching ambience. Here, everything is bold and impactful with a touch of experimentation – including the bar cocktails. From the concise list, the Pomodoro Mezcal, a smoky take on a Bloody Mary, confused my vodka receptors, but the Spicy Margarita with jalapeño was the unequivocal star. Food-wise, Langosteria casts a wide net in pursuit of freshness and quality, hauling its catch from Italy, Spain, France and Scotland. Locavore advocates will scream, but the quality is undeniable. My Sicilian red prawn starter – butter-soft and topped with wafer-thin slices of pecorino – was beautiful. The mains included Langosteria classics like the King Crab Special Edition 2007 and the Brittany Lobster "Spicy Blue”; I plumped for the crispy-skinned black grouper Chateaubriand, its saltiness offset by tangy-sweet caponata (Sicilian aubergine, olive and caper relish). My langoustine with lobster in a puddle of zingy lemon butter was perfectly al dente, but the Milanese turbot with asparagus and saffron proved somewhat immemorable. I chased it all with a glass of Ferrari Brut from a wine list that features most of the Champagne heavy hitters alongside an impressive, Italian-dominant selection of reds and whites. Portions are generous throughout, and for guests of the Raffles hotel, it's just a short stagger to their rooms upstairs. Noo Saro-Wiwa Address: Langosteria, Whitehall Place at The OWO, London, SW1A 2BD Website: langosteria.com Willet's, Chelsea At the back of The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel, is an elegant wooden staircase that King Edward VII (when he was the Prince of Wales) ascended to visit his lover, the Victorian actress and socialite Lillie Langtry. It still stands as a testament to the history (and discretion) of this particular 1880s Chelsea townhouse, and today, though less steeped in scandal, it is as regal and luxurious as ever. The Cadogan is also home to Willett’s, a new British bistro that seems set to become a hotspot in its own right, even amongst those not staying upstairs. Studio Shayne Brady, the interiors team behind the renovation, has modernised while remaining true to the hotel's history – bathing the space in calming blues and greens. Executive chef Michael Turner (a Gordon Ramsay alum) is producing à la carte dishes that showcase the very best of British produce in unfussy, delicious dishes. The sourdough crumpets with gentleman’s relish and dressed Dorset crab were the definite showstoppers and are destined to become signature dishes. Mini but mighty, I’d have been more than happy with plates of those alone. Seasonality and locality are buzzwords thrown around quite loosely these days, but Willett’s really does do credit to everything that is brilliant about the produce of the British Isles. I'd also recommend the succulent Beef Wellington and the Colchester oysters. We’ve no doubt that this restaurant will become as legendary as some of the hotel’s historic residents. Cass Farrar Address: 75 Sloane Street, London, SW1X 9SG Website: belmond.com Dante, Mayfair Devotees of all things Stateside were intrigued when one of America's best cocktail bars, New York City's Dante, jumped across the pond in 2025 to pop up at grand dame Claridge’s. Rather than tire and bloat at yet another cross-Atlantic collab, the gourmands kept coming. And so, a year later, the hotel restaurant closed its doors for a facelift any Mayfair resident of a certain age would approve of, led by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, with a fresh palette of green-and-blue tones and fantastical, botanical murals by Beth Rodway, to welcome Dante as a permanent resident of the neighbourhood's slickest hotel. We follow Billecart-Salmon Champagne with a taster of the Negroni Rosa, a watermelon concoction that tastes like a swig of the summer to come. A host of NYC favourites are now on the menu – we sample delicate caviar tarts and champagne pearls and are taken aback by the gargantuan grilled king prawns, their smoky, chilli-butter scent enveloping our booth. If a dish is preceded by the restaurant’s name, you know it’s one the chef’s hedging their bets on. And so the Dante smash burger arrives: a juicy patty coated in provolone cheese and topped with sweet caramelised onion, beside perfectly crispy chips awaiting their saucy demise. Burger devoured and Parmigiano Reggiano-doused veal Milanese inhaled between us, we call on our second stomachs for pudding with a side of spectacle. An espresso martini arrives, my face staring back at me in cocoa dusting courtesy of the bar’s cocktail-printing sorcery, alongside an uber-indulgent sticky toffee doughnut that illuminates our woozy cheeks with a whiskey flambé. It's a fiery finish to a meal I’ll be dining out on for a long time to come. Connor Sturges Address: Dante Mayfair, Claridge's, Brook Street, London W1K 4HR Website: maybourne.com Best new London restaurants in June 2026 The Sea, The Sea, Chelsea When we walk into Pavilion Road’s The Sea, The Sea – already a familiar name in Chelsea, but now a restaurant serving far more than just drinks and oysters – we don’t know what to expect. Above the ground-floor raw bar, tables are bathed in light, and the design is minimalist, but we quickly learn that all attention is poured into the fare. The menu spotlights lesser-known fish, plus whatever catch is locally abundant from the seafood suppliers they've built trusted relationships with. We start with cold sake and a tin of Imperial (as a caviar enthusiast, I love that the sour cream comes pre-topped with chives), followed by butter-soft Isle of Skye scallops with flowering currant. Often, the raw bar usually outshines everything else to me, but three warm dishes – cuttlefish ragu with green almond, smoked Chalkstream trout on a Jersey royal mash, and a rice vinegar-steeped John Dory with maitake – are impossible to top. The ragu is nothing like we imagine: no pasta, just clean-cut cuttlefish with an unbelievably flavourful squid ink salsify that results in an immediate repeat order. Come dessert, don’t look beyond the potato ice cream with smoked eel. It sounds hard to wrap your head around, and for that reason, you must order it. Tamara Southward Address: 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW Website: https://theseathesea.net MA/NA Mayfair A new opening in Mayfair comes with glitzy high expectations, which we immediately felt as we were swept through the doors of MA/NA by a suave-suited doorman. He guided us through the long, winding bar space with a house DJ and down to our table under huge bonsais and gold statement lighting. A martini is poured table-side as we browse the extensive menu divided into small plates, robata (meats from the Japanese grill), sushi, steak cuts and large plates. We ordered to share: rock shrimp tempura in a glazed sticky sauce, juicy chicken thigh skewers from the robata grill, a 12-piece sushi platter with fresh cuts as selected by the chef (which could also pass as a piece of art) and the crunchy duck salad with sweet pomegranate. But, our favourite dish, which – fair warning – comes with a big price tag, was the Japanese A5 Wagyu slices served on a hot Himalayan salt stone, which not only flavours, but sears the meat from its heat. Melt-in-the-mouth slices of the finest beef, packed with flavour. MA/NA is on par, if not tastier than some of London's favourite high-end Japanese spots, with equally flashy guests and interiors. Sophie Knight Address: 30 Upper Grosvenor Street, London, W1K 7PH Website: manarestaurants.com Buvette London, Neal's Yard 14 years since its New York debut, chef Jody Williams has brought Buvette (and with it, the spirit of the West Village) to the cobbled streets of Covent Garden – slap bang in the middle of Neal's Yard. This charmingly chic bistro – complete with curated antiques and a black bicycle parked out front – somehow manages to strike just the right balance between familiar and fancy, with a day-to-night menu focusing on locally-sourced produce. We start with a crisp glass of bubbles as we make our selection, following the house suggestion of sharing three to five dishes between two. Plates are indulgent yet remarkably delicate; a vibrant ratatouille, fresh steak tartare, garlicky escargot, and decadent dauphinois. The standout is, unsurprisingly, Buvette's signature croques; we opted for the forestier, a vegetarian riff on the original, paired with a generous pour of white wine (French, naturally). To end, tarte tatin and a mousse au chocolat, followed by a perfectly chilled martini made just the way you like – a highlight among the well-executed classic cocktails on offer. I can’t wait to visit again, whether for a flaky morning croissant and espresso or another evening encounter with that croque... Drew Burns Address: Buvette London, 2 Neal's Yard, London WC2H 9DP Website: buvette-london.com Ornella, London Fields Foodies and film fanatics flocked to Lupa when it opened its doors in Highbury – an Italian feeding frenzy from restaurateur Ed Templeton and chef Naz Hassan, fuelled by The Gentleman star Theo James’ involvement. The reviews were promising, and bookings soon became hard to come by, so it came as no surprise when the trio announced a follow-up – Ornella. On the corner of a leafy suburban street in London Fields, this new arrival is an edible love letter to Milanese fare that the capital’s food scene has long been crying out for, named in honour of the late singer Ornella Vanoni. Inside, it’s simultaneously cosy and sexy, diners tucked into banquettes and huddled around circular tables illuminated by flickering candlelight. Proceedings start over punchy sbagliato and caffè amaro cocktails – easy on those, mind – before the fluffiest focaccia in town arrives, warm and doused in glittering olive oil, alongside wafer-thin slivers of salty mortadella and coppa. There’s a choice of four starters – shoutout to the sea bream tartare, I hear, from my companion – followed by five ‘primi’ dishes. We slurp on salty onion broth and twirl our forks to catch shavings of cheese in the simple yet moreish butter and Parmesan tagliatelle, all washed down with generous pours of Venetian Manzoni Bianco. Naturally, onto secondi, a satisfyingly crisp chicken Milanese, used mostly to mop up heaps of silky mashed potatoes that likely contain more butter than potatoes (no complaints from us). We saunter into the night, hands in circular motions on our stomachs, remarking on how beige and calorific our spread became. No regrets at all, mind, as we plot our return to get snug in one of Ornella’s corners when the mercury drops, if not before. Connor Sturges Address: Ornella, 51 Wilton Way, London E8 1BG Website: ornella.restaurant Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. Here, a communal oval table sits opposite the kitchen, where an intimate group sit watching folds of dough being expertly handcrafted into pasta and breadsticks by the chefs in their whites. Inspired by the Baroque palazzos of Southern Italy, the restaurant is adorned with custom-made Murano chandeliers hanging from tall ceilings, held up by dramatic pillars adjoined to a waffled terracotta ceiling, which makes me think of a gelato cone. The scene here on a Tuesday evening is mostly out-of-town pals sharing plates, business comrades and on this occasion, a Hollywood A-lister, but the winning majority here were couples holding hands across tables and huddled in booths. We start by nibbling on the longest breadsticks I’ve ever seen - simple and all unique, the only concern is filling up on them, but they are surprisingly light. Next comes an injection of colour with the Pipi Cruski Limone Di Rocca Mayo, a traditional dish of fire-red peppers that are fried and best enjoyed slovenly dipped into lemon butter. Despite the colour, these aren’t spicy and have the most excellent crunch. Among the tables, we tuck into an antipasti of Orkney scallops, which are tender but fragrant alongside Batutta Di Manzo Inglese, a refreshing mix of chopped beef, salad leaves, pomegranate seeds and large shavings of black truffle. Mouths still full but contentedly chatting, it’s easy to see the inspiration behind this place. With excellent company and ambience, come and come again, but definitely share the hand-made pasta with native blue lobster sauce and T-bone among the table, while you snack on humble traditional Sicilian vegetables and of course, an entire bowl of zucchini sticks. To finish, the showstopping Tiramisu is necessary - presented to the table in a family-style bowl, the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ Kumori, Soho Slap-bang in the heart of Soho, Kumori is a 30-seat handroll bar where most of the action happens at the counter, creating an intimate, immersive feel. Inside, the space feels a little like stepping into a spaceship – all brushed-metal surfaces and iridescent pink and purple lighting. From the plump made-to-order handrolls to the carefully curated soundtrack, everything about Kumori feels cool, fresh and considered. Knees brush as we pore over the tick-box menu, leaving me spiralling as I weigh up how many of the handrolls I can reasonably fit in; there are simply too many good options. The cocktail list is an equally delicious debate, eventually landing on a yuzu mezcal margarita and sitting back to settle in for the show. Behind the counter, chefs move with speed and precision through a menu curated by head chef John Randy De Guzman (formerly Nobu, Tobi Masa and Katsuya). Each roll is served from chef to patron the moment it’s made, turning dinner into a kind of live theatre. Lucy Bruton Address: Kumori, 26 Denman Street, London W1D 7HX Website: kumorirestaurant.com Best new London restaurants in May 2026 Tavern, Shoreditch I’m still thinking about those little melted cheese-filled choux buns that kicked off dinner (the chunion puff), and the dense brown butter muffin that we finished on. But also every course we inhaled in between, which was cooked on open flames from the team behind Michelin-starred Restaurant St Barts in Farringdon. Nest, the high-end tasting-menu restaurant that once sat on this site, is no longer open. The trio behind it, Johnnie Crowe (Co-founder), Brendan Appleby (executive chef), and Kirsty Easterbrook (head chef), have moved away from fine dining, rebranding and reopening as Tavern, a much more casual affair with a nose-to-tail concept using seasonal British produce. I loved the new bistro-style interiors mixed with oldy-worldy pub furnishings. Dark, mismatched wooden chairs, scattered with shaggy sheepskins, are tucked beneath linen-topped tables with flickering candles. Kick things off with a Tavern Pickleback cocktail – a dirty martini infused with pickle juice, served with a cocktail stick of cured meat inside. Small plates (actually on the larger size) are flung out of the kitchen quickly; order the fire bread coated in wild garlic and, obviously, the chunion puff to start. For mains, we loved the asparagus with a dollop of buttery hollandaise and cured egg yolk, the pork and cuttlefish sausage with squid-ink mustard and the huge joint of smoky sirloin with a side of charred leaves, beetroot and horseradish. For dessert, have the black koji custard tart, bitter and sweet at the same time. Sophie Knight Address: Tavern, 374-378 Old Street, London, EC1V 9LT Website: tavernlondon.co.uk The Latimer, North Kensington The Latimer is a true family effort. It's been recently brought to life by Rochelle Canteen co-founder Melanie Arnold, St John and Sessions Arts Club partner Jon Spiteri, and their three children, Lorcan, Fin, and Molly, who have brought their own prowess to London hotspots Caravel and Koya, respectively. Given this resume, I already knew I’d be in good hands when it came to the food, but the clan have also captured a remarkably warm neighbourhood feel. Though it’s been open for just over a week, when we visit, guests here walk around comfortably with a sense of knowing the place. We ordered grilled asparagus in a herb sauce we’d drink by the bowl if we could, confit trout with green beans and new potatoes, and our must-have: unbelievably tender pork belly skewers braised in cider, served with a dollop of applesauce. Grilled-to-perfection sea bream with tiny green and yellow tomatoes in a delectable aioli, and a courgette linguine tossed in stracciatella followed. There are two desserts – an amaretti crumble and a chocolate mousse. Plus, I’m impressed by the drinks here – at £12, they’re decently priced for West London and the chicest thing about the pub. I opt for the Westway, a tequila-and-blood-orange shrub short drink, but mentally bookmark South of the Border, a black coffee-and-reposado tequila drink, for when I’m next here on a weekend. Tamara Southward Address: 274 Latimer Road, London W10 6QW Website: thelatimer.co.uk Bar Etna, Newington Green Does London really need another hype-y pizza joint? Having been left as cold as a next-day margarita by a couple of recent openings, I was sceptical – but having spent the evening being charmed and carbloaded by the team at Bar Etna, I can attest that it absolutely does. Perhaps I shouldn’t have been surprised – this is the dream-team project from Four Legs’ Ed McIlroy (Finsbury Park’s Tollington and The Plimsoll) and Joe Beddia (owner of Philadelphia-based, Bib Gourmand-garlanded Pizzeria Beddia). Their special relationship has resulted in an East Coast pizza bar with mid-century Milanese design and top-notch seasonal British ingredients. The downstairs bar is reserved for walk-ins, while upstairs is (slightly) more formal tables, where we huddle knee-to-knee with strangers in front of an open kitchen from which servers twirl out piping pizzas. The menu is no-fuss: three spritzes plus a special (a tomatini-inspired affair on our visit); negronis or vermouth on tap; an Italian-focused wine list; a couple of snacks; and four thin-crust, Italian-American style pizzas to choose from. Creamy “judion” (butter) beans arrive floating in silky olive oil and liberally doused with salt and lemon zest – perfectly simple and perfectly done, a hint of what’s to come. The must-order tomato pie is a Philly staple of salty, herby tomatoes spread on springy focaccia. My fellow diner deems it “the best, most upscale version of primary school traybake pizza you’ve ever had”. For pizza, we go for a simple Number One (tomato, mozzarella and Neal’s Yard coolea), which elegantly manages the dance between a thin, crispy base and a satisfying amount of flop. The Number Two (cream, cantabrian chillis, greens, coolea) is our favourite, with just the right amount of chilli heat, but the appropriately volcanic Etna Curry Pizza blows my socks off with one bite; it’s not for me, but those made of stronger stuff might enjoy this playful tribute to a curry house saag paneer. A stainless steel coupe of espresso soft serve is tiny and chic and just right to cut through all the carbs. One night after opening, Bar Etna was heaving, with a real house party feel. With plans for late-night pizzas by the slice on Fridays and Saturdays, I can already tell that the pavement outside will be spilling over this summer – and with the recently opened The Gold Tooth (from the pair behind London Fields’ Papi) and existing favourites Cadet and Yield nearby, Newington Green is fast becoming one of the buzziest food spots in this part of town. Olivia Squire Address: 47 Newington Green, London N16 9PX Website: instagram.com/bar.etna.london Idalia at Pillar Hall, Olympia There’s something sparkly happening in West London. Last month saw the opening of Pillar Hall – a landmark new live music venue, 30,000ft restaurant and speakeasy set within a truly magnificent Grade II-listed space, as part of Olympia’s tidy £1.3 billion regeneration. Originally designed in 1886 by architect Henry Edward Coe, it was built for exhibitions, concerts and even the circus. Vivienne Westwood staged her first catwalk show here; Britain hosted one of its earliest film screenings; and now, 140 years on, it’s back with a new outfit for a fresh dose of razzle-dazzle. At its heart sits the sweeping restaurant, Idalia. The name is an alternative moniker for Aphrodite that was rather more in vogue in the 1880s. The vast, gleaming dining room is all verdant glamour, inspired by the nearby gardens of Kensington and Olympia, with space for 300 – so not your quiet Tuesday supper spot. The sparkling wine list is all English and excellent, but do start with one of the cocktails, which are playful, theatrical things served in everything from pink-crusted globes to glass handbags as an homage to Dolce & Gabbana. Of course, it’s a fine dining experience. In the kitchen, Samantha Williams – formerly Angela Hartnett’s executive chef – delivers a modern British menu with the odd Asian interlude. Reasons why, unsure, but why not, I say – and to be fair, the Asian stuff is really good. A bowl of Gochujang chicken thighs are juicy, crispy and drizzled in zesty sriracha mayo, while the whole roasted Turbot, which arrives theatrically and is deboned tableside, comes with a heaping scoop of shichimi togarashi butter oozing atop the skin and some fresh pickled daikon. It’s melty-soft and perfect for sharing, best served with a side of the beef tallow chips – the swankiest fish and chips you’ll eat all year bar none. Finish with the pistachio cheesecake, which is truly humongous and has famously racked up quite a reputation in only the first week of opening. This is a thoroughly grand affair perfect for your next big do – and such a glitzy night deserves a little flourish. Charley Ward Address: Pillar Hall, Olympia Way, London W14 0EY Website: pillarhall.co.uk Fenix, Mayfair I’ll never say no to a Greek salad, but a salad plus endless dips, pittas and charcoal-fired meats and seafood? Count me in. Fenix is a smart Greek-Mediterranean restaurant in the heart of Mayfair (right next to Green Park station), serving sharing plates with a slightly modern twist. The menu is split into spreads, salad, cold dishes, meze, open fire, pasta and rice and sides, and the choice is overwhelming – in the best way. At first glance, I knew I'd have trouble choosing from the vast menu, and there were multiple extra dishes I’d have chosen if I had endless stomach space, but in the end, we went for a little bit of everything. Start with the dips – the spicy feta is creamy with a bit of a kick, but the smoked taramasalata was the real star of the show; full of flavour, a perfect smooth texture and just gorgeous spread across pillowy pita. We saved a little bit of our dips for the meze (the halloumi tempura and caramelised aubergine with tahini miso are must-orders) and added spicy sea bass carpaccio, spicy sweetcorn and orzo with langoustine and feta to finish things off. There wasn’t a dish I regretted, although in hindsight I was probably too stuffed for the crème brûlée – but who can say no to a sweet treat? The space is massive, but it still feels intimate. During our Thursday night dinner, we were catered to by multiple members of staff (all of them friendly and knowledgeable) and our reservation was stretched out for nearly three hours, without ever feeling rushed. The decor is clearly slightly themed towards a taverna (think raffia and wood, plenty of greenery and paved flooring) but avoids being gimmicky thanks to the chic combination of textures and light colour palette. I’d come back here with friends visiting London to show them a cool spot in the city, and for a menu with an endless list of crowd-pleasers. Address: Fenix, Stratton House, 80 Piccadilly, London W1J 8HX Website: fenixrestaurants.com Café Jikoni, Stratford It’s rare for a toastie to be anything more than a rushed, forgettable meal, but at Café Jikoni, that all changed. The Goan aubergine achaar and Mony’s cheddar toastie was one of the best bites I’ve had this year, and without question the finest toastie I’ve ever eaten. The staff insisted we try it, and despite my initial scepticism at choosing a sandwich over something more elaborate, I was quickly proved wrong. It was spicy, oozing, and bright with freshness. To me, the mark of an exceptional chef lies in their ability to elevate the humble. Ravinder Bhogal is a clear master of this, able to refine even the most staple of dishes. Born in Kenya to Indian parents, she is an award-winning food writer, TV presenter, journalist, cook, and restaurateur, and her breadth of experience is evident in every dish. Jikoni Marylebone has long been an essential part of London's dining scene, and now Bhogal has expanded the concept with an all-day café and restaurant housed on the lower ground floor of the new V&A East Museum in Stratford. The striking building feels like a natural home for her food: elevated yet relaxed, inclusive, and creative. Standouts ranged from the nibbles – such as the Shambaa pickles and umami-rich oregano fries – to larger plates like butter beans aglio e olio, topped with irresistibly crunchy pangrattato, and a deeply comforting massaman curry. As someone who eats predominantly plant-based, I found Jikoni sets a high bar for vegetarian cooking, proving it can be just as inventive, flavourful, and satisfying as any meat-based dish. The tofu massaman and butter beans were particularly vibrant and memorable. From the drinks list, the sweet, smoky strawberry margarita and a satisfyingly dry martini are both worth your time. To finish, I watched the sun set over the canal while indulging in an intensely rich Vietnamese coffee brownie, alongside a picture-perfect yuzu, pandan, and strawberry iced bun. Address: Café Jikoni at the V&A East Museum, 107 Carpenters Rd, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, E20 2AR Website: jikonilondon.com Best new London restaurants in April 2026 Teal by Sally Abé, Hackney Tucked along a leafy Hackney street, Teal by Sally Abé feels immediately at home among neighbourhood pubs, cafés and delis, just a short stroll from London Fields. With its soft green interiors, potted plants and light-filled dining room, the space strikes a balance between relaxed local charm and quietly confident fine dining. This is the latest opening from Sally Abé, whose résumé spans some of London’s most respected kitchens, including Restaurant Gordon Ramsay, The Ledbury and The Harwood Arms. Here, her cooking leans into British produce with a sense of nostalgia, revisiting historic touches such as the £1 “penny lick”, a playful nod to Victorian-era street treats. The menu opens with thoughtful bites, including a standout Locket’s savoury: a salty-sweet mouthful of Stilton on toast, with a fruity finish. Starters showcase the kitchen’s finesse, particularly a delicately balanced asparagus tartlet with Old Winchester, and a Dorset crab royale lifted by peas and lovage. Mains are richer and more robust, from an artichoke and hazelnut vol-au-vent to beef sirloin with wild garlic, Cornish mussels, and a deeply flavoured haunch of deer. Desserts are a highlight. A marmalade ice cream sandwich walks the line between bitter and sweet, while a marshmallow teacake paired with Earl Grey custard offers a playful finish. While traditional British menus can lean heavily towards meat, Teal makes a strong case for its vegetable dishes, which stand confidently alongside their counterparts. The wine list is thoughtfully curated yet accessible, with English options such as Sussex sparkling wines appealing to the local crowd. Service is warm and assured, completing a restaurant that already feels like a natural fixture in the area. Address: Teal by Sally Abé, 52 Wilton Way, London Fields, E8 1BS Website: tealbysallyabe.com Taverna Ermou, Marylebone Taverna Ermou is the closest you’ll feel to being in a Greek taverna in London. Tiled chequered floor, marble tables topped with a little candle, traditional chairs made of wood and straw and lots of framed hand crochet doilies often seen in old-school Greek homes. Staff dressed in white shirts and black aprons run around serving a packed out and very loud restaurant off the already busy James Street in central London. This is the second branch of Ermou, following the original in Athens. It’s warm, welcoming and slightly chaotic – a recipe for a fun evening with friends. The menu is like the interiors: extremely traditional. Expect classics like tzatziki, Greek salad, and super succulent chicken souvlaki. Plates are meant to be shared, served on stainless steel platters and thrown in the middle of the table – we were happy to find there's no skimping on portion sizes either. Every dish was big enough for at least three or four people to share happily. You’ll want to order a bunch of dips, we can’t recommend the deconstructed spanakopita dip enough – a warm spinach and feta paste served with crispy bread. Then order mezze plates, including the Saganaki, which we have seen pop up all over our Instagram: a runny graviera cheese coated in a flaky kataifi phyllo sprinkled with pistachios and spicy honey. A fresh salad and a few bigger plates from the grill and pasta section, such as spiced beef and lamb kebabs, charred octopus and rich creamy crab orzo. We’ve also heard great things about the brunch menu. This all-day dining spot might have just taken the lead as the best Greek restaurant in London. Sophie Knight Address: Taverna Ermou, 38-40 James Street, London W1U 1EU Website: ergonfoods.com Burro, Covent Garden Burro – or butter, in Italian – certainly lives up to its name. Simple ingredients reign supreme here, but in our three-course dinner, we had anchovies with butter and crostini, sole with a butter-and-prosecco sauce, and garlicky Jersey royal potatoes swimming in the good stuff. Personally, I had no complaints (the more butter, the better), but diners should be warned that it’s easy to lean towards heavy dishes… although, isn’t that what lovely Italian dining should be about? It’s very easy to over-order when the menu starts with a selection of antipasti so tempting you could ask for one of each, but I’d certainly recommend the aforementioned anchovies, plus pillowy-fresh foccacia and melty Salumi. When it came to Primi, we misjudged; the fettuccine with duck and porcini ragù was heavy and a little salty; in all honesty, I had hoped for a little more flavour or fun. The sole lifted my spirits a little, but it was dessert – rhubarb granita with vanilla cream – that really left me wanting more. It’s rare for me to skip a tiramisu, but in this case, I was ready for something a little bit lighter, and thank god, because I stumbled upon one of my favourite puddings in a long time. The restaurant is undoubtedly set for big things: its location in Floral Court in Covent Garden is pretty perfect, and comes from a known name in the industry, Conor Gadd, co-owner of much-loved Highbury restaurant Trullo. This is a more suave, grown-up version, where theatre-goers mingle with after-work diners, and the vibe inside is relaxed and fun – helped along by a great team of staff who happily share suggestions. High ceilings, fancy tablecloths, and art dotted across the walls add to the opulence. I'll certainly return to try the constantly changing menu, but I'll be hoping the granita remains. Abigail Malbon

item.title: My favourite Airbnb: I had my ‘friendmoon’ at an art-filled Renaissance haven in the Tuscan hills
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.20
Most people's memories of their wedding day is that it passed in a blur and a flash. The adrenaline, excitement and emotion all kicks in and you're whirled from one moment to the next without any time to process or soak it all in. I had been told this by many (many) people before I celebrated my own nuptials in May this year, so I made a point of stretching out my celebrations for as long as I could feasibly get away with. For fun, and as a massive thank you, we whisked our bridesmaids and groomsmen to a celebratory ‘friendmoon’ straight after the wedding. We got married in Italy and this was an excuse to spoil our wedding party, show our gratitude, and cheers to their vaillant organisational efforts. With heads still aching from the day before, we drove out into the Tuscan countryside, passing through charming Chianti villages, tootling down long, winding roads carved into hillsides and meandering through avenues lined with Cypress trees. Down one such lane lay Villa Tinaccio – our home for the next few days. This Renaissance villa is one of Tuscany’s most impressive estates. Owned by the same family since the early 14th century, it’s a haven of classic Italian charm – think soaring alcoves, manicured gardens and endless views of the countryside. The family have looked after the building well, carefully restoring crumbling corners, renovating defunct hosting spaces into sprawling bedrooms and adorning each majestic hallway and empty wall space with what must surely be one of the region’s most remarkable art collections. We entered through the main courtyard to be welcomed by an iron-faced Anthony Gormley statue, standing to attention and surrounded by a U-shaped building. Behind the bronze figure lies the east wing, where the family stays when they visit their country estate, and opposite that is the west wing. This was our digs for the next few nights – a vast expanse with three dining rooms, two living areas, seven bedrooms, and a newly renovated annexed wing. Not in any way aligned with the uni halls we'd shared with a clutch of this group not so many years ago… Alongside the Gormley, there is a staggering collection of other artwork to admire. A stone structure from sculptor Richard Long stretches across one corridor; one of Loris Cecchini’s Waterbones installations extends across the loggia and, come sundown, large-scale light installations by Italian artist Massimo Uberti blink to life in the garden. A stay really was like living in our own private art gallery – every wall and corridor is adorned with jaw-dropping art from world-renowned artists. But while the villa is home to many-a masterpiece, the garden is surely the estate’s magnum opus. A stone balcony proudly overlooks a saltwater pool, fringed with sun loungers, manicured hedges and lemon trees. A family of turtles – a protected local species – call these gardens their home, quietly roaming the grounds, munching on grass here, snoozing in the sun there. As the newlyweds, we got to stay in the recently renovated ground floor suite. The space is immense, with soaring wooden ceilings, flagstone floors, towering armoires and massive tapestries draped on the walls. It even had its own private sitting room, with an impressive selection of books ranging from Italian history to holiday reads to borrow for your stay. The bathroom is a sight to behold, with two (!) marble bathtubs, his-and-hers sinks, and an entire wall covered in a floor-to-ceiling mirror. Other bedrooms varied in size, some bright and airy with butter-yellow walls and freshly picked flowers from the garden, others a deep magenta colour with low-slung wooden beams and shuttered windows looking out across the rounds. Days here passed slowly – breakfast on the loggia, morning swims in the pool, strolls through the gardens. The villa was ours should you wish to spend the stay in complete seclusion, but the caretaker lives down the lane and can help book private chefs, wine tastings or excursions. Our chef for the week was the wonderful Anna Cieno, who whipped us up incredible multi-course feasts featuring crispy courgette flowers stuffed with buffalo ricotta and salty anchovies and creamy gazpacho with taggiasche olives and a caper berry tapenade, to creative takes on classic dishes, like a lasagne-cum-millefeuille made of carasau bread, buffalo mozzarella and confit cherry tomatoes drizzled with basil oil.

item.title: The most exciting hotel openings in Europe this summer, recommended by the editors who were first through the doors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.04
New hotel openings are something that gets us over-excited at Conde Nast Traveller, and we're exceptionally lucky to be the first people through the doors at some of the world's most hotly anticipated places to stay. In Europe, the summer season is well underway, and spots we've had our eyes on for months are now welcoming those guests committed to living their Eurosummer dreams. From 11-bed boutique hotels in the Menorcan valleys to Greek resorts and converted palazzos in Italy, these are the best of the region's new openings, tried, tested and (crucially) recommended by the editors. Editor's picks Best in Spain: Binidufa, Menorca Best in Greece: Santa Marina Arachova, Athens Best in Italy: Orient Express Venezia, Venice Best in France: Zannier Île de Bendor, near Provence - Read Full ReviewThis feel-good spot has embraced Mallorca’s lightness and carefree attitude by showcasing the work of its artists and creatives – the very people who have helped shape the island into the hotspot it is today. But Mandarin Oriental’s Asian heritage runs through its veins, so its dedication to care, service, and attention to detail remains. In Mallorca, this attitude is delivered with a Spanish softness so pure it feels infectious. The sound of the waves is like a backing track throughout a stay here – the property, which spans three hectares, clings to the rusty orange cliff and has direct access to two tiny but perfectly formed calas. There are two pools, too: one overlooked by the Mediterranean restaurant Lepocc and another for families with a breezy Greek restaurant at its foot. Rooms are bright, spacious and decorated in sunshine tones to reflect the surrounding rocks, and greens – inspired by the pines and the ever-changing colours of the sea. Take a boat from the private pier to Puerto Portals to experience the glossy side of the island but be sure to make time for the spa, too. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewIf there was one place in Europe missing a Four Seasons Hotel, it was Mykonos. The brand’s second Greek property – following the 2019 opening of Four Seasons Astir Palace in Athens – has exceeded expectations. Set on the island's quieter side, away from the throng of nightlife but close enough that guests interested can visit with ease, it’s the brainchild of Greek architect Nicos Valsamakis, and has been designed to mimic a traditional Mykonian village. Boxy white buildings tumble down the hillside towards the hotel’s private beach, and cobbled courtyards with trailing pink bougainvillaea add warmth. Pops of painted blue and – surprisingly – postbox red create that quintessentially Aegean aesthetic, and local details infiltrate every room. The food is stellar, as is the service, but there isn’t a shred of pretence about any of it. Somehow, the brand has created a boutique feeling in a resort setting, and there’s no better combination in my eyes. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewNo one wants to see the decline of a much-loved friend, and so it was a relief when I learned that Four Seasons had taken over the running of Hotel Danieli. One of Venice’s most glamorous addresses, it has stood on the Riva degli Schiavoni, next to the Doge’s Palace, for well over five centuries. It has suffered in the past from a kind of medieval typecasting – dark opulence with heavy damasks and a lot of deep reds, lavishly gilded woodwork, and the kind of furnishing that would require six strapping gondoliers to shift. You almost expected the waiters in the Bar Dandolo to appear in tights and codpieces. By the beginning of our own century, the Danieli’s famed splendour was getting a little thread-bare, so when Four Seasons arrived in 2023, they took the decision to close the hotel for renovation, only opening its doors again in August 2026. The result is a triumph. I would venture that at no point in its history has the Danieli looked this good. Elaborate chandeliers were sent back to Murano for refurbishment; the Academy of Fine Arts restored the painted ceilings; and local artisans refurbished the grand staircase, Corinthian columns and decorative stonework. Designer Pierre-Yves Rochon has transformed the rooms by bringing the colours and the light of the Venetian lagoon into expanded suites and gracious living areas – celadon green, softs blues, the champagne tones of Venetian skies. Everywhere there are mirrors, expanding space, playing with Venetian light: those undulating reflections, those scorci or glimpses of people, panoramas, passing boats, the sense of mirages, that are so much a part of Venice. Few hotel reopenings have been as hotly anticipated, and fewer still have succeeded so spectacularly. Stanley Stewart - Read Full ReviewAmong a sea of uniform properties on the island, Fouquet's Mykonos really does stand out. On paper, it follows a tried-and-tested formula: the aesthetic draws on its natural surroundings, suites are built into the island’s landscape, and its food and wellness offerings are superb. But it’s the design here that sets it apart. Unlike its neighbours, Fouquet's isn’t afraid to add colour, pattern and statement artwork to the white- and stone-hued architecture, making things that little bit more fun. At the Roka pool and beach restaurant, loungers come in rusty orange and sunshine yellow hues that mimic the skies at golden hour, and throughout the shared spaces, bold, conversation-starting artwork and sculptures – including an original Salvador Dalí – add charisma. There are only 60 suites, plus three enormous private villas, and my beachfront bungalow is so large I could cartwheel across it like a gymnast at the Olympics. The private terrace is decked out with plush loungers and the walk-in wardrobe is as indulgent as a private shopping suite. Built a little higher into the craggy rockface are equally beautiful, slightly smaller suites with picture-perfect private plunge pools overlooking the sea. After sunset, those looking for a sophisticated scene with Ibiza-worthy music (and a subtle rather than outlandish party vibe) will find no better dinner spot than Roka, the on-site restaurant. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewHope, an 1867 hunting lodge and collection of cottages whose revamping into an exclusive-use retreat has been 15 years in the making, is arguably the most ambitious opening yet from conservation pioneer WildLand. Akin to a Scottish safari lodge, its latest outpost treads lightly on the land and directs guests’ attention outwards wherever possible: through floor-to-ceiling windows; bracing dips in lochs and hikes in munros; and a gloriously tactile, proudly of-its-place design referencing British craftsmanship and the great Scottish wilderness on its doorstep. Days are organised not by schedules, but by elemental “rhythms” – earth, fire, water – that flow through everything from the activities to the music playing. On the grounding “earth” day, a sound bath in the subterranean, supervillain-style Earth room makes me feel like I’m melting into a moss-textured rug. “Water” day opens with a walk into a freezing loch, emerging renewed to a crackling campfire and ginger shots and a run to the outdoor cedar sauna. Guests might want to thread together an itinerary with WildLand’s nearby properties, Lundies House and Kinloch Lodge, or drive the North Coast 500 road. But really, this is a place you come to forget the rest of the world, and the daily immersions in nature and cossetting interiors are more than enough to justify staying in one place. Olivia Squire - Read Full ReviewThat overworked trope, hidden gem, actually makes sense when you enter Aria Hotels’ adults-only resort, which teeters above sheer cliffs of capital Manolas on Santorini’s under-the-radar sister island, Thirasia. Apart from zingy fresh vegetables and fruit grown in the island’s mineral-rich volcanic soil, and bread and dakos rusks baked fresh in islands ovens, everything has to be ferried over from the mainland, so logistics are crazy – waiting until the morning ferry arrives to get milk for your morning coffee is standard, but that’s all part of the fun. 11 cave-style suites with graceful domed roofs and arched interiors, whitewashed like snow inside and out, are modelled on the island’s traditional yposkafo cave houses. Clinging by their toes to the edge of a cliff in capital Manolas, they gaze out over the taverna-lined turquoise horseshoe curve of Korfos Bay to Santorini opposite. Carefully styled by the owner, interiors are immensely well thought out. High ceilings frame, cool tiled floors and curved interior windows, curtains and textiles are sourced from local loved Athens company Kamarinos Design, and bespoke silk artworks were handcrafted by artisans Zografos from Soufli in northern Greece. This is a place to chill, baby, chill. Slinky bamboo sun beds by the infinity pool with views over island capital Manolas (where most of the 150-something inhabitants go about their lives blissfully removed from world outside), invite you to linger. I was entranced by those spectacular views, the cluttered of Manolas’ blue-trimmed whitewashed houses linked by narrow steps leading up and down between blue-domed churches above the scimitar curve of Korfos Bay. Best enjoyed whilst sipping handcrafted cocktails whisked up by manager Filipos and his amiable staff. Heidi Fuller-Love - Read Full ReviewDown a suitably grand wide driveway where grazing sheep stretch out in the sprawling grounds near Winchcombe, you’ll find the newly renovated Dumbleton Hall. This 19th-century Cotswold stone estate has entered an ambitious new chapter following a major restoration inside and out. Built on a historic wool fortune – the Cotswolds area is well loved for its wool products, as well as its lavender – the manor house has long been a literary and cultural hub, having hosted the likes of Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell, and John Betjeman, among others. Now, within the old stone exterior, it’s a thoroughly refreshed take on country living, with maximalist Belle Époque-inspired interiors (they’ve somehow made leopard print rugs work in an olde worlde country manor) with far-reaching bucolic views across the hotel’s peaceful grounds and lake. It’s a true taste of the good life, made a little more elevated – settle in by a roaring hearth, tuck into a seasonal British plate, then sip slowly on something in the Library Bar, which is lined wall to wall with books. It stands out against neighbouring Cotswolds heavyweights by deftly combining the grandeur and scale of an old estate scale with an intimate ease that evokes staying at a stylish friend’s country seat over a stuffy old hotel. Charley Ward - Read Full ReviewLuura is the first outpost from a new hotel group of the same name, and if its debut – on the west coast of Paros – is anything to go by, it’s one to keep an eye on. Just 13 days old when I arrive, it already has the confidence of a far more established spot, only without any of the showiness. Forget the usual Greek-island formula of whitewashed minimalism: the design is earthy and tactile, with honey-hued limestone, dark wood, rich linens and striking artworks inspired by the island woven into the landscape. There’s an emphasis on all things local that feels genuine and considered, whether it’s the handmade furniture and ceramics dotted about the hotel, or the fresh produce sourced from Paros’ farmers and cheesemakers perfectly plated at the buffet breakfast. Speaking of which, the food is a knockout; at Lenea, Mediterranean dishes come with Lebanese touches; at Mimi Kakushi, celebratory Japanese plates are served with killer sunset views. The key, though, is the people: warm, utterly charming staff, and a creative, easygoing crowd add to the sense that even this early on, Luura will quickly become the kind of place you can linger longer. Add thoughtful wellness and suites designed down to the smallest detail, and Luura makes one heck of a case for this quieter corner of Paros. Sarah Allard - Read Full ReviewThere’s something wonderfully transportative about arriving at Binidufà. It’s built into a verdant valley on a private estate in the depths of the Menorcan countryside, and as we drive through one of the island’s traditional wooden gates on the approach, the experience feels surreal – almost otherworldly. It’s the second hotel in the Vestige Collection to open on this family-owned estate in as many years, and while there’s a distinct commonality between the two, Binidufà is undeniably special. There are only 11 rooms, scattered across the grounds, and a huge amount of space, both inside and out. All have private terraces and bathrooms big enough to live in. I can’t help noting how private it would feel here, even at capacity. Guests are openly encouraged to flit between the valley and the hilltop, where sister hotel Son Ermità sits like a crown and boasts show-off views that span earth, sea, and a very impressive sky, especially at night. Mesura, the restaurant at Binidufà, is plant-based and champions locality. Creative veggie and vegan dishes (with the option to add a fish or tofu topping) are designed to share and change with the seasons. It’s a concept that feels wholly fitting to its fairytale setting, and I surprised myself by deeming the pumpkin and beetroot dishes so good that I ordered them two nights in a row. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewSublime is famed for being the place to stay in Comporta, so when it announced a new villa-first opening a stone’s throw from the original property, it’s fair to say interest among the Conde Nast Traveller editors piqued. With the promise of even more private space than the original hotel, Monaco-born Beefbar as the main restuarant, slick wellness facilities and a stellar family offering, it feels different enough to its sister property (now renamed Sublime Terracotta) to feel like a totally different hotel. All 43 villas and 124 rooms are peppered throughout 51 hectares of land, which will, in time, be immersed in jungle-like vegetation and feel wholly private – there’s quite a bit of growing to be done before that’s the case, though. Facilities are king, and are shared between the two hotels, so building a Comporta itinerary without so much as veering away from Sublime is entirely possible, especially if restaurant-hopping is on your agenda. There are 6 in total here, the most famous being Sublime beach club, to which the hotel runs shuttles throughout the day. To me, Sublime Sands felt reminiscent of Soho Farmhouse but with a Portuguese twist, and that’s a good thing. The main courtyard, glass-walled restaurant, indoor/outdoor pool and snazzy kids’ club all sit within easy distance of one another and guests can grab an e-Bike to glide through the grounds to their accommodation with ease. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewThe visual pageantry within the 15th-century Palazzo Donà Giovannelli is evident from arrival, as the private motoscafi docks outside the unique pink-and-white chequered façade – the mid-19th-century handiwork of influential architect Giovanni Battista Meduna, and, until recently, hidden under plain paint. This is just one of the many gems uncovered by Aline Asmar d’Amman, the visionary powerhouse, architect and interior designer behind Orient Express Venezia. To listen to Aline poetically describe this eight-year-long restoration project, where she witnessed stones, one by one, be removed, restored and put back in place, along with layers of paint peeled back to reveal original frescos, is to be drawn into the romantic mythology of this palace. There’s an enveloping comfort and warmth to the hotel, a notable feat when many of Venice’s palaces can feel dusty, cold, and dare I say, haunted. The Corte del Conte, the palm court-style lobby, is a dazzling spectacle of soaring beams, Murano chandeliers and plush velvet seating. There are 47 rooms and suites, all singular in their layout and design. My favourite is the jewel-box Cherubini Suite, a vision of loveliness with a rediscovered frieze by Sebastiano Santi running along the wall in the sitting room, and a blue-domed ceiling with a Murano chandelier in the bedroom. Orient Express has landed Heinz Bek, the famed three-Michelin-starred German chef, to oversee the dining experience, including his namesake restaurant. For a taste of the original Orient Express, The Wagon Bar is a pocket-sized Art Deco speakeasy reminiscent of a railcar. Lauren Burvill - Read Full ReviewThis newly redesigned hotel lies a few miles off the coastal town of Bandol on Île de Bendor, a seven-hectare island snapped up in 1950 by drinks entrepreneur Paul Ricard. The eccentric creator of pastis, turned his island into a hedonistic mini-world filled with creativity, nature and communality—and now his descendants are continuing that spirit in partnership with the Zannier hotel group. Zannier Île de Bendor leans into its Provencal roots, with a 1960s retro elegance that embraces the local community. Here, the feel is of a car-free village where guests visit the art gallery, attend craft workshops, rejuvenate in the spa’s Iyashi Dôme, and snorkel. At the three restaurants, the fare ranges from pan-Mediterranean and Asian fusion to fine-dining Provencal cuisine. The 93 rooms and suites are divided into three uniquely ambient blocks, including a cute cluster of converted fishermen’s houses fronted by picket-fenced gardens. The fabulous rooftop terrace promises exquisite cocktails and sunset views of the rocky coastline. Noo Saro-Wiwa - Read Full ReviewFinca de la Bobadilla isn't technically a brand new opening, but it's a completely different hotel to what it was last year, after extensive rennovations and top-tier inclusions to its offering. Pulling into its 350-hectare estate, I’m met with a sign: ‘Hotel 2.5km’, and it puts the sheer size of the property’s grounds into perspective. There are just 73 rooms here, but the property itself is bigger than I imagined. There’s a fountain in the courtyard, a chapel with the largest privately owned organ in Europe and a Mezquita Cordoban-inspired ceiling in reception. And despite having elements of grandeur, there’s not a shred of pretence. Instead, a sense of homeliness filtrates the air. The aesthetic is beautiful and natural: think stone, wood and glossy ceramic tiling sourced in nearby towns, all bathed in natural light. Over the coming days, I realise the sound of water can be heard from just about anywhere I venture – a feature I’m told is typical of the Alhambra of Grenada, the closest city. If checking in and staying at the hotel is your MO – especially if you’d class yourself as ‘outdoorsy’ – there’s more than enough to keep you entertained for days. Horseback hacks through the estate are among the most popular pursuits, as well as excursions on foot or bike, either guided or self-led. Padel, pickleball and tennis courts are also available to book. The main pool is sublime, and the garden that surrounds it is dotted with plush loungers and thatched umbrellas, making it tempting to stay for hours on end. The spa is well worth visiting, too, equipped with a dry sauna and an infra-red sauna, a heated indoor pool and a dynamic pool with massage jets that promise to rid any post-flight stiffness. If that’s not going to do the trick, book a treatment with one of the on-site therapists. Visit our best family-friendly hotels in Spain guide for more on its children's offering. Sarah Leigh Bannerman - Read Full ReviewAirelles Palladio Venice is the first hotel from the Airelles group to open in Italy and the result is French grandeur in an authentically Venetian setting. It comprises four historic buildings from the 16th and 17th centuries. The Palladio building was designed by Andrea Palladio in 1561 and originally housed the Istituto delle Zitelle, famous for its lace (the ruff worn by Louis XIV at his coronation was made here). At the centre of the property is the church of Santa Maria della Presentazione, a gem with an octagonal dome and exquisite frescoes. Interiors are inspired by the city’s grand palazzos, with brocades, Murano glass and antiques artfully placed in a way that makes each room completely unique. For food lovers, this is a dream destination, and home to some of the world’s top chefs: Jean-Georges Vongerichten, Nobu Matsuhisa, the irresistible pâtissier Cédric Grolet, and the Italian chef Norbert Niederkofler, whose restaurant in Brunico has won three Michelin stars. Wellness is also a big deal here. The 1,700-square-metre, three-story Spa by Guerlain is the biggest wellness space in Venice. Sara Margo - Read Full ReviewThe largest hotel investment ever made in Crete, Ikos Sani Group’s eco-friendly 414-key sports-oriented beachfront property is their sixth venture in Greece, and is a welcome addition to the Ikos brand’s truly all-inclusive portfolio of luxury resorts. It’s an easy 45-minute drive from Chania Airport, but still manages to sit in a rural area renowned for its pristine beaches. Kissamos is a hopping-off point for the flamingo-pink sands, turquoise lagoons and dune-studded island scenery of Elafonisi (it gets busy in summer so go early). I’d need several pages to list all the activities in this resort, which focuses heavily on sports, both land and water – with free bikes available from the sports centre, cycling around this vast property is a workout in itself. You can also challenge your kids to a game of five-a-side football, padel or tennis, do some cardio in the gym, take out a sailing boat, learn to windsurf or join some of the classes ranging from TRX and Zumba to aqua aerobics and beginners’ yoga. After your exertions, book a massage (complimentary if you’re a Deluxe guest) in the cool, dimly lit spa, where enticing fragrances from Anne Semonin Paris products and soothing music are the backdrop for ice rooms, a salt room, thermal suite and sauna. Back in the rooms, interiors decked out with solid wood desks and low sturdy tables, well-upholstered sofas, jute mats and rugs on floors, wicker lampshades, ceramic bedside tables and natural fibres, feel earthy and rooted. This understated luxury suits the nature-focused surroundings, dotted with gnarled olive trees and flanked by vast gardens planted with sturdy drought-resistant local plant varieties. Don't miss those all-inclusive extras, including complimentary day loan of a Mini Countryman to explore the surroundings. Heidi Fuller-love - Read Full ReviewPerched on a hilltop in the heart of Chianti, between Panzano and Greve in Chianti, La Darbia occupies an idyllic sweep of land that spans 15 hectares of olive groves, woodland, wildflower meadows, and undulating lavender fields. Scattered throughout are 17 suites unfolding across the hillside in clusters of ancient stone farmhouses. No two rooms are alike, their proportions and personalities dictated by the quirks of the original buildings, but all claim equally lovely views. Some occupy the farmhouses on the lower slope, overlooking the cobbled courtyard and Mediterranean herb gardens, while others are slightly further up and offer panoramic views of the Panzano valley. Ambling down to breakfast from my hilltop suite, past fragrant herbs and wildflowers, I felt like I was staying in a little Tuscan village rather than a hotel or retreat. Meals are served at the terrace restaurant, with views stretching towards hilltop bastion Panzano. Executive chef Sebastiano Pagliaro oversees an ever-changing menu that draws on Chianti's rich agricultural heritage and the nearby Tuscan coast, showcasing regional cheeses, local meats, and freshly caught fish from Livorno. If your preferred holiday pace involves doing very little, this is an excellent place for it. La Darbia is as much about being immersed in the landscape as it is any organised activity, and most guests seem content to simply spend time outdoors. Walking paths thread through the lavender fields, which are dotted with forty beehives – home to the two million bees that produce the estate's honey. Laura Kettlewell - Read Full ReviewSanta Marina is a true family affair, created by Elias Papageorgiou, who is behind the namesake hotel in Mykonos. The venture here began with their own family house, a mountain retreat away from the heat and chaos of Athens and on the doorstep to some of the best skiing in the country. Its location in the hills above the traditional stone village of Arachova is a gateway into the rural mountainous region of Central Greece. There are just 20 rooms along the lower and upper floors of the main building, as well as two villas on the grounds, which are connected to the hotel facilities via panoramic stone terraces. Dining reflects the intimate size of the hotel, with all meals coming out of one main restaurant, though you can choose to eat in-room or upstairs in the lounge area by the fire. I recommend the restaurant for breakfast, which is a great buffet spread, while the other spaces lend more atmosphere especially for dinner. Arta Ghanbari - Read Full ReviewWith the structure of a typical Andalusian village, OKU (built on the site of a former hotel, to which new parts have been added) has a sloping layout: the highest part, at the top of the hill, is under construction and will house a spectacular area dedicated to young children, with a water park, a gazebo, suites for families. There are also tennis and paddle courts and, for golf fans, OKU Andalusia plans to collaborate with nearby golf courses. Currently the resort has 105 rooms and all beds face the sea, but by 2026 there will be 255, distributed in 14 categories, plus a spectacular villa. All rooms are rustic yet modern in style; the solid wood furniture comes from Bali and has been handcrafted, and ceramics, wicker lamps and raffia rugs are all items I dream of taking home. The breakfast is arguably the most exceptional I have ever tasted. Not only for its tremendous variety, but for its exquisite product quality and beautiful presentation. The best part? Having it first thing in the morning watching the sunrise on the terrace.
