When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. item.title: How To Turn a Long Flight Into Useful Personal Time
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.29
A long flight can feel like dead time because it sits between two places and belongs to neither. Yet it is also one of the few stretches in modern-day travel when everyday demands temporarily lose their grip. The trick is not to fill every minute but to offer a small menu of activities that fit different energy levels. A downloaded book, a notebook, a favorite album, and a short game of PlaySolitaire each offer a different way to experience the journey. That compact game loop matters because it creates a clear beginning and ending when the hours ahead feel shapeless. Stop Planning the Flight Like a Workday Travelers often board with an ambitious list. They plan to finish a novel, clear a laptop folder, watch three films, and arrive with a new language skill. This turns a quiet journey into a performance test. Cabin conditions rarely cooperate. Sleep may be broken, concentration can fade, and the person beside you may need to move just as you settle into something demanding. A better plan is flexible. Choose several low-effort options and let your attention decide which fits the moment. Build a Menu Instead of a Timetable A useful flight menu has contrast. Bring something to read, something to listen to, something to write, and something to play. Download what you need before leaving home because a plan that depends on perfect onboard internet is not much of a plan. Keep choices easy to reach. If every activity requires unpacking half your backpack, you will likely return to scrolling through the entertainment screen without choosing anything. Choose Activities With Natural Endings Open-ended entertainment can cause time to feel longer. Endless feeds and large game worlds provide no clear stopping point, so an hour disappears without feeling complete. A chapter, a crossword, a journal page, or a single hand of solitaire has a finish line. PlaySolitaire works well in this role because its rules are familiar and each round stands on its own. You can put it away when the meal arrives without feeling as though you have abandoned a larger mission. Load the game before departure so the cached version can be reopened if your flight lacks reliable Wi-Fi. Alternate Attention With Real Rest Not all quiet moments need an activity. After reading or watching something, close your eyes for a while. Look out the window when the view allows. Stretch when it is safe to move around the cabin and drink water regularly. The aim is not to defeat boredom at all costs. It is to move gently between focus and rest so neither becomes exhausting. A good activity should support that rhythm rather than call for constant attention. Leave Part of the Journey Unclaimed The most memorable travel days are rarely controlled minute by minute, and the journey can follow the same principle. Leave space for a conversation, an unexpected film, or simply doing nothing. Long flights become easier when they stop being a problem to solve. With a few carefully chosen options and permission to change your mind, the cabin becomes a temporary room of your own. You may not use every hour productively, but you can arrive feeling that the time was yours. This article was published in partnership with PlaySolitaire.io.

item.title: Review: CNOC Thru-bottle
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.44
The CNOC Thrubottle is a one-liter reusable bottle designed to replace the one-liter Smartwater bottles that many backpackers and thruhikers use today. It shares the same thin shape and 1 liter (33 oz) capacity as a Smartwater bottle, and it's compatible with Sawyer water filters and other bottles with a 28mm thread. It also has a tethered cap, pull lanyard, and exterior fluid markings. - Weight: 2.2 oz - Capacity: 1000 ml (33 oz) - Material: HDPE - BPA Free: Yes - Screw-cap: Yes (28mm compatible) - Dimensions: 2.9 x 12 inches - Heat-Tolerance: Safe up to 212°F, but keep exposure short to limit material fatigue One-liter Smartwater bottles are popular with backpackers and thruhikers because they're easy to pull out and replace in backpack side pockets; they're squeezable and thread-compatible with Sawyer water filters and other filters with 28mm threading. Smartwater water bottles are technically recyclable, but many end up in landfills when discarded. The CNOC Thrubottle is an alternative to Smartwater bottles that shares their benefits but goes beyond them in ways that backpackers and thruhikers can appreciate. - Graduated liquid markings along the side in both ounces and mL for rehydrating freeze-dried and dehydrated meals. - Has a tethered cap so you can't lose it. - Has a pull cord, which makes it easy to pull the bottle out of a pocket - Safe up to 212°F (100C), but keep exposure short to limit material fatigue. - Curbside recyclable - Constructed from durable materials, including long periods of sun exposure While the ThruBottle is reusable and could keep a lot of Smartwater bottles out of landfills (even though they're technically recyclable and returnable in many states), are any of these added features and capabilities must-haves? Not really. - The liquid measurements are useful, but you can slap a $5 sticker with the measurements onto a Smartwater bottle and still stay ahead pricewise since a 1L Smartwater bottle costs $3 and the Thrubottle costs $14. - The tethered cap is a win if you take your Sawyer filter off the bottle, although that's rare for some people. In any event, 28 mm caps are pretty easy to come by since other water and soft drink companies use them widely. - The pull cord is just nice to have, but not essential. No one is going to stop to use it to re-attach the Thrubottle to a backpack - The hot water capability isn't all that useful because the bottle doesn't have a wide mouth, which makes it difficult to put things like tea bags in or get them out Final Verdict While all of these features are nice-to-have, none of them will prevent you from losing the CNOC Thrubottle if it falls out of your backpack. But if you can avoid losing it, it's an excellent alternative to a Smartwater bottle or other commercial 28mm-compatible water bottles. Disclosure: CNOC provided a bottle for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. One of the things I dislike most of the Smartwater bottles is the sound they make when compressing them… not unique to most plastics but when it’s stored in certain locations (for example front chest pocket) it will sometimes make a soft popping/cracking noise as part of the plastic is continuously compressed and relaxed. Does the CNOC make similar sounds? Might be worth the $10 to me for that reason alone. The plastic isn’t as crinkly , so not that I’ve found. You will probably go through 50 smart water bottles before this wears out so it pays for itself many times over…I bought them so I could get out of my pack half empty which was tough with a used smart water bottle as they get weaker over time and I am probably drinking those shed microplastics.. So true.

item.title: ‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.56
Renaissance art without the crowds in Italy Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna won me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel near Via delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. The Palazzo dei Diamanti was almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkin cappellacci, a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty. John One of Germany’s greenest cities Next to flashy Munich or cool Berlin, Hanover in northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallery Sprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – the Great Garden at Herrenhausen – impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multicultural Linden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at the Teestübchen. Ulrike The Algarve’s city of crafts Bursting with Portuguese charm, Loulé is 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported by Loulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations. Sue Unesco sites in northern France Arras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: the belfry of the Hotel de Ville and the Vauban Citadel. Exploring the Boves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods. Bryan Boese Artistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful south Malmö is easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. The Western Harbour contains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraper Turning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafe Hollandia offered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. The Disgusting Food Museum next door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)! Elisabeth Brilliant beach and seafood in Sardinia If you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love in Cagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark of Bastione St Remy delineating the ancient Castello district and serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, and Trattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back. Martha Stained glass wonder in north-west Spain In León, colours grab your attention and take away words. León cathedral completely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-century San Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast. Deborah Norway’s art nouveau gem Ålesund is one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramic Aksla mountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunning Geirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all! Teresa Stansby The French city with a bit of everything I spent five days in Saint-Malo this August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (on Instagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C. Sophie Amos Winning tip: a watery Dutch master of a city Leiden starts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls. item.title: TSA brings its new 'e-gates' to Newark. But are you eligible to use them?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 7.12
TSA brings its new 'e-gates' to Newark. But are you eligible to use them? As the Labor Day travel rush kicks off, airport security may look a little different for travelers at one of the biggest airports in the New York City area. This week, the Transportation Security Administration brought its new "e-gates" to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) for the first time. It's a new setup that allows passengers to pass through Transportation Security Administration without ever stopping to speak with an officer. The automated gates are live for certain United Airlines passengers passing through Newark's Terminal C. EWR is one of the nation's first airports to pilot this new high-tech security process. Earlier this summer, the TSA began trialing similar technology at Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT). I just tried the TSA's new e-gates: Here's what it was like Passengers using the e-gates no longer have to hand their IDs to a TSA staffer. Instead, they walk into a booth and have their photo taken, and then the translucent gates typically open in a matter of seconds. View this post on Instagram Who can use the TSA e-gates? In Charlotte, the e-gates are available to all passengers registered for TSA PreCheck. Access in Newark is limited to United flyers who have opted in to the faster TSA PreCheck Touchless ID program. That biometric program allows passengers to pass through security without showing an ID. Instead, the TSA snaps a photo and compares the image to passport information already on file. Travelers using the e-gates at Newark can essentially pass through the initial security line without pulling out an ID or boarding pass, or speaking to an officer. Then those passengers (and their bags) will be screened as usual. How to use the e-gates in Newark To use the TSA's e-gates at Newark, you'll need to be flying United. And, you'll have to opt in to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID with the airline. Here's how to do that. The TSA has now trialed e-gates at three major airports: EWR, CLT and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA). So far, the process has been slightly faster than a normal security line; the TSA has said the automatic gates save about 3 seconds per passenger on average. It may not sound like much, but as thousands of flyers go through security each day, those saved seconds add up. The e-gates also free up officers to assist travelers in other lanes. Travel lines go high-tech TSA isn't alone in turning to higher-tech processes to speed up airport lines. In recent months, the paid security service Clear has also rolled out its own version of e-gates at dozens of airports nationwide. It comes as airlines, government agencies and private security companies have increasingly been relying on biometric photos to cut wait times at major hubs. Earlier this summer, TPG reported that U.S. Customs and Border Protection was trialing camera capture technology for Global Entry. That new process verifies passengers' identity as they walk into the customs hall, eliminating the need for the fast-track program's blue kiosks. Meanwhile, some airlines have begun using facial recognition at certain airport gates, allowing flyers to board without scanning a boarding pass. At TSA checkpoints, passengers can always opt out of having their photo taken. Photography — and use of the new e-gates — is optional. The TSA hopes to eventually bring the e-gates technology to more cities. Related reading:

item.title: One of our favorite points brands just opened a hotel in Japan's premier ski destination
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.12
One of our favorite points brands just opened a hotel in Japan's premier ski destination Moxy is going to the mountains. Marriott today announced that its latest Moxy location is now open in Niseko, the heart of Japan's alpine ski region on the northern island of Hokkaido. The opening — one of the most anticipated points hotel debuts this year — is an interesting addition to Niseko's otherwise upscale hotel portfolio, which includes a Park Hyatt and a Ritz-Carlton Reserve. Moxy tends to be a more casual brand with a youthful vibe and a focus on lively shared public spaces (you often check in at the bar) and pared-down accommodations in creative configurations, some of which feature bunk beds for larger family or friend groups. The new hotel has 310 rooms, and from what we can tell so far, they only come in two categories: - Moxy Niseko Loft with one queen bed and two twin bunk beds - Moxy Niseko Twin with two twin beds The latter is a mere 194 square feet and, like you'll find in many other types of Moxy rooms, the sink is in the main room while the water closet with a toilet and walk-in shower is in a glassed-off space of its own. As for the Queen Loft room, it is also listed at 194 square feet and includes a queen bed by the window with a small sofa and a lofted twin-size bunk bed above it. There's no closet area to speak of in either room, but instead a wall with pegs, a folding table and a luggage rack, so it might be tough to find a place to stow your ski gear. As for the rest of the hotel, the interior design was inspired by Hokkaido's mountain landscapes with colorful touches of Kawaii, or "cute," pop culture references thrown in. The hotel has a grab and go counter for meals on the run, but its main restaurant is the Moxy Bar & Cafe, which is a laidback-looking space serving breakfast, lunch and dinner. The hotel also features a small 24-hour fitness center for folks who don't get their fill of exercise skiing in the winter or hiking in the summer. The new Moxy Niseko is located within the central Niseko Village ski resort with easy access to the Niseko Village gondola at the base of Mount Niseko Annupuri, putting the area's many ski trails in easy reach. Visitors will also find tons of nearby restaurants, shops and onsens to have a relaxing soak after a day out on the slopes. The hotel is also easy to reach from two different Japan Rail stations, which put it within a two-hour train ride from New Chitose International Airport (CTS), the region's main hub. So why bring Moxy to this particular part of Japan when many of the brand's outposts tend to be in major cities or near airports? (The four other Moxy locations in the country are in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka). The brand has recently expanded to some other nature-first destinations such as Banff in Canada and a planned opening in Vietnam's beachy Phu Quoc. "Niseko's year-round appeal, global reputation and adventurous spirit make it a natural fit for Moxy," said Cristiano Rinaldi, Marriott's chief lodging product and services officer in Asia Pacific excluding China, in a statement. "This opening brings the brand's playful social energy to one of Japan's most celebrated mountain retreats, creating a stay experience that is approachable, design-forward and deeply connected to the destination." Moxy's entry into this particular hotel market also means travelers have another reasonable budget option for their next Japan ski (or summer hiking) trip, which is a boon considering how expensive some of Niseko's other accommodations can be. Rates at the Moxy Niseko in the next few months start at a mere $88 per night. Rates in January through March, when the powder tends to be best, start at $192 per night (though most nights are priced at $400). Points rates have not yet been made available. Compare that to the Park Hyatt Niseko Hanazono, where rooms start at a whopping $1,550 per night this January, and you might be willing to sacrifice a few creature comforts (and cram into a smaller room with your ski gear) in order to experience Japan's winter wonderland. Hopefully points rates will be loaded into Marriott's system soon. And when they are, you can bet several members of the TPG team will be looking into winter trips to Japan and how a stay at the Moxy Niseko measures up. Related reading:

item.description:

Baby on board: Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards just made it much cheaper to fly with lap infants on award tickets If you're looking to redeem points and miles for airline travel and have a lap infant traveling with you, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program just made an incredibly generous policy update. For long-haul international Atmos Rewards redemptions, including those operated by partner airlines, lap infants will now only be charged government-mandated international taxes when the award ticket is issued on "027" stock, meaning issued by Alaska or Hawaiian. Lap infants are defined as passengers under the age of 2 on the date of travel of all flights of the trip who do not require their own seat. They will continue to fly free on Alaska-operated domestic award flights (including Hawaiian Airlines flights) when accompanied by an adult. For some other airlines, lap infants are charged 10% of the adult revenue fare, plus taxes and fees, whether an adult passenger redeems miles or pays cash for international flights. On short-haul international services, where cash rates are just a few hundred dollars, lap infant costs are affordable. However, it becomes more expensive to redeem for long-haul business-class flights. So even if you find a sweet spot international business-class redemption for 50,000 points, for example, you'd need to pay 10% of the cash fare to bring a lap infant along. That means on a $3,000 one-way business-class fare, you'd spend $300 for a lap infant who doesn't have their own seat and probably won't eat or drink anything offered on board. If you are traveling internationally with a lap infant on an award ticket, this 10% fee, which is common across the industry, can be a significant added expense to your points and miles redemption. That's why this surprise policy change from Atmos Rewards is so generous and so welcome. It not only covers international flights operated by Alaska (which is steadily adding pins to its route map) but also the impressive roster of Atmos Rewards partner airlines, including British Airways, Japan Airlines, American Airlines, Icelandair and Starlux, giving you more choice to save when you travel with your family. Bottom line Atmos Rewards now has the most generous lap infant award policy of any major loyalty program. On long-haul international redemptions, you pay only government-mandated taxes and fees for a child under 2 traveling on your lap, which are usually very low, with no percentage of the adult cash fare and no points payable. That applies to Alaska and Hawaiian metal and flights operated by partner airlines, and lap infants must be added by phoning Atmos Rewards. Lap infants on international revenue fares are still subject to the 10% charge, so consider redeeming Atmos Rewards points instead. Related reading:

Ending soon: Highest-ever bonuses on no-annual-fee Chase Ink business cards Editor's Note Both the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are strong small-business options, with flat-rate or bonus-category earning structures that can add up quickly. And new applicants of either card can currently earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. It's the highest welcome offer we've seen on either card, but the offers are ending soon. If you've been considering one of these cards and can comfortably meet the spending requirement, now may be a good time to apply. Keep in mind that these are business credit cards. You don't need a large company with employees to qualify — even freelancers, sole proprietors and those with side gigs may be eligible. However, you will need a legitimate business to apply. Turn cash back into Chase points While the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash technically earn cash back, you can convert that cash back into Chase Ultimate Rewards points if you also hold a premium card such as a Sapphire card or the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees). Doing so can dramatically boost value, since points can be redeemed for travel at elevated rates or transferred to airline and hotel partners. (Note that while the Chase Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (see rates and fees) is also a cash-back card, its cash back cannot be converted into transferable points.) Ink Business Unlimited Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the highest offer we've seen on this card, but it's ending soon, so don't wait to apply. Annual fee: $0 Earning rate: 1.5% cash back on all purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Unlimited is a great option for small businesses and sole proprietors who don't have spending concentrated in specific spending categories. Regardless of category, you'll get a flat 1.5% on purchases. While it's not the best flat-rate option for business owners, it does come in handy if you have Chase Ultimate Rewards points-earning credit cards to turn that 1.5% cash back into 1.5 points per dollar spent (a 3.1% return, based on TPG's September 2026 valuations). To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Unlimited. Apply here: Ink Business Unlimited Ink Business Cash Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the best offer we've seen on this card. Like the offer on the Ink Business Unlimited, this bonus won't be around for much longer. Annual fee: $0 Earning rates: - 5% cash back at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 2% cash back at gas stations and restaurants (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 1% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Cash is great for anyone who spends a lot at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services. These are common expenses for many small businesses, so most business owners should be able to maximize rewards with this card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Cash. Apply here: Ink Business Cash Ink Business Preferred Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome bonus is worth $2,050 when you take advantage of Chase's transfer partners. Other redemption options include redeeming your points through Chase Travel℠ and for cash back, but these options offer less value: up to $1,750 (depending on your booking) and $1,000, respectively. This bonus is one of the better offers we've seen for the card, so any time it's offering at least 100,000 points (as is currently the case) is considered a good time to apply. Annual fee: $95 Earning rates: - 3 points per dollar spent on shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, travel, and advertising purchases with social media and search engines (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases across these categories each year, then 1 point per dollar spent) - 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases Who should apply: Small-business owners with significant spending in the above bonus categories will be happy to earn up to 450,000 points per year on those purchases. This card also provides access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners, so it can provide value even without pairing it with another Chase card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred. Apply here: Ink Business Preferred Ink Business Premier Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This has been the standard bonus on this card since it launched in late 2021; we have not seen any elevated offers, so now is a good time to apply. Annual fee: $195 Earning rates: - 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more - 2% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: This card is ideal for small-business owners looking for a card with a flexible spending limit. That means you must pay the bill in full each month and cannot carry a balance. If you can pay your balance in full each month, you'll enjoy the unlimited earning potential on this card. It's worth noting, however, that the rewards from this card cannot be combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Premier. Apply here: Ink Business Premier Are these bonuses worth it? One of these cards could be worth considering if you have a major purchase coming up that you want to use to earn one of these welcome bonuses, or if you want to take advantage of their earning rates sooner rather than later. While these cards won't add to your Chase 5/24 total, you need to be under that number to apply for any cards with Chase. If you've opened five or more personal credit cards (from any bank) in the past 24 months, you will likely be declined when applying. Business credit cards — or cards with significant welcome bonuses — tend to have higher spending requirements to achieve the bonus. If you can meet that requirement, the welcome bonus is almost always worth the effort. Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions Are you eligible for a Chase Ink welcome bonus? Chase has different welcome-bonus eligibility rules across the Ink Business card family. For the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited: If you've previously had either no-annual-fee card, you won't be eligible for the welcome bonus on the other. In other words, having the Ink Business Cash can make you ineligible for the Ink Business Unlimited bonus, and vice versa. This restriction doesn't affect your eligibility for an Ink Business Preferred or Ink Business Premier welcome bonus, provided you're otherwise eligible. For the Ink Business Preferred and Ink Business Premier: The restriction applies only to the specific card. If you've previously had the Ink Business Preferred, you may not be eligible for another Preferred bonus, but you can still be eligible for the Premier bonus, and vice versa. You can also still be eligible for a Cash or Unlimited bonus if you've never had either no-annual-fee Ink card. You'll also need to be under 5/24, meaning you've opened fewer than five new personal credit cards across issuers in the past 24 months. While Chase has never publicly acknowledged this rule, they do enforce it. Finally, you must have some type of business to qualify for an Ink card, since they are business credit cards. You don't need to own a fully-fledged corporation; freelancing, gig work and sole proprietorships may qualify. Bottom line If you can combine your Ink rewards with an existing Ultimate Rewards account, these welcome offers can become even more valuable since you'll have access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners. Just make sure you're eligible under Chase's welcome-bonus and 5/24 rules and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making purchases your business wouldn't otherwise need. The welcome offers on the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash are ending soon, so if you've been considering either card, now may be a good time to apply. Otherwise, the right Ink card for you will depend on your business's spending patterns and which earning structure best fits your needs. He'll use it on upcoming American trips with his wife and daughter, and appreciates being able to add authorized users with their own Admirals Club access. You can add up to three authorized users for $175 each. They receive Admirals Club access when flying American or an eligible partner and can bring up to two guests, though they don't access partner lounges. Since Admirals Club day passes cost $79, this can be a valuable perk for frequent American flyers. The Citi / AA Executive offers valuable airport and inflight benefits: Enhanced airport experience: You and up to eight travelers on the same reservation get priority check-in, airport screening (where available) and priority boarding. First checked bag free: On eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries, the first checked bag for you and up to eight companions is free when traveling on the same reservation. Since American typically charges at least $45 per bag each way, this provides meaningful savings even for occasional check-bag users. Inflight and Admirals Club credit: Receive up to $100 back annually on eligible purchases. Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit: Up to $120 statement credit when you pay an eligible fee with the card (once every four years). I recommend Global Entry, which includes TSA PreCheck. To receive the credit, book an eligible American Airlines Vacations travel package or experience through AAVacations.com using your card. Eligible packages must include at least two components — a flight and hotel, a flight and a rental car, or a hotel and a rental car. This isn't as flexible as a general travel credit, so don't book a package solely for the benefit. But if you already book vacation packages or bundle flights with hotels or rental cars, the credit provides significant value. TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson is particularly interested in this benefit because he already uses American Airlines Vacations: "I've been a huge advocate for AAVacations over the years and I will definitely take advantage of this new perk." Automatic hotel and rental car elite status The Citi / AA Executive also offers complimentary Omni Hotels & Resorts Champion Status (enrollment required), which includes an annual free night reward after a qualifying stay,* and Avis President's Club status (enrollment available through Aug. 31, 2028). *A qualifying stay consists of two or more consecutive nights booked directly through Omni Hotels & Resorts at omnihotels.com. Benefits of Omni Champion Status can include complimentary one-level room upgrades and early check-in and late checkout (when available), while benefits of Avis President's Club include car upgrades, expedited service and complimentary additional drivers. I wouldn't recommend adding the card to your wallet just for these perks, but they're valuable additions if you already stay at Omni or rent with Avis. You'll earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each milestone: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points (up to 40,000 bonus points per qualification year). This benefit is most valuable for frequent American Airlines flyers who already earn enough Loyalty Points to reach these thresholds. Cardholders can receive up to $15 in Lyft credits per month, or $180 annually, after taking three eligible rides that month. I consider this one of the weaker benefits of the card because the three-ride requirement means you can't simply take one Lyft trip and receive the monthly credit. How to earn and use your rewards The is most rewarding when you use it strategically rather than putting all your everyday spending on it. Earning miles on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive With the Citi / AA Executive, you'll earn: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases 1 mile per dollar on all other eligible purchases Spend $150,000 in a calendar year and you'll earn 5 miles per dollar on American Airlines purchases for the remainder of that year. You'll also earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. The boosted earning rate on American's hotel and car rental portals is attractive if you regularly use those services, particularly since these purchases also earn Loyalty Points. Clint uses AAdvantage Hotels and likes the elevated earning rate: "I end up booking a lot of AAdvantage Hotels because of the generous Loyalty Point earning rates, so this is an added benefit, too." However, don't use the Citi / AAdvantage Executive for most everyday purchases — the base earning rate is weak compared with many other cards. If you're trying to maximize flexible rewards, you're generally better off using a card that earns transferable points on everyday spending and reserving the Executive for purchases where it offers a meaningful bonus or benefit. Redeeming AAdvantage miles AAdvantage miles can be redeemed for flights on American Airlines and its Oneworld and other airline partners. Award flights operated by American and Fiji Airways are dynamically priced, so the miles required vary by flight and date. All other partner awards follow AAdvantage's fixed, region-based award charts. For example, you can book a one-way business-class award on Qatar Airways from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to Hamad International Airport (DOH) in Doha for 70,000 AAdvantage miles (and just $35 in taxes and fees). Where the Citi / AAdvantage Executive falls short The 's biggest drawback is its $695 annual fee. It's easiest to justify if you regularly use Admirals Clubs; otherwise, you may struggle to offset the cost. The card also isn't ideal for everyday spending. Most purchases earn just 1 AAdvantage mile per dollar, and AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as Amex or Chase points, which transfer to multiple airline and hotel programs. Skip this card if lounge access isn't a priority, or if you want flexible rewards across broader categories. Citi / AA Executive vs. Citi / AA Globe If you want American Airlines benefits without unlimited Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is the clear alternative. For a lower $350 annual fee, the Globe includes four Admirals Club passes yearly. One pass covers one adult and up to three children under 18; passes work at multiple lounges within 24 hours on American or Oneworld flights. The Globe also offers preferred boarding, a free first checked bag on eligible domestic American itineraries, and an annual companion certificate (starting year two) with substantial strategic value. Choose the Globe if you're an occasional American traveler who wants lounge access a few times a year. Choose the Executive if you regularly visit Admirals Clubs — unlimited access easily justifies the higher fee. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, that welcome offer is worth roughly $1,813. This is the highest offer we have seen in the card’s history, making now a great time to apply if you can comfortably meet the spending required to earn the welcome offer. Citi's 48-month rule prevents you from earning a welcome bonus if you've received one on this card within the past four years. The clock starts from when you receive the bonus, not when approved or activated. Citi also applies this 48-month restriction to certain conversions from other Citi accounts. Other cards to consider if you don't want the Citi / AAdvantage Executive The is a strong choice for frequent American Airlines travelers, but it isn't the right fit for everyone. Here are a few alternatives: If you want a lower annual fee: The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® offers a straightforward way to earn AAdvantage miles while receiving core American Airlines benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select. If you want Oneworld perks without being tied to American: The is a strong option for travelers who want to earn Oneworld elite status while taking advantage of benefits with Alaska Airlines and its partners. To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit. If you want transferable points and lounge access: The (see rates and fees) earns transferable Citi ThankYou points and offers premium travel perks, including lounge access. It can be a better fit for American loyalists who want more flexibility from their rewards. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Elite. The information for the Citi Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Bottom line The is fundamentally an Admirals Club card, with additional perks that can help frequent American Airlines travelers offset its $695 annual fee. The card makes the most sense if you'll regularly use Admirals Club access and can take advantage of benefits like Loyalty Point bonuses and authorized user lounge access. But for travelers who rarely fly American, don't use airport lounges or prefer the flexibility of transferable points, there are better premium travel cards for your wallet.

item.title: Flighty app gets some upgrades: Why this flight-tracking app is a go-to travel companion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.22
Flighty app gets some upgrades: Why this flight-tracking app is a go-to travel companion Editor's Note I know it's superstitious, but I always text myself my flight information ahead of a trip so I can track my route on JetLovers.com. Somehow, I'm convinced it wards off a canceled flight. I've also previously used Google Flights or another of my favorite apps, Flightradar24. But a new player in the flight-tracking space has made me a convert. Flighty is an app that helps me track my flights day-to-day and keeps an ongoing record of my travels worldwide. The paid version even provides a year-end summary that's fun to look back on. And Flighty just got some other new upgrades: In July, it unveiled a new gate prediction service. Often, Flighty will know your gate before you do. It has also launched Connection Assistant, which provides step-by-step guidance to help you manage your airport transfers. And last year, the app introduced a feature that, in many cases, lets users see why their flights are delayed. Flighty tracks late aircraft issues and airspace congestion to help predict delays hours in advance — helping you get a jump on potentially switching flights or even skipping the trip altogether. Here's everything you need to know about the Flighty app and its latest updates. What is Flighty? Flighty is an Apple iOS app that launched in 2019. It shares real-time updates on your flights, including delays and cancellations. Oftentimes, it knows when a flight is having issues before your airline app does. "I love Flighty because it organizes all my flights and lets me know about changes many times before the updates show on the board at the airport or at the gate," said Mike Panzarella, formerly the chief operating officer at Rocket Dollar. He said he started using Flighty in January 2023 and swears by it. "It helps you feel calm and helps you understand issues before the throngs of others do ahead of you, which is fantastic," he said. "It simplifies travel. It's almost like having an assistant or travel agent for $49 a year." There are paid and free versions of Flighty. The free version gives you real-time updates on delays or cancellations and will alert you to gate changes, departure and arrival times, and when to check in. You'll also be able to track your flight, but you won't get push notifications or many of the other advanced functionalities. The paid version has many more bells and whistles. Here are just a few of Flighty's features: - It automatically pulls in future and past flights from your calendar. - Passenger flights are displayed on the screen when you open the app. - You can import flights via email or sync with TripIt. - It gives you a countdown to your trip. - It supports all airlines worldwide, up to 365 days in advance. - It displays your booking code and check-in information. - Cancellation and schedule change monitoring starts 365 days in advance, and live tracking starts 48 hours in advance. - It will alert you to airport delays, late plane arrivals and other issues. - It shows you taxi, takeoff and landing times. - A progress bar displays while you are in flight. - It predicts your gate, often before the airline posts the information. - The app gives you step-by-step directions for connections. - Upon landing, you'll be made aware of your arrival gate and baggage claim carousel. "Flighty was named an Editor's Choice app by Apple within days of launch, won an Apple Design Award in 2023, and was a runner-up for iPhone App of the Year," according to the company. Indeed, I've found it a useful tool and especially fun because it appeals to my AvGeek interests. Flighty 4.1 This summer, Flighty unveiled several cool new features. Among them is a new step-by-step process for your connections. Flighty has inside information on almost every airport on the planet and can tell you if you need to clear passport control, recheck bags, change terminals and even if you'll need to go through security a second time. It also gives you clear time requirements. No more asking agents or fellow passengers where to go next. It could also help you get through transfers more quickly. "Making a connection is easily one of the most stressful moments of flying," Flighty CEO Ryan Jones said. "Knowing a connection is theoretically possible doesn't help anyone. What helps is knowing what it actually takes to reach your next gate. The new Connection Assistant shows you exactly that, so you can move through any airport like you've done it 100 times, even if it's your first." The company says the Connection Assistant feature, "combines Flighty's best-in-class flight tracking data with airport-specific procedures and statistical modeling of millions of prior flights, and then turns it all into guidance for your exact trip." Connection Assistant shows the typical connecting time and instructions based on your passport information. Flighty 4.0 In an August 2025 app update, Flighty added the ability to better predict delays and let you know why your plane is delayed. The app uses aviation authority data and machine learning to provide early warnings of delays and, in many cases, tell users the exact cause of the delay. Flighty analyzes late-arriving aircraft data and monitors airport airspace to predict delays or cancellations. The team says the new data collection means subscribers can learn how long a delay will actually be, rather than relying on airlines, which do not always provide the most accurate information about when a flight will actually take off. According to Flighty, late aircraft, air traffic control congestion and ground stops account for the majority of delays. "Flighty 4's monitoring predicts and deciphers those delays to give travelers what they've always wanted — a clear reason why their flight is delayed," Jones said. How much is Flighty? The upgraded version of Flighty is called Fighty Pro, and it costs $4.99 a week if you pay as you go. Jones says this option is perfect for less frequent flyers or those looking for information about individual trips. However, most users opt for the annual plan, which offers a hefty discount, bringing the annual total to $59.99. You can also buy a lifetime membership for $299. (I ended up buying a one-year membership because I wanted to give it a good test run, but wasn't ready to commit to a lifetime. Now I wish I had.) If you want a family plan, you can choose one for $15.99 per month, $119 per year, or $449 for lifetime access. Flighty lets you know when your flight is delayed Flighty will let you know if your flight is delayed in many cases. This can keep you from getting to the airport earlier than you need, thus saving you valuable time. According to the company, the No. 1 cause of delays is a late plane. The app automatically monitors flights for 25 hours prior to departure. Flighty will also alert you to airport delays and other issues with your flight. A good example of this is shown in the screenshots below. Flighty alerted me to a delay several hours before my flight to Cancun from San Francisco, and I was able to take my time getting to the airport. However, I have found that Flighty isn't perfect at tracking all delays. A long-haul flight between New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Honolulu's Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) was held up for nearly three hours, with nary a notification from Flighty. Flighty did let me know when we pushed back from the gate, but failed to follow the flight after it was further delayed due to a mechanical issue, and returned to the gate. In fact, to this day, Flighty still shows the flight departed on time, even though we ended up leaving more than three hours late. The company said this can happen if a flight returns to the gate and the airline marks the following departure as a separate flight. Flighty is working to address this in a future update. Still, despite the imperfections, the app provides valuable information that most third-party tracking companies don't offer. For example, its "Where's My Plane?" feature tracks your plane starting 25 hours before your flight and is consistently reliable. With this feature, you can better anticipate a delay, giving you time to make other arrangements (if needed) before a formal announcement. Flighty notifies you while in the air Flighty lets you know which gate you are leaving from or arriving at, as well as any gate changes that occur on the day of travel. The app can also be used while you are on a flight. It will let you know if your flight is on time and how much time you have left. On a recent Atlanta flight, Flighty told me that my plane would arrive a bit early. The app can track delays while you're in the air, as shown by this notification for a flight from New Orleans to New York City. Flighty not only let me know that my flight was delayed but also how late the plane would arrive. Another example of an inflight delay notification came when I flew Hawaiian Airlines' brand-new Dreamliner from Honolulu to San Francisco. As you can see, the flight was slightly late. In addition to showing the new arrival time, Flighty displayed a nifty map of the San Francisco Bay Area and a view of San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that day. These features can be helpful or at least interesting when you are flying and may save you from opening another app. They can even update you when you aren't connected to the internet since the clock remains active in the app. For a traveler like me who gets anxious during travel, Flighty is super helpful. I feel like I'm always well-informed during my trips and a little ahead of the game compared to other passengers. Flighty can keep your friends and family in the loop You can also invite friends and family to share information with you on Flighty. Simply invite friends via a text message. Once they accept, you can set custom alerts and keep track of their flights, and vice versa. Flighty will update you if your friends and family have a flight change, cancellation or delay, or if any other issues arise, depending on how you've customized the settings. "No other service has ever successfully built 'friends for flying,'" Jones said in a press release. "They all try to make it social and public. But that's not what users want. They want to share with just a few friends and family, all privately, without signing up for a new service." Flighty will also give you data on your upcoming flights Flighty also provides useful data on your upcoming flights. You can see whether your flight is on time and the flight plan, among other options. Flighty can provide data on your past year of travel One of the app's best features is "Flighty Passport." This option lets users view and share their personal travel map, mileage and other fun stats from their past year of flights. It will even pull data for your lifetime of flying. As you can see, it shows flights from both my current travel year and prior years. According to Flighty, I've flown more than 870,000 miles on 33 different airlines. That's a pretty big undercount, but more on that below. The app also tells you how many hours you've lost to delays, both by the year and over your lifetime. In total, I've lost a whopping 87 hours to delays, according to Flighty. Flighty is an AvGeek's dream One of the best things about Flighty is all the information the app has about your flights. It's wildly appealing if you are any kind of AvGeek. The app tells you your most common aircraft type, the number of different jets you've flown, detailed information on each of your flights and lots of other interesting aircraft stats. These are only a few examples of what you'll find in the app. Flighty isn't perfect As I mentioned above, Flighty doesn't pick up all delayed flights, but there are a few other quirks that have frustrated me and some other users. Panzarella told me that Flighty lost a record of one of his travel segments after an Aeromexico flight he was on was diverted. "The final and original destination was never picked up from the diversion airport," he said. "It doesn't accurately reflect my flight totals for the year." He told me he even flagged it to Flighty, but it was never adjusted. "The recovery flight from a diversion is a separate flight," Jones said in an interview with TPG. "The app tells you this and presents a button to search for the recovery flight." Panzarella told me he'd had better luck by using a simple trick. "I integrated it with Tripit, and it's seamless," he said. "Tripit ingests my emails and then publishes them to Flighty automatically." I've found that the app hasn't found all of my historic flights either. Some of my flights aren't integrated with my work and personal calendars, and Flighty has had a hard time finding many of my flights, especially from years past. My lifetime totals are wildly inaccurate, and even last year's stats are missing a few flights. There is good news on that front: It looks like you can now add flight records manually. That's a welcome addition to the app. TPG reader Alex Setzler told me you can also email your itinerary to track@myflightyapp.com.
